News.title: North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un is ‘extremely obese’ after gorging on steak and lobster diet, South Korean spies say
News.content:
Next

KIM Jong-un is “extremely obese” according to spy agencies, who say his lavish diet of steak and lobster could lead to an early downfall.

Already facing international sanctions and regime instability, the North Korean dictator now faces a new threat – chronic obesity.



The supreme eater weighs more than 310lb (140kg) at just 5-foot-7-inches, putting him at serious risk of cardiovascular disease, according to South Korea‘s National Intelligence Service (NIS).

Kim’s heavy smoking and body mass raise serious international questions about who would succeed him as leader of the volatile nuclear-armed state if he were to suddenly die.



His health follows a hereditary pattern as both his father, Kim Jong-il, and grandfather, Kim Il-sung, were obese and heavy smokers.

They both died of heart attacks.

Speculation over Kim’s health first reared in 2020 when he missed a commemoration of his late grandfather’s birthday.

He was away from the public eye for about 20 days, fuelling rumours that he was seriously ill after surgery.



But while he may be at risk, Seoul politician Youn Kun-young said Kim has shown no obvious difficulty with physical activity.

Kun-young said: “It is assessed that there are no signs of health issues, given the close monitoring by (his) dedicated medical team.”

A chef who worked with Kim’s personal chefs during a North Korea-US summit revealed the leader has the taste for the most luxurious of foods.

Paul Smart, a former executive chef at Hanoi’s Metropole hotel, said in 2019: “He likes caviar, lobster, really luxurious product.

“Foie gras, he really likes to indulge in cuisine.”



But as Kim feasts on crustaceans and tender cuts of meat, North Koreans have battled repeated food shortages in recent years.

The UN said food insecurity in the DPRK is a key humanitarian concern.

The questions surrounding Kim’s health come months after the NIS said it believed his daughter is poised to be named North Korea’s future leader.

Kim’s daughter, believed to be named Kim Ju-ae and roughly 13 years old, has been accompanying her father to an increasing number of events, including weapons tests, military parades and factory openings.

State media said she is her father’s favourite child but until she is old enough, experts say Kim’s merciless younger sister is more likely to be installed as leader.



Michael Madden, director and founder of NK Leadership Watch, said Yo-jong has been groomed to be Kim’s immediate successor – and would eventually hand over power to his daughter, Kim Ju-ae.

Powerful Kim Yo-jong, 38, could rule the hermit kingdom with an iron fist with insiders revealing she has been influenced by their father most hardcore aides and advisors.

Experts say her rule could be even more ruthless than her brother’s.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Should Ju-ae one day take control of North Korea, she would become the first female leader in its dynastic history.

Madden said: “The most important detail is that Yo-jong would be a transitional leader and regent until Ju-ae was prepared to assume power.”

News.title: Christa Pike execution allowed after Supreme Court overturns last-minute halt to lethal injection for ‘Satanic’ killer
News.content:
Next

CHRISTA Pike’s execution has been allowed to proceed after the Supreme Court overturned a last-minute stay to put the “Satanic” killer to death.

The state of Tennessee’s order is set to expire at midnight local time and if time runs out, a new execution date would need to be set.



Pike’s execution was dramatically halted just one hour before she was due to be put to death by lethal injection on Wednesday morning.

The now 50-year-old had been scheduled to die after she was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.



Witnesses had already gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when a federal appeals court stepped in and stopped it.

But the Supreme Court has now allowed the execution to move forward in Tennessee, overturning the last-minute stay.



The 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals had initially voted 2-1 to issue a stay.

That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.



But Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh granted the application to vacate the stay of execution.

The Supreme Court’s three liberal justices, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the ruling.

Sotomayor called the court’s decision stunning, as it clears the way for the execution to happen before her still-pending legal challenges to her conviction can be properly considered.

The state’s execution order expires at midnight, according to Kelley Henry, a Nashville-based attorney experienced with Tennessee death penalty law.

If time runs out, the state Supreme Court would need to set a new date.



Pike, who was 18 at the time, and her boyfriend were convicted of the 1995 stabbing and beating of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.

The case garnered widespread attention back then in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body.

That stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.



But, if the execution goes ahead, it will make her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in at least 200 years.

The US Supreme Court had rejected a bid to halt her death on Tuesday, while Tennessee Governor Bill Lee had already denied her request for clemency.

Before the execution was halted, Pike had declined to choose a special last meal.

She had also written that she was “at peace” as the execution approached, saying, “I am not afraid to die. I am only nervous about the process.”

Her victim’s mom May Martinez says she has waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.



“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” she added.

She and her husband are understood to have traveled from Florida to witness the execution.

Pike was just 18 when she killed Slemmer, a fellow student at a job-training program in Knoxville, on January 12, 1995.

She is said to have lured Slemmer to a wooded area where she used a box cutter and large chunk of asphalt to attack her.

Prosecutors said she feared Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend.



Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.

Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole.

Pike was the only one sentenced to death – she was convicted of murder and conspiracy and sentenced to death in 1996.

She has not denied the killing but said she was “a mentally ill 18-year-old kid”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her supporters say her age and mental illness at the time should be mitigating factors.



She also had a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler.

News.title: Three rushed to hospital after mystery package sent to Polish army HQ near Ukrainian training base – as site evacuated
News.content:
Next

THREE people have been hospitalised and 130 evacuated after a mystery package – containing nothing but a postcard – was sent to an army HQ in Poland.

An envelope sent from Germany was delivered to the Military Police base in the town of Nowa Dęba, about 70 miles from the southeastern border with Ukraine.



No substance spilled out when staff opened it this morning, according to local media.

Despite this, two officers and a civilian working at the army base suffered irritation on their hands and faces, and were hospitalised.



Another four people who did not have any symptoms were isolated as a precaution.

Polish Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) teams were deployed to the scene to investigate the unknown contents.



There were concerns that the base may have been targeted because of its proximity to Camp Jomsborg, a training facility for Ukrainian and NATO personnel.

But a statement from the military published this afternoon confirmed that the envelope was not dangerous.

It said: “We inform you that the examination of the package ruled out the presence of chemical, biological, and radiological agents.

“Two soldiers and a military employee, after examination, were discharged from the hospital; the tests showed no signs of poisoning.”



This comes days after the government began distributing instructions on how to respond to air attacks amid fears that Russia will open a second war front in Poland.

Magdalena Roguska, deputy head of the Ministry of Interior, said that the manual aims to prepare civilians on what to do after receiving emergency situation alerts.

The Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski also revealed he had an evacuation backpack ready.

“I have stocks of rice, I have a hand pump at home, and I have also made preserves from fruit from my own garden,” he told Fakt newspaper.

“I have the safety instructions, and I have also thought through where the nearest place of shelter is.



“Everyone should also know how to apply a dressing. That is useful even in peacetime.”

Asked whether people should prepare a bag with emergency provisions, Sikorski said: “We have all received the safety instructions.

“If the state tells a citizen, ‘Listen, these are unsettled times, it is better to be prepared’, it does no harm to listen to that. That is my appeal – to listen to it.”

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has repeatedly warned of potential hybrid attacks from Russia on European countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland.

Other European leaders have shared his warnings.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Poland, Romania, Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania have seen an increase in air raids and the use by Russia of long-range Shahed drones and low-tech, primarily decoy, Gerbera drones.

Intelligence chiefs also say they could soon be incorporated into hybrid attacks on vital infrastructure, such as undersea pipelines, power grids and communication cables.

News.title: Why Burnham’s support for rejoining EU is huge political gamble – & issue voters actually care about he should focus on
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Why Burnham’s support for rejoining EU is huge political gamble – & issue voters actually care about he should focus on







Next

COULD Britain really be about to rejoin the European Union?

Ten years since the referendum, Andy Burnham has attacked Brexit as “harmful” and says he will consider “options” for a closer relationship with Brussels.



Significantly, this includes the “possibility” of promising a second referendum in Labour’s next election manifesto.

This from a Prime Minister who only a few months ago said reopening old wounds over Brexit would only sow further division.



So what has changed his mind?

Burnham insists that the decision to leave the EU has damaged the UK economy and hampered growth by making it harder to trade with the continent.

But this fails to mention how other major EU countries have also experienced sluggish growth in the decade since the referendum – it is a stagnant bloc.

More likely, the PM probably sees electoral mileage in showing support for rejoining the EU as it could peel left-wingers in the Lib Dems and Greens back to Labour.

But it is a huge political gamble given the party has also been bleeding support to Reform since the election, especially in those Red Wall seats in the north that voted to Leave.

We can reveal that some Cabinet Ministers are already getting nervous about fighting a new Brexit battle and appearing to be trampling on the previous democratic vote.



And does the public really want to be getting bogged down in Brexit arguments once again?

One area Labour should really focus on is immigration, which IS a top priority for voters.

Yesterday saw France pull the plug on the “one in, one out” scheme cooked up by Sir Keir Starmer to send back small boat migrants in exchange for some of Europe’s asylum seekers.

But after just a year, the Home Office announced yesterday the deal is dead after only a handful of people were ever returned.

And so the challenge of stopping Channel crossings goes on…

News.title: Andy Burnham admits double-whammy of rising petrol and energy prices will hit Brits hard
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has admitted a double-whammy winter of pain is on the way as average energy bills hit £2,000 a year — and diesel now selling at £2 a litre.

When asked if the UK was in an energy crisis that could go on for months, the PM said: “I don’t think that is an overstatement, to be honest.”



Mr Burnham is weighing up options to ease families’ financial burden but has previously said that Chancellor John Healey has little room for manoeuvre in his Budget next month.

The PM also appeared to open the door to stopping a fuel duty hike set to kick in this January, saying: “I’m considering anything that might help people.”



It comes as analysts warn that average energy bills could hit £1,999 from January 1 amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

And the RAC says the average pump price of diesel yesterday stood at a record 199.72p per litre.

This passed the previous all-time high of 199.09p that was set in June 2022.

A litre of diesel now costs on average 57.3p more than it did at the start of the US-Iran war on February 28.

Industry chiefs have repeated calls on Labour to approve two new North Sea oil and gas fields, Jackdaw and Rosebank.

EDF boss Simone Rossi said: “We should use resources to create jobs and tax receipts.”

News.title: More than 150 homes evacuated & bomb disposal unit deployed after ‘suspicious items’ discovered at home in fraud arrest
News.content:
'BOMB' SCARE More than 150 homes evacuated & bomb disposal unit deployed after ‘suspicious items’ discovered at home in fraud arrest







Next

MORE than 150 homes have been evacuated and a bomb disposal unit deployed after “suspicious items” were found at a property.

Cops said the discovery was made as they arrested a 70-year-old man in Worle, near Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, on Wednesday afternoon.

The man was arrested on suspicion of fraud by false representation and remains in custody.

Officers had located “suspicious substances and items” after conducting searches of the property and quickly called the bomb disposal unit to the scene.





Around 153 properties were evacuated by 9pm as dozens of families were displaced in and around Becket Road.

A 100m cordon was also put in place as a precautionary measure.

Avon and Somerset Police said later the items had been “tested and destroyed” by the Explosive Ordinance Disposal Unit (EOD).

They added that it was thought to be an “isolated incident”.

However, families were unable to return to their homes as the cordon remained in place overnight and the EOD carried out an “in-depth search” of the property.

North Somerset Council posted a statement to social media directing those evacuated to a refuge centre.

The local authority said: “Police have confirmed that the cordon will remain in place overnight while investigations continue at the property.

“Anyone who can’t return to their home within the cordoned area, and doesn’t have other accommodation available tonight, should go to The Campus, Highlands Lane, BS24 7DX, where an overnight rest centre has been set up.”



A spokesperson for Avon and Somerset Police said earlier on Wednesday evening: “As part of an ongoing investigation into fraud offences, officers have arrested a man, aged 70, on suspicion of fraud by false representation in Becket Road, in Worle near Weston-super-Mare, this afternoon.

“During searches of the property, some suspicious substances and items were located.

“As a precautionary safety measure, a 100m cordon has been put in place and the Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit is enroute to the scene.

“A number of properties within the cordon have been evacuated and we are working with colleagues at the local authority to find a suitable location for those who have been displaced.”

News.title: Kids set to be told from primary school age how to get into work to avoid a life on benefits
News.content:
Next

KIDS are set to be told from primary school age how to get into work to avoid a life on benefits.

Jobs tsar Alan Milburn will call on Ministers to give kids early exposure to different careers to broaden their horizons and help end the youth inactivity crisis.



The recommendation to introduce mandatory work experience with dedicated curriculum time will be in his landmark review to help fix the NEETs travesty.

Mr Milburn fears that teaching youngsters about the workplace and providing hands-on experience has been an “afterthought” and the changes will help make them “work ready”.



The former Health Secretary spoke to The Sun as he visited Thornhill Community Academy in Dewsbury, west Yorkshire, where Channel 4’s Educating Yorkshire was based.

He said: “Just familiarising kids in primary school, maybe not from as young as four, but just familiarising them with what work means, what the possibilities are.



“Because all too often, children are growing up with a very narrow view about what the possibilities are for them.”

He added: “Particularly if they come from a poorer background.

“And partially, this is about getting employers in to primary schools and just beginning to lay the trail of breadcrumbs.

“So that youngsters are getting a sense about, ‘I could be doing this rather than that, I could be being a nurse, but I could be being a doctor.



Yeah, I could be thinking about going into veterinary medicine’.

He added: “I don’t think you want to be heavy-handed about it, but you do just want to begin to give youngsters a real sense of what they might be.”

Mr Milburn insisted he had “buy-in” from both Andy Burnham and John Healey in solving the Neets issue which sees one million 16-24 year olds not in education, employment or training.

He added that parents fearful of their children missing lessons should see it as an “investment” in their futures.

His proposals in his report that could be out within weeks include experience of work starting at the beginning of primary school.



Then in the first three years of secondary school pupils should have meaningful experience with employers.

When pupils are 14-16 years-old they should have a traditional work placement and be given employer feedback.

Mr Milburn added that the work experience can be part of the solution to get them away from benefits and the first step into work.

He said: “But for most youngsters, surely we can’t be ruining their life chances and saying, “Oh, it’s ok to be on benefits.

“We want youngsters to be in work, and by the way, they want to be in work.



“We know that eight and 10 young people who are NEET, they want to be working or they want to be training.

“And we’ve just got to make that possible. And this is part of the way that we do that by making sure that work experience is embedded in the curriculum. It’s not like an afterthought.”

Children’s Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza who was also on the visit said: “I’ve heard from children all over the county – they are ambitious, they want to do well and they want good jobs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The buzzy students at Thornhill Community Academy are no different.

“If we are serious about helping more young people into work, we must give them the advice, guidance and, vitally, the work experience to help them achieve their ambitions.”

News.title: Hero Israeli plumber who controlled plane after ‘co-pilot stabbed captain during hijack’ learned to fly from TV show
News.content:
Next

THE hero Israeli plumber who took control of the plunging Flydubai plane has revealed he learned to fly from a TV show.

Yaniv Hayoun was among the passengers who helped thwart “Israel’s 9/11” after they overpowered the knifeman who allegedly stabbed the pilot and planned to crash the flight.



Incredibly, Yaniv has revealed he knew what to do with the controls after watching Air Crash Investigation – a TV show on major aviation disasters.

He revealed what went on inside the plane to Israel’s PM after safely landing in the country on Wednesday.



Yaniv told Benjamin Netanyahu: “We pinned him down to keep him secure and then I jumped into it (the cockpit) and pulled the controls.”

Incredulously, Netanyahu asked how he knew to pull in a backwards motion, to which he stated: “I watch Air Crash Investigations Mr Prime Minister.”



Prior to their sit-down conversation, Yaniv received a hero’s greeting at Tel Aviv airport from the Israeli president who hugged him tightly as blood remained splattered on his clothing.

Yaniv told how he helped subdue the alleged knife-wielding co-pilot, after barging into the flight deck.



He said: “I pushed the door; the pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door so it was hard for us to open.

“We pulled him out – it was a matter of seconds.”

He then called his friends for help, putting the assailant in a chokehold before dragging him out from the cockpit and grabbing the controls in an incredible show of bravery.



When the plane began to level as he gripped the controls, an off-duty pilot told Yaniv that he would take it from there.

Prime Minister Netanyahu praised the hero for his “tremendous resourcefulness”.

Speaking from the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump praised Yaniv’s “amazing” actions, revealing him to be a plumber.



The incident caused the aircraft to plummet 17,400 feet in less than two minutes, flight tracking data shows, with passengers believing they were going to die.

Graphic video taken onboard the plane showed a gruesome scene as passengers and crew aided the wounded pilot.

The captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, suffered serious injuries in the incident which has now been dubbed by officials as “Israel’s 9/11”.

Machchhar has about 15 years of experience flying for commercial airlines and had logged almost 10,000 hours on Boeing 737s, according to his social media.

He bravely fought to defend the plane – and the 174 passengers on board – while being attacked with a blade.



Despite his wounds, the veteran pilot managed to unlock the door of the cockpit and alert the crew of the ruthless attack.

This bought just enough time for Yaniv and other passengers to burst through and subdue his co-pilot.

The two off-duty pilots were onboard the aircraft as a potential regional rerouting meant the flight may have required a longer path, The Jerusalem Post reports.

This would push the original crew past their legal duty hours, making extra staff necessary.

There is no indication that their presence was due to an advanced security warning.



Authorities suspect the incident may have been an attempted terrorist attack, Israeli officials and an Israeli source familiar with the situation told CNN.

Israel’s defence minister Israel Katz said early intelligence suggests the co-pilot wanted to carry out a “jihadist terror attack”.

The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar is in stable condition and is being treated in a hospital in Tabuk.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has praised the captain for his “extraordinary bravery.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said on X: “My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery.



“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back… preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster. He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”

News.title: Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the veteran broadcaster and campaigner had "changed countless lives".

Dame Esther hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items.

She launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness. Later in life, she became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In December 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic.

But in a statement given to the Press Association earlier this month, she said that despite having "spent the money and made the plans" to go to Dignitas, she had since reached the point where she was "too physically fragile to make the journey".

She added that the law must "change and change quickly", as she renewed her plea ahead of the latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, which failed to pass through the Commons.

News.title: How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment
News.content:
Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".

She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved.

"I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.

She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.

They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".

Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.

She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton.

The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.

Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended.

"That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.

The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.

That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments.

"In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.

News.title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, says Milburn
News.content:
Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK.

Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds.

However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support.

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026.

Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible".

Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday.

As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons".

He told the BBC this could be achieved by employers giving talks in primary schools and offering taster sessions to children.

"It'd be good if employers came into schools and said, 'Look, this is what's going on, these are things that are possible.'"

Milburn says that for Key Stage 4 pupils - aged between 14 and 16 - experience must be given in a real workplace with employer feedback.

News.title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
News.content:
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break.

In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight.

Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025.

"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down."

In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says.

She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers.

But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model."

Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world.

For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them.

"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones.

A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time.

Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health.

A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness.

There are several theories as to why that might be.

AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people.

"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors is back - here's what you need to know ahead of the first show
News.content:
The Celebrity Traitors is back for a second series, and viewers will see the likes of Michael Sheen, Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Amol Rajan at the round table along with Bella Ramsey, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama and King Kenny.

There are 21 celebrities taking part in total - two more than last year - and there will be an extra episode after the huge popularity of last year's series.

The extended 75-minute debut episode starts at 20:00 BST on Thursday, with Claudia Winkleman again hosting the murderous game.

Viewers can expect some fresh ideas, and executive producer Sarah Fay said they "always want to push the envelope" with the show's elaborate tasks.

"We're always trying to evolve existing ideas to bring them into a new life or coming up with different cultural references," she told the show's press launch.

News.title: Vape prices to rise as new tax takes effect
News.content:
The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people.

The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of Â£2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price.

The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people.

The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking.

The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine.

Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by Â£2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping.

News.title: BBC should not overspend on shows such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, MPs say
News.content:
The BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, an influential group of MPs has said.

It is one of several issues raised in a wide-ranging report about the BBC's funding and future, published by the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee.

Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform.

The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming". Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said.

Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report , externalcomes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for.

Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding".

But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo".

The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired.

"At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said.

The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer".

The BBC said it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming.

News.title: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness.

Young people claiming Universal Credit who are fit to work but have not worked for six months continuously would face new rules to qualify for payments, including daily attendance at a job centre or courses.

The party says the scheme would help tackle the almost one million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.

But anti-poverty charity Trussell warned that people on Universal Credit could not afford basic essentials, which harmed their ability to find and keep work.

Under the Tory proposals, those aged 18 to 24 who apply for Universal Credit but have not previously worked for a continuous period of six months or more, for at least 16 hours per week, would instead have to take part in a "Get to Work" scheme.

Rather than Universal Credit, they would receive a "Get to Work Allowance" paid at the same rate but requiring daily attendance at a job centre, on work experience or work readiness courses.

They would be assigned a manager and have to take part in job search workshops and interview preparation sessions.

The programme would last six months, or less if a participant secures a job - but those who are still unemployed after half a year on the scheme would have their benefit cut by 30%.

Young people on Universal Credit who have previously worked for six months, have health issues or care responsibilities or are estranged would be exempt.

The party has also said it would look closer at whether parents' earnings and savings should be factored into welfare payments for their children.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the measures were designed to "show some tough love" to reduce the number of Neets.

"Too many young people are leaving school and signing straight onto benefits - this is a waste of their potential and a disaster for our economy," the Tory MP said.

News.title: We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early
News.content:
Dame Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, called the scheme "shameful" and said she's had "no assurance that the danger perpetrators pose has been properly considered and assessed with meaningful input from victims".

"Ultimately, we cannot ignore the fact that the early release scheme has caused untold damage to victims' confidence in the justice system," Dame Nicole added.

She said Prime Minister Andy Burnham "must take urgent steps to address this" and called on the probation service to be given "the resources it needs to safely manage more offenders in the community". She also called for additional funding for domestic abuse services to support victims.

A recent report raised serious concerns about electronic tagging, which can be used to monitor offenders' movements in the community. It found almost half of tags were not fitted on time.

Alice told the BBC she had been looking to buy a doorbell with a camera fitted to help make her feel safer, but said she cannot afford one. "I don't feel prepared in the slightest and I don't feel safe," she added.

"I think the early release scheme is a joke to victims and survivors, who spent years preparing for trial, going through evidence and re-traumatising themselves to go to court, just for the perpetrator of their crimes to be released after just 33% of their sentence".

The MoJ said: "Anyone who is released faces the toughest-ever controls on their movements, including world-first restriction zones and the largest expansion of electronic tagging, with victims having a say in their perpetrators' licence conditions."

News.title: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says
News.content:
The government believes that Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC. He did not provide further details.

Iran has responded, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the UK leader was "barking up the wrong tree".

"I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all," he wrote on social media.

Asked why the suspects had been released on bail - a decision which has been openly questioned by President Donald Trump - Burnham insisted the men were subject to the "strictest possible bail conditions".

Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said: "I will tell you, I would have said, 'don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."

But Burnham said: "I think people need to understand that when it says released - that isn't as people might think. It's obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions.

"The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that."

Burnham's comments come after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor".

News.title: Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the European Union.

The prime minister told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now" but the UK needed to "consider the options" for its relationship with the EU as "where we are isn't good enough".

It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year.

The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing Burnham of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years".

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason, Burnham was challenged over whether he was reopening divisive arguments about rejoining the EU, despite promising not to in May.

In response, the PM said: "No, I'm not proposing that, am I? I am saying that in a context when we're looking at a 10-year plan for Britain, Britain needs to consider the options as to where we will be.

"That is way before you even get to anything that's put before the public, this is about now just looking at what are the broad options for our relationship."

He suggested these options could include staying "exactly as we are", a closer relationship similar to that being discussed by the EU and Canada or rejoining the EU customs union.

However, Burnham stressed that "to leap back to a proposal and a referendum on it wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

Pressed over whether including an in-out referendum in a future Labour manifesto was a possibility, Burnham said: "Yes, things are possible. I think where we are isn't good enough."

News.title: UK-France 'one in, one out' migrant scheme scrapped
News.content:
The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped.

The pilot scheme allowed the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who were believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

Only around 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago.

The BBC understands the government would have liked the scheme to continue, but felt it did not reach the desired scale.

A Home Office spokesperson said "lessons learned" would be used to "accelerate efforts" to return small boat migrants with no right to remain.

"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the spokesperson said.

"However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK."

The government would continue working with France to tackle small boat crossings, the spokesperson said, adding that "real progress" had been made with numbers "significantly down on last year".

The French Interior Ministry told the BBC: "We are discussing with the British the terms of exit from the agreement."

News.title: Bayeux tour to include audio account of tapestry
News.content:
Osman, who has no sight in either eye, contacted the museum via solicitor Leigh Day to ask whether audio-described tours would be available.

The law firm told him the museum had said self-guided visits would be prioritised over tours and events.

The British Museum said this was because there are limits on how many hours of light to which the tapestry can be exposed - and this in turn restricted visitor numbers.

Osman is seeking damages and a declaration that he was discriminated against and an order requiring the museum to change its policies.

He also said relevant staff should be given disability awareness training and he hoped the legal action would "help make sure blind and partially sighted people are properly considered" when major exhibitions are planned.

His solicitor said the Equality Act placed obligations on service providers to anticipate the needs of disabled people and take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage.

"Our client is asking for the same opportunity as sighted visitors to experience this exhibition."

A British Museum spokesperson said the museum was "committed to making the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition as accessible as possible" and had worked with specialist access consultants.

Provisions currently include a sensory map to help visitors prepare for their visit, as well as dedicated tours during the exhibition run which will include an in-person audio-described tour, the spokesperson said.

"We are also exploring including a separate audio-described tour as part of the exhibition's app-based audio guide."

The 70m (230ft) embroidery, which depicts the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of 1066, is on loan from France and is on display at the museum until 11 July 2027.

News.title: Residents near RAF Fairford left 'like sitting ducks'
News.content:
A couple, who asked not to be named, claims Whelford villagers were warned to stay home on Saturday night - hours before the alarm was first raised by a farmer.

The pair were evacuated from their home the following morning, after the vans were found abandoned at the end of their driveway.

But when the husband stepped outside, he said he was confronted by armed police.

"I was trying to get my wallet out to say, 'look I'm a resident here'," he said.

"Then one of them got out of the vehicle and put a gun on me, in my direction.

"Then the other officer also got out, put a gun on me, and said 'Who's asked you to leave?'."

The couple said they and and their terrified child were briefly trapped inside their home before managing to escape through a neighbour's property.

After being allowed to return home, the pair saw the van doors had been "blown off" and their contents emptied, with water butts and oil drums strewn on the ground.

"All of a sudden, you see on the news the five suspected terrorists have been released," the husband said.

"You're thinking, 'Is this for real?'.

"We've all been panicking for the best part of a day and a bit. Are our homes going to get blown up? Could we have been blown up?"

The family say they are "angry" over an absence of communication from authorities in the days leading up to the incident, alongside the lack of reassurance afterwards.

News.title: Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.

An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

It comes as the Independent Football Regulator â set up by the government in 2025 â said the case had raised "serious issues".

The regulator suggested it would be exploring options â including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club â once the disciplinary process was completed.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing â which could take months to convene â to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.

Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.

Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

News.title: Met hands Grenfell fire investigation file to CPS
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has submitted its final investigation file into the Grenfell Tower fire to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies.

These include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.

Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) and the Department of Housing have both been referred to the CPS following the fire which killed 72 people at the tower block in North Kensington, west London.

The CPS said charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which is on 14 June 2027.

RBKC said it had been informed by the Met that it had referred the council to the CPS for three offences: corporate manslaughter, section 3 of Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, and acting contrary to the Regulatory Reform (fire safety) Order 2005.

The council said in a statement on Wednesday: "They have told us that the CPS will now independently review the evidence, and they will decide whether to charge the council with those offences."

Elizabeth Campbell, leader of the council, said their "commitment to candour, openness, and accountability has not changed".

A Texas man was arrested in the early hours of Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the State Capitol in Austin, authorities said.

The Texas Department of Public Safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack" for Thursday in the city.

The tip came in Tuesday evening, and SWAT officers arrested the suspect at 3am Wednesday at a residence in Converse, Texas, near San Antonio.

Benny Caldera Jr. was jailed on a $75,000 bond. He could face charges including felony terroristic threat against a public servant, the DPS statement said.

Messages were left seeking comment from an attorney listed for Caldera.

Authorities say a 40-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas State Capitol ( AP )

Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing the ongoing investigation.

DPS notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.

Texas Senate Secretary Patsy Spaw said in a notice that there will be increased security at the Capitol during the investigation.

Gov. Greg Abbott said the state DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.

"Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol," the governor said in a statement on social media.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed legislation Wednesday that would have penalized Californians for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctor’s offices and other spaces people generally consider private.

The legislation also would have required companies making smart glasses or other wearable devices, starting in 2028, to include a light or some other feature that indicates that the person is video or audio recording. It would have banned the sale of technology designed to help people conceal a recording light or sound on a smart device.

Newsom wrote in a letter explaining his decision that the bill's definition of a wearable recording device was too broad. He noted that the state already bars people from recording someone without their consent in spaces generally considered private.

Meta Ray-Bans, smart glasses that were rolled out in 2021, have especially grown in popularity, with more than 7 million of the AI-powered devices being sold last year. State Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes, who wrote the bill, said it would've helped the state respond to the technology’s rapid growth.

“Whatever we can do to protect an individual’s right to privacy, we have to do,” she said.

The bill would have been the first of its kind in the nation and built upon the state’s extensive privacy protections. California is one of about a dozen states that already requires both parties’ consent before a conversation can be recorded via audio or video.

Reyes’ proposal was designed to clarify that it applied to smart glasses and make it easier for someone to tell when those devices are recording. Any person who violated the bill by secretly recording someone would have faced prison time or fines of up to $1,500. A company that made devices that didn't comply with the bill would've faced fines up to $2,500.

But TechNet, a group of executives from companies including Meta, Google and Amazon, said the legislation, known as SB 1130, would have been unfair to businesses and customers.

“California already has extensive laws governing unlawful recording, and as currently written, SB 1130 is not the right approach to addressing these concerns,” TechNet Executive Director Robert Boykin said in a statement.

Meta touted the benefits of its smart glasses in response to Newsom's veto, including an initiative providing the devices to blinded veterans to help them read documents and identify objects.

“We’re still in the early days of building this technology and we’re committed to continuing prioritizing privacy as we build,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement.

About a dozen states, including California, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, require someone who wants to record a conversation to get the other person’s permission.

It’s important to strengthen privacy laws for these wearable smart devices because it’s not as obvious to tell when a person is using them to record compared to when someone is filming with their phone or a camera, said Justin Brookman, the director of technology policy for Consumer Reports.

In a letter to lawmakers earlier this year about the bill, Consumer Reports referenced a TikTok in which a woman recounted her experience getting a wax when she realized her technician was wearing smart glasses. The technician told the content creator, Aniessa Navarro, that the glasses weren’t on, but the experience was still unnerving, she said in the TikTok. The Consumer Reports letter cited a separate event in which a woman said she was secretly filmed with smart glasses at a gym and harassed online after the video was uploaded to social media.

“The stories are enough to cause alarm, and we need to do something as soon as we can,” Reyes said at the end of the legislative session.

A model has sued Victoria’s Secret, claiming the company used too much of her face in an Instagram ad for perfume without permission and without additional compensation.

Sydney Roper, who has modeled for Peter Millar’s G/FORE golf apparel brand for about six years, alleges in a lawsuit filed in federal court in California Tuesday that Victoria’s Secret used her “recognizable likeness” in the ad “to attract consumer attention and promote purchases.”

Despite the company purchasing only an “unrecognizable parts-model appearance,” in which less than 30 percent of Roper’s face would be shown, about 95 percent of her face appeared in the ad, according to the lawsuit obtained by The Independent.

“These models are exploited and taken advantage of on a daily basis. They go up against these big companies. The models are afraid to take on the big companies because they don't want to be blacklisted,” Roper’s lawyer Perry C. Wander told The Independent.

open image in gallery A model has sued Victoria’s Secret, claiming the company used too much of her face in an Instagram ad for perfume without permission and without additional compensation ( Getty Images )

“My client has been doing it for a long time, and she just doesn't let anyone take advantage of her anymore at this point in her career,” Wander continued. “So she was really adamant to pursue the case.”

When Roper’s agency demanded an extra $3,000, including a $500 agency fee, for using more of her face in the ad, Victoria’s Secret “did not respond, removed the linked , and offered no apology,” the lawsuit read.

“Taking an  down does not pay the model for the use already made,” Roper’s legal team wrote in the complaint.

The Independent has reached out to Victoria’s Secret for comment.

The complaint stems from a perfume ad that was part of Victoria’s Secret Joyride campaign that rolled out this summer.

open image in gallery The company agreed to only show less than 30 percent of Sydney Roper’s face, but about 95 percent of her face was in the ad, according to the lawsuit ( Getty Images )

Roper’s agency agreed to a four-hour modeling shoot for the campaign on April 3 in exchange for $1,000 plus a 20 percent agency fee, according to the lawsuit.

A company representative allegedly confirmed to Roper’s agency in an email that “all will remain unrecognizable” and said that only part of her face, including her nose and lips, would be shown, along with her hands and an arm.

But, according to Roper’s estimate, about 95 percent of her face was allegedly shown in the ad. “Her visible eye, nose, lips, and facial features made her recognizable notwithstanding partial shadow,” the lawsuit read.

“My client discovered an Instagram post of the Victoria's Secret perfume video ad that was posted by Victoria's Secret, and it had her full face. She's pouring perfume on her chest, and you can see her full face,” Wander told The Independent. “The original contract was with a modeling agency that does just bits and parts of models, not a full face.”

open image in gallery ‘These models are exploited and taken advantage of on a daily basis,’ Roper’s lawyer said. ‘My client has been doing it for a long time, and she just doesn't let anyone take advantage of her anymore’ ( Getty Images )

Wander said a model showing her full face for a national or international perfume campaign could be paid tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of dollars.

“We don't know if this was an inadvertent mistake or they decided to just publish the video of her full face, hoping that she either wouldn’t notice or would actually be excited that her whole face was in the ad,” the lawyer said.

Roper is now seeking “accountability for the unauthorized commercial use of her likeness and the breach of the negotiated restrictions,” according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit requests an unspecified amount of damages, profits attributable to the “unauthorized use” of Roper’s likeness and attorneys’ fees.

A Louisiana boy who survived a stabbing attack that left four others dead made an emotional return home with a police escort as local authorities dubbed him a “superhero.”

The Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office shared a video on Facebook Tuesday of the boy returning to his home in Houma, about an hour’s drive southwest of New Orleans, from the hospital after being seriously injured in the attack.

The boy, wearing a neck brace and a Spider-Man baseball cap, was seen shaking the hands of cops and saying “thank you” for helping him to safety.

“This young man and his family have endured unimaginable loss,” Terrebonne Parish Sheriff Tim Soignet said in a statement. “Today, we stand beside them as he comes home, and we will continue to stand beside them in the days ahead. To this young survivor: you are not alone. Your community is with you, we are with you!”

Members of the sheriff’s office and Houma Police Department had turned on their flashing lights and sirens to escort the boy, calling it “a welcome home for a ‘superhero.’”

open image in gallery A Louisiana boy who survived a stabbing attack that left four others dead has returned home via police escort as local authorities dub him a 'superhero' ( Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office )

open image in gallery Police shared a video Tuesday of the boy returning to his home in Houma, about an hour’s drive southwest of New Orleans, from the hospital after being seriously injured in the attack ( Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office )

Deputies rushed to Ashland Drive in Houma on September 12 to find the boy with stab wounds. He was airlifted to an “out-of-area” hospital in critical condition, the sheriff’s office said at the time.

As police investigated, they found four others dead inside nearby homes from a series of stabbings. A 47-year-old Houma resident, Kaegan Jude Solet, was later arrested in connection with the stabbings and charged with four counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted first-degree murder.

A neighbor named Dulce recalled the moment the boy ran to her house to get inside and find help as the man accused of stabbing him trailed close behind.

“She saw that the boy went running to the back door,” Dulce’s niece, who translated her aunt’s words into English, told WWL Louisiana.

open image in gallery A 47-year-old Houma resident, Kaegan Jude Solet, was later arrested in connection with the stabbings and charged with four counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted first-degree murder ( Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office )

The man who had followed the boy “had wrapped the kid by his shoulders and pushed him down, then hit him again,” Dulce’s niece said, adding that the boy eventually passed out.

Dulce and her family, who were eating dinner with her when the boy rushed over, called the police.

Solet was identified as a person of interest the same day that the stabbings took place. The next day, the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office confirmed that he was taken into custody.

On September 15, the sheriff’s office said Solet was released from medical care, sent to a local jail and booked on the murder charges.

open image in gallery On September 15, three days after the attack, the sheriff’s office said Solet was released from medical care, sent to a local jail and booked on the murder charges ( Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office )

When sharing the video of the boy returning home from the hospital after his horrific ordeal, the sheriff’s office said, “We ask the community to continue lifting up the victim and his family while respecting their privacy as he recovers.”

One Facebook user said, “Someone take him to Disney.”

“Choked up and crying like a baby. Bless his heart,” another wrote.

A third commented, “What an amazing police force we have, with all the hell that that sweet baby has been through our police officers escort him home and made him feel special.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a sweeping “State of the Force” address to service members on September 30, using the platform to issue blunt directives on military standards — including a jab at “beardos” — while detailing plans to overhaul the armed forces.

“We are no longer the woke department or the weak department,” Hegseth declared at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. Hegseth said that a “simple translation” of his message meant the Pentagon would exclude some groups, including trans service members, and “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”

He laid out six major initiatives aimed at shifting the Defense Department — which the Trump administration moved to rename the Department of War — toward rapid modernization and autonomous warfare. And instead of the hundreds of generals and admirals who sat through his previous address, this year’s audience comprised lower-ranked active-duty officers and non-commissioned officers.

“Allow me to lay it out simply for the anti-American losers in our media,” Hegseth said. “You, this group, are ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.”

During the address, Hegseth outlined several structural changes to military operations:

open image in gallery In a September 30 ‘State of the Force’ address to service members, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued blunt new directives on military standards ( Getty )

Autonomous Warfare Command

The Pentagon is establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command designed to scale up robotic and automated combat systems across all branches. Set to operate as a four-star combatant command by October 2027, the effort builds on recent drone deployments in the Middle East.

“The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” Hegseth said. “The autonomous robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades.”

The initiative will be directed by Defense Innovation Unit Director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser.

Project Meridian

open image in gallery The new military directives range from establishing tech advisory panels with Elon Musk to launching dedicated cadet corps at five partner universities ( Reuters )

Hegseth announced the creation of Project Meridian, a 120-day panel set up to figure out what military technology the U.S. will need for future battlefields. However, he offered few specific details during the address about what capabilities the initiative would actually focus on.

The panel will be co-directed by Elon Musk, defense entrepreneur Palmer Luckey, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, with facilitation by the department’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael.

“Those three great Americans are going to be joined by a team of senior leaders, handpicked private sector leaders and subject matter experts from across our nation’s unmatched innovation, academic and policy ecosystems,” Hegseth said.

Next Great American Base

open image in gallery Instead of the hundreds of generals and admirals who sat through Hegseth’s previous address, this year’s audience comprised lower-ranked active-duty officers and non-commissioned officers ( AP )

Plans were unveiled for a massive, off-grid military installation spanning hundreds of thousands of acres. Hegseth promised a “transparent” bidding process to launch what he called a new “gold standard” military facility built for the first time in 40 years.

The department is inviting state governors to compete for the site, favoring whichever state eliminates regulatory hurdles and provides the most favorable land package. The design requires classical architecture, following executive orders on federal buildings.

Given President Donald Trump’s affinity for major real estate developments and putting his name on buildings, the project has sparked speculation that it could be named after him.

America’s Corps of Cadets

open image in gallery Physical fitness standards will be strictly enforced across all service branches, with gender-neutral, male-equivalent benchmarks required for all combat roles ( Getty )

To expand officer commissioning sources, the military is launching “America’s Corps of Cadets.”

The program establishes specialized cadet programs at five partner institutions: Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University, and Hillsdale College. Designated as “Distinguished Military Colleges,” these schools will receive priority status for officer commissioning.

Hegseth praised the schools for producing “patriotic leaders of character” and criticized other legacy institutions as “anti-American, DEI-worshiping, woke factories.”

Despite holding degrees from Princeton and Harvard, Hegseth explicitly targeted Ivy League institutions.

“You see, the Ivy League faculty lounges, they’ll never understand you, and that’s OK because they could never ever do what you do,” he told the audience.

FORTRESS America

open image in gallery Under the FORTRESS America initiative, all major military installations will be required to generate independent power and harden infrastructure against cyberattacks ( AP )

The administration is launching “FORTRESS America,” short for “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy Supply, and Survivability.”

Framed by Hegseth as a “national insurance policy,” the policy mandates that major U.S. installations develop independent power sources capable of operating if the commercial electric grid fails.

It also directs the domestic mining and manufacturing of essential materials, including rare earth metals, microchips and propellants, to eliminate reliance on foreign suppliers.

Office of Religious Affairs

Hegseth announced the creation of a dedicated Office of Religious Affairs reporting directly to the defense secretary, saying the unit would “protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support.”

The office is designed to oversee departmental policy regarding religious support and chaplaincy programs, which officials stated would focus on troop resilience while maintaining voluntary access to services across all faiths.

A gang rape allegation at Cornell University has brought fresh scrutiny of fraternities at the Ivy League school, which has a history of misconduct cases followed by efforts to reform the Greek system.

Authorities reopened an investigation Monday as outrage built over a woman’s lawsuit filed Sept. 16 against the Chi Phi fraternity, the university and the seven students she says assaulted her. She told police in November 2024 that she was assaulted at the fraternity house the month before, and prosecutors decided at the time not to prosecute anyone.

The Associated Press generally does not name people who say they have been sexually assaulted. The woman’s lawsuit uses a pseudonym for her.

The Chi Phi chapter has been barred from campus, and its national organization said Wednesday that the Cornell chapter unanimously voted to remove the accused members from its rolls within days of the woman filing a police report. Cornell has said its investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled.

It's a horrifying but familiar story on many campuses, said Elizabeth Allan, a professor of higher education at the University of Maine and director of the school’s Hazing Prevention Research Lab. She said failed reforms show "how entrenched some of the behaviors are and that we need to take an approach that’s transformative.”

The university in Ithaca, New York, has rolled out reforms in response to hazing deaths, lawsuits and arrests in its Greek system.

In 2019, Cornell required Greek life chapters to hire independent event monitors and submit to random security spot checks, among other changes, after freshman Antonio Tsialas was found dead at the bottom of a gorge. His parents’ lawsuit said he and other fraternity pledges were hazed by being forced to drink dangerous amounts of alcohol.

Cornell has had fraternities — and problems — since its founding in 1865, said Adam McCready, a University of Connecticut associate professor who studies fraternities and sororities. One of the first confirmed hazing deaths happened at Cornell in the 1870s, he said.

Over time, the fraternities built what he described as “palatial mansions that dictate the social environment on campus.”

Fraternities have a long record of hazing and abuse cases

In 1997, a Cornell student alleged in a lawsuit that he suffered weeks of paddling and beatings. The following year, a half dozen Cornell students were arrested over allegations that a fraternity pledge was taken from his dorm room, blindfolded and bound with rope and duct tape.

In 2012, a fraternity was found guilty of hazing in the alcohol poisoning death of a Cornell student. After the death, Cornell University moved to eradicate risky pledging practices.

At the time, more than one quarter of Cornell students were members of fraternities and sororities. These students graduate and turn into donors, McCready said. “It can be a challenge to making change if there’s pressure not to do so,” McCready said.

In 2018, a fraternity chapter was placed on probation over a contest that members dubbed the Pig Roast in reference to the weight of the women they slept with.

Cornell again took steps to reign in fraternities, moving to ban hard liquor from chapter houses and require live-in advisers.

But in 2022, allegations of a sexual assault and students being drugged at off-campus housing affiliated with fraternities led Cornell to temporarily suspend fraternity parties. Fraternity leaders were supposed to use the time to "implement stronger health and safety plans,” the university had said.

The gang rape allegation followed two years later.

Advocates call for a stronger response

Cornell has said it is committed to implementing recommendations from a task force that launched last year on campus sexual assault. The university has also pointed to the expulsions and suspensions it implemented in the case.

But that is too little for advocates of sex crime victims.

The people the woman says gang raped her were allowed to write essays to Cornell “to mitigate their conduct,” the woman's lawsuit said. That's unacceptable, said Maha Ibrahim, a director at Equal Rights Advocates, a nonprofit that represents survivors.

“There's no schema where that’s an appropriate response to a gang rape,” Ibrahim said.

Allan said the case highlights a need to better understand what contributes to this kind of violence and misconduct, not just in groups, but communities, institutions and society.

“The lack of understanding around consent issues are broad-reaching and we have to be taking a public health approach to change behavior, change attitudes" in more sustainable ways, Allan said.

____

Leah Willingham in Boston contributed to this report.
