A copilot on a flight to Israel stabbed a captain on Wednesday before passengers pushed their way into the cockpit and wrestled with the attacker. The FlyDubai plane fell rapidly, and a passenger said he grabbed the controls and pulled upward, like how he had seen on television. Other crew members soon took over, and the jetliner made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

It was not clear what motivated the attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saudi Arabia arrested the copilot. The passengers from the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv were met with cheers in Israel as they completed the journey on another flight Wednesday evening.

Here's a look at the airline in which the altercation took place.

Airline is owned by the Emirati government

FlyDubai, the sister airline to Emirates, is a government-owned carrier run by the United Arab Emirates that operates a fleet of 98 Boeing 737 aircraft, according to its website. The airline flies to the Mideast, Africa, Europe and Asia, including the Indian subcontinent.

In November 2020, FlyDubai began offering commercial flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai, a rare route at a time when other airlines in the region stopped flying to Israel, a UAE ally.

The airline reported carrying 15.7 million passengers in 2025 and reached a total revenue of AED 13.6 billion ($3.7 billion).

Stabbed captain helped passengers overpower attacker

In the chaos of the attack, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24. Most of the plane’s rudder was ripped off the tail during the sudden drop.

Netanyahu identified the wounded captain as Smit Machchhar of India. The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in stable condition.

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” Netanyahu said on X. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco is particularly popular in south Asia that is placed between the cheek and lower gum. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

News.title: ‘Pooled’ TB testing could save money and improve diagnosis, study finds
News.content:
Mixing phlegm samples from multiple patients in “pooled tests” for tuberculosis could halve costs and help find millions of missing cases, according to a major new study.

While most advances in fighting TB come with a large price tag, the shift in strategy could dramatically boost access to diagnosis and save money, experts said.

TB is the deadliest single infection globally, killing around 1.3m people every year, despite being both preventable and curable.

The gold standard in diagnosis is rapid molecular testing, which detects genetic material from the bacteria causing TB in patient sputum samples within hours. But each sample needs a specialist diagnostic cartridge that costs around US$8, beyond the budget of many poorer countries even before recent aid cuts.

In a pooled test, samples from multiple individuals are tested in one cartridge. If the result is negative then all of them are reported to be negative, but if the result is positive each is re-tested individually.

Results published in The Lancet Global Health found the strategy, with up to four patients in each pool, used half as many cartridges as individual testing – 7,028 compared to 14,362. It detected 84.9 per cent of people with TB compared with 88 per cent for individual testing.

The study involved more than 14,000 people whose symptoms suggested TB in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria and Vietnam.

Sports.title: Maths may suggest Man City get a 456-point deduction to end up in non-league – but football doesn’t work like that
Sports.content:
Next

FOUR points deducted for Forest. Six for Everton. Another two for Everton. Six for Leicester.

So what happens when Manchester City are found to have breached the rules 114 times?



Four multiplied by 114 is a 456-point deduction.

Manchester City would be relegated so far down the football pyramid they would be in National League North.



Except it doesn’t work like that.

There is no Premier League list pinned to the wall saying: one ­financial breach, four points; two breaches, eight; 114 breaches, please report to the National League.

The four-point calculation is not a rule. It is what happens when you take recent points deductions and try applying an average to a case which is anything but average.

That is important because 114 ­findings does not mean 114 identical PSR breaches.

The charges cover different rules, different seasons and different types of conduct over nine seasons.

So 456 points is not the answer.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

But it is useful because it shows how ridiculous it would be to try to find the answer by multiplying ­previous sanctions.

And then you read the judgment and sat in every ­Premier League meeting where it has been discussed — as I have — this affair stops being a maths problem.

The Independent Commission found that a series of City’s sponsorship agreements were “shams”.

The club’s accounts between 2009-10 and 2017-18 had wrongly recorded more than £830million as income when it should have been treated as equity contributions. Expenses were also understated.

The accounts simply did not provide a true and fair picture of City’s financial position.



Then comes the sentence that blows away any suggestion this was simply a dispute about accounting terminology: “By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the PL rules.”

There isn’t much ambiguity there.

It doesn’t say City misunderstood the rules or that they were complicated.

It doesn’t say somebody forgot to tick a box.

The commission also found that, when the accounts were restated, City failed to meet the relevant break-even requirement by a “very substantial amount” in every season covered by that charge.



City made “concerted efforts to stop and frustrate” the investigation and breached its duties of co-operation in most of the respects alleged.

So while a 456-point punishment may be absurd, it does not follow that the punishment should be modest.

That is the trickiest part of this entire business.

What is the Premier League actually intending to punish?

The number of rules broken? The number of seasons involved? The financial advantage? The sporting advantage? The deliberate nature of the conduct? The attempt to frustrate the investigation? Or all of it?



Look at Forest and Everton.

Forest received four points for a PSR breach.

Everton’s original ten-point deduction was reduced to six on appeal.

A separate Everton breach resulted in another two points.

Those cases establish that points deductions are not fixed. They also don’t establish that four points is the exchange rate for cheating.



Football does not work that neatly. And nor does compensation.

This is where the old Carlos Tevez case comes back into the conversation.

West Ham were fined £5.5m over the registration arrangements involving Tevez and Javier Mascherano. They were not docked points and avoided relegation, while Sheffield United went down in 2007.

After years of legal wrangling, West Ham paid Sheffield United around £20m in compensation.



Punishment and compensation are two different things.

That matters because if another club can demonstrate it suffered a direct financial loss as a result of City’s conduct, why should that question disappear?

We have seen the principle tested again with Burnley being awarded £26m in their compensation claim against Everton, who are appealing.

But there is a very large difference between saying ‘we were harmed’ and proving ‘this is the damage you caused us’.

Football is basically one enormous Sliding Doors movie.



If City had not done this, who ­finishes where?

Who gets into the Champions League? Who wins the title? Who stays up?

Who signs which player?

And does the manager who gets sacked in November still get sacked if the league table looks different?

You cannot simply redraw every Premier League table since 2009 and announce new winners.



Sporting history does not come with a reset button.

Then there are the players.

The commission found that in ­certain arrangements terms relating to remuneration and image-rights ­payments ought to have appeared in players’ contracts but did not.

That is a regulatory issue.

Players weren’t sitting with a calculator and a copy of the Premier League handbook.



They sign contracts, they don’t ­prepare the club’s accounts. There is the increasingly popular idea City should get some enormous points deduction and “work it off” over ­several seasons.

What is this — football community service? A points deduction is a sanction, not a mortgage.

You don’t hand Manchester City a 456-point overdraft and tell them to make monthly repayments.

The commission has to decide what sanction is appropriate for the actual findings and the rules governing those historic breaches.



What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

That is a much harder task but it is also the only sensible one.

A punishment designed simply to make people gasp does not necessarily make sense.

If City get a points deduction, explain the number. If it’s a fine, explain why money is sufficient.

If there are sporting sanctions beyond points, explain what they are intended to achieve.

If other clubs have suffered demonstrable financial losses, deal with compensation separately.



The Premier League has spent years telling its clubs that financial rules matter.

Clubs have lost points, paid fines, been relegated, and have been forced to sell players.

Clubs have watched European football disappear from their budgets.

Now the biggest case of all has arrived. And the commission’s judgment does not describe a club which ­simply got its sums wrong. It describes overstated income of more than £830m, sponsorship arrangements called “shams” and accounts that did not give a true and fair view.

It says City clearly intended to ­circumvent the rules and the club made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the investigation.



Those are the facts the punishment has to answer. Not 456 points or whatever number looks most frightening on the front page.

There is a temptation in football to think justice means making somebody suffer as much as possible.

It doesn’t. Justice means making the punishment make sense.

If the sanction is too small, every club that has played by the rules will ask what the point was.

If it is simply enormous because enormous looks good, City will ask what the logic was.



And if there is no logic, the argument never ends and the appeals rumble on for years.

So, the Prem needs to do something much harder than produce a spectacular number. It needs to explain it.

Explain what advantage was gained.

Explain how the duration and seriousness of the conduct have been weighed and why the sanction is proportionate.

And explain why another club committing the same offence would be treated the same way.



That last bit is the one I would put in bold. Because every owner in the Premier League is watching. Every chief executive is watching. Every supporter is watching.

They want to know whether the rules mean what they say and whether they are same for everyone.

The answer cannot simply be the biggest punishment anyone can ­imagine. Nor can it be the smallest punishment the lawyers can defend.

It has to be one that can survive scrutiny from Manchester City, from the other 19 clubs, from the courts and, most importantly, from supporters who want to believe the competition is run on a level playing field.

This is not about finding a number that makes everybody happy. There probably isn’t one.



So what would I do?

I would go for a 50-point deduction, an £83m fine — roughly 10 per cent of the £830m by which sponsorship income was overstated — and a three-year restriction on registering new players.

Not because 50 is some magic number but because the punishment has to hurt on the pitch as well as in the accounts department.

Crucially, I would still leave City something to play for this season.

A 50-point deduction would put them in an extraordinary fight for survival. But it would not make relegation a mathematical certainty from the moment the punishment was announced.



That matters. Punishment should be severe, but football should still be allowed to happen.

Make Manchester City fight for every point, make them earn their way back from the hole they have dug and let the rest of the season determine whether they survive.

I would also expect City to face at least one season excluded from European competition, subject to Uefa’s own process and jurisdiction.

I would go after individuals, too.

The commission says a number of important witnesses called on behalf of the club gave false evidence, with some giving evidence they knew to be untrue and were therefore dishonest.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

That should potentially mean a ­suspension from holding senior football positions.

You cannot tell every club in the Premier League that financial integrity is fundamental and then punish only the corporate logo on the shirt.

Sports.title: Man City ace Erling Haaland’s eye-watering fortune revealed thanks to top brand deals and share in two planes
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL star Erling Haaland, the Premier League’s top scorer last season, has netted a £19.6million fortune.

The 26-year-old Man City ace has built his vast wealth while his club remains mired in a financial scandal.



Figures show his image rights firm, York Promotions, has cash deposits of £5million and assets and investments worth more than £12million.

Assets include a share in two planes worth £2.1million.



Haaland earns £500,000 a week on the pitch.

Top players earn extra cash from clubs from the sale of merchandise like shirts that bear their “name, nickname, slogan and signatures, image, likeness, voice, logos, get-ups, initials, team or squad number”.

The in-form striker has deals with big-name brands Nike, EA Sports, Midea, Breitling, Dolce & Gabbana, Red Bull, Beats by Dre, TAG Heuer, Prime Hydration, Hyperice, and the Norwegian Seafood Council.

Leeds-born Erling runs the company with his dad and manager Alfie, who also played for Man City.

Top tax accountant Julia Hoyle – an associate of Haaland’s late agent Mino Raiola – is also listed as a director.

The ace has been linked with a move to Barcelona or Real Madrid after it was found Man City arranged “sham” contracts with commercial partners.



The contracts were part of a “disguised funding scheme” to inflate club revenue by more than £900million.

The disgraced club now face possible relegation.

Sports.title: Crazy moment Lionesses hero Williamson picks ball up and gives away penalty as Arsenal crumble in Champions League
Sports.content:
Next

ARSENAL squandered a two-goal lead to drop crucial Champions League points against Paris FC following a Leah Williamson howler.

The 29-year-old gave away a penalty following a bizarre handball incident at the end of the match.

With the Gunners leading 2-1 in the 86th minute, goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez kicked the ball to Williamson, who set herself to take a goal kick.



The England captain put her hand on the ball, prompting referee Iuliana Demetrescu to swiftly give a penalty.



Despite protests from Williamson, the spot-kick stood and was converted by Maeline Mendy to level the score.

Arsenal had led the match 2-0 thanks to goals from Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway, but Clara Mateo capitalised on a high defensive line to get Paris back into it.

The Gunners came close to seeing the game out for the win, but the late error saw them drop points for the first time in this European campaign.

It was also the latest in a run of disappointing results and performances.

Reflecting on the bizarre moment, Russo said: “It was a mistake, obviously it wasn’t intended at all. We let them come back into the game in the second half probably way before that moment.”

Head coach Renee Slegers did not show up for the post-match press conference after the disappointing end.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK



Instead, her assistant, Aaron D’Antino, spoke to the media.

Reflecting on the result and performance, he said: “It’s incredibly disappointing, or frustrating I should say, because we felt like for large periods of the game we had good control.

“They are a counter-attacking team, that is their threat, so we were aware of that. And yes, the first moment we conceded the first goal, we can defend it better from the first phase.

“But there were periods of the second half that we were really happy with our attacking intent and that’s a key area that we’ve been working incredibly hard on and we thought we got some good rewards.

“And then the way that the game ends is incredibly disappointing. We didn’t think it was a penalty, we don’t think the goal kick had actually been taken from what we had seen.



“But it goes to VAR and apparently that’s a penalty.”

Slegers now finds herself under increasing pressure following a slow start to the season.

The Gunners currently sit seventh in the WSL table with just five points from their opening four games.

They have scored just two league goals during that time.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp responds to Man City guilty verdict after ex-Liverpool boss once joked he’d hold open-top bus parade
Sports.content:
Next

JURGEN KLOPP is not preparing for any late title parties amid the Manchester City scandal.

The Germany boss, whose side face Serbia on Friday, had previously joked he would join an open-top bus parade to celebrate should Liverpool be awarded any championship honours due to the Cityzens being stripped of any.



The Premier League have found City guilty of ALL charges of financial rule breaches over a nine-year period, which started in 2009.

During Klopp’s time in charge at Anfield, his Liverpool team finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola’s City on three occasions, albeit only one of those came within the period under investigation.



But while others are calling for the honours won during that time to be taken away from City, the ex-Reds chief appears to have no interest in being rewarded retrospectively.

Klopp, who ended Liverpool’s 30-year wait for the title in 2020, said: “I haven’t given it much thought.

“I can wait and see how it plays out quite calmly.

“My respect for Pep Guardiola and the football City played during the time we competed against each other — and the level of opposition they provided at the highest stage — is far too great for me to simply say now that they ought to face some kind of punishment.

“Naturally, I have nothing to do with that matter anyway.

“But when you talk about a legal process that has already dragged on for so long, you can imagine — and I suspect there will be appeals or other complications — that it’s going to take ages yet.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“So, I am a long way off from preparing for any outcome, and I don’t really have a strong feeling about it one way or the other.

“It’s not as if I need to have won the Premier League a few more times.

“I am completely at peace with what happened and what we achieved.

“We battled it out on the pitch, and I can’t comment on anything else because I don’t know the exact details of the case.



What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. Sports.title: ‘Star in the making’ – Chelsea wonderkid scores late winner for England u18s as fans think he’s going right to the top
Sports.content:
Next

CHELSEA youngster Ryan Kavuma-McQueen scored a 91st-minute winner as England Under-18s clinched a 2-1 victory against Korea Republic on Wednesday.

The 17-year-old came off the bench on the hour mark, shortly after the Young Lions had taken the lead thanks to a strike from Newcastle ace Sam Alabi.

Ji-Seong Lim then equalised for Korea Republic in the 70th minute, but Kavuma-McQueen won it late with a deflected shot into the top-right corner.



Excited Chelsea fans were quick to comment on the goal, with one person writing: “Absolute star in the making.”



Another said: “What a player!”

A third commented: “Kavuma-McQueen leaving it that late, my heart did not need that. Give me academy lads doing this over another random signing any day.”

While a fourth wrote: “Who else can do it better than him?”

The win saw England U18s progress to the UEFA Friendship Cup semi-finals.

Kavuma-McQueen has been enjoying his first taste of regular first team football this season.

He is currently on loan at Portsmouth in the Championship and has made seven first-team appearances.

During that time, the teenager has scored one goal and provided one assist.



Kavuma-McQueen has made just one senior appearance for Chelsea, in last season’s FA Cup quarter-final against Port Vale.

Sports.title: Man City’s sponsor threatens legal action against Premier League after guilty verdict over financial breaches
Sports.content:
Next

ETIHAD Airways – the chief sponsor of Manchester City – has threatened legal action against the Premier League after the club was found guilty of financial breaches.

In a long statement on Wednesday night, the sponsor said it was going to “seek the relevant legal counsel… to protect its interests”.



It is claimed £900m was hidden in “sham” deals across a nine-year period, after City were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges.

Now the airline has hit out at the Prem saying it “categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements.”



It slammed the Premier League for having “created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings.”

They said the Premier League had not been in touch nor given the airline “accuracy and fairness of information relied upon in reaching conclusions.”



“Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly.”

The airline said the selective release of information and a lack of clarity and transparency had been damaging to Etihad.



“The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented.”

Etihad Airways is one of the flag carriers of the UAE with the football club being owned by the country’s vice president and member of the royal family Sheikh Mansour.

The threat comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham weighed in saying he would be “really concerned” to lose Manchester City’s billionaire owners.

He told the BBC: “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.

“Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. I can’t intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that.”



Legendary manager Pep Guardiola has also broken his silence saying he was “here” for the club – “more than ever”.

He said: “I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran, the players, staff, Enzo and you, our unique supporters.

“Let me be clear: we will get through this together.”

The Prem’s statement on the charges said an Independent Commission had found City “guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation”.

Those charges relate to the period between 2009 and 2018, with Guardiola joining the club in 2016.



One punishment for the club could be the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) forcing Sheikh Mansour, the vice-president of the United Arab Emirates, to sell the club.

City have won a total of eight Prem titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League under his ownership.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Premier League did not comment when approached by The Sun.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo LEAVES Portugal camp amid feud with manager Jorge Jesus as thousands track his private jet
Sports.content:
Next

CRISTIANO RONALDO sensationally QUIT the Portugal camp after being an unused sub against Norway and then refusing to train amid a major bust-up with the new manager.

The legendary superstar, 41, spent the full 90 minutes watching from the sidelines as his team-mates ran out 2-1 winners in Oslo.



A seething Ronaldo demanded showdown talks with new boss Jorge Jesus on Wednesday.

Now, though, the Al-Nassr forward has walked out on the training camp later today.



Ronaldo, 41, wrote on Instagram to his 679million followers: “After the press conference of the national team coach, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team camp.

“In due time, I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team, to which I have always devoted myself.



“Now is the time to wish Portugal and all my team-mates good luck, without exception.”

And fans wasted no time trying to track his private jet – and saw it was on the move.

According to FlightRadar24, his Bombardier Global Express aircraft was flying from Madrid to Copenhagen this evening – with nearly 5,000 people keeping tabs.

It took off from the Spanish capital at 7.49pm local time and was due to land in the Danish capital at 10.18pm.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Portugal play Denmark in the Nations League tomorrow night before rounding off the bumper international break at home to Norway on Sunday.

The first Norway game last weekend was the first time in 18 years that Ronaldo was named in Portugal’s matchday squad but did not get on the pitch.

Jesus planned to bring him on for 30 minutes – but opted against the plan.

And when he did replace starting striker Goncalo Ramos on 81 minutes, it was Francisco Trincao who came on.

Record stated an emergency meeting between Ronaldo, Jesus and Portuguese FA chief Pedro Proenca was called for earlier today where they thrashed out their differences.



But it seems the icon was not happy with the outcome and on Wednesday evening was waiting for his plane to take him back to Madrid – after allegedly not taking to the field for training either yesterday or today.

Instead, he was spotted leaving Parken Stadium in a van with two members of backroom staff.

Jesus doubled down on his decision not to play Ronaldo against Norway – but insisted there was no issue between the pair.



The manager, who replaced Roberto Martinez after the World Cup, said: “There was no incident whatsoever.

“Any player – and I was a player myself – when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don’t get on, no-one is happy about that.

“Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It’s nothing to make a fuss about.



“If everything goes according to plan [against Denmark], it will be Goncalo who plays.

“If I need [Ronaldo], he’ll come on. If I don’t need him, he won’t.”

The feud comes just a week after Ronaldo committed his future to playing for his country – as he chases down 1,000 career goals – and admitted he will step away when he is no longer wanted by the national team.

Ronaldo revealed: “I had a conversation with our president, with our coach.



“I still believe that I’m able to help the national team to reach what they want, and will finish when I feel like I’m not doing anything here.

“I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football.

“This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Jesus, who won the league title with Ronaldo at Al-Nassr last season, added: “As long as he’s playing and is in a condition to be selected, I will pick him, within certain limits and under the conditions that I consider best for the national team.”

Sports.title: Price books Clayton showdown at World Grand Prix as Aspinall races through
Sports.content:
Gerwyn Price set up an all-Welsh quarter-final showdown with Jonny Clayton with a straight-sets win over Ross Smith at the World Grand Prix, as Ryan Joyce and Nathan Aspinall also progressed in Leicester.

Price, among the tournament favourites after Luke Littler's shock early exit, followed his opening-round victory over Sebastian Białecki by dropping just four legs to despatch Smith at the Mattioli Arena.

The 2020 champion was outscored by Smith - having posted the highest average of the first round - but dropped just four legs during his 3-0 win, securing him a meeting with World Cup of Darts partner Clayton on Friday evening.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gerwyn Price set up an all-Welsh quarter-final at the World Grand Prix with Jonny Clayton, with the Ice Man boasting about his record against his compatriot

Clayton opened with three consecutive ton-plus checkouts and made four in total during a 3-1 victory over Wessel Nijman, where a 93.08 average and some remarkable finishing pushed him past the 12th seed.

Ryan Joyce breezed into the quarter-finals with a straight-sets victory over Danny Noppert, as Luke Woodhouse - who stunned Littler in the first round - was knocked out after losing 3-0 to Nathan Aspinall in a one-sided contest.

How Price and Clayton set up all-Welsh showdown

Price averaged 101.61 on Monday night but was over 10 points lower against Smith, where he recovered from being broken early with a 13-darter to match it in the next and then claim the opening set in a final-leg decider.

The world No 4 took out an 86 finish on his way to winning the second set and nailed an 80 checkout early in the third, where Smith took out 116 to break and extend the match before Price closed out victory on D18.

Image: Gerwyn Price and Ross Smith

"I don't think it was a great game and I don't think we played brilliant," Price admitted to Sky Sports. "What we did do in patches was start well and finish well, but the bits in between were a little bit rubbish.

"I know he [Clayton] is chasing a Grand Slam spot, so the pressure is on him. I think he got lucky first round - hopefully he doesn't get lucky in the next round!"

Clayton won the opening set in straight legs after three consecutive ton-plus finishes, immediately breaking with a 112 checkout, taking out 116 to hold throw and then nailing a 125 finish on the bullseye.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jonny Clayton sealed the first set against Wessel Nijman with a stunning 125 checkout, finishing in style on the bullseye

Nijman responded to Clayton pinching a leg with a 90 finish to take the second set in a final-leg decider, before 'The Ferret' regained the lead by starting the third with another bullseye finish to take out 126.

Clayton, who posted eight maximums alongside his impressive finishing, then reeled off four of the next six legs to reach the quarter-finals for a third consecutive year.

"My scoring was good but, to be fair, Wessel [Nijman] missed a few chances on doubles and he gave me a few chances," Clayton told Sky Sports. "The two bullseyes were good, the 126 was good and I have a big smile."

Sports.title: Somerset pair Overton and Luff win PCA awards
Sports.content:
Somerset duo Craig Overton and Sophie Luff have won the headline accolades at the 2026 PCA awards in partnership with Toyota while emerging England stars Sonny Baker and Tilly Corteen-Coleman also received coveted honours at Exhibition White City.

Overton saw him collect a PCA awards quadruple, winning the PCA Men's Player of the Year trophy, the PCA Men's Domestic Overall MVP, the Rothesay County Championship Player of the Year and selection in the IG PCA Men's Team of the Year.

The 32-year-old, who has scored 951 runs, taken 76 wickets and 45 catches across all three formats this season, becomes the first Somerset player to secure the award since Nick Compton in 2012, beating competition from the notable shortlist of players including Joe Clarke, George Hill and Dan Lawrence.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Overton had to face the last balls of The Hundred match from his brother Jamie!

He also scored a memorable unbeaten 79 in the Vitality Blast quarter-finals to take Somerset to Finals Day.

"It's a phenomenal feeling. To be chosen by your peers to win this award is very special; it means so much to me," said Overton.

"To be able to put in consistent performances has made it a great year. My bowling ticked along and after I scored that hundred at Essex in the second game of the season my form with the bat carried on throughout the summer. The quarter-final against Yorkshire was where I felt like this year is the one where everything's going my way and everything clicked.

"I felt like I got in a groove where my body was in a good spot, not 100 per cent because of the schedule, but mentally I felt like I was in a great spot to be able to go out and perform when games come along near enough every other day."

Image: Sophie Luff emerged victorious from her peers to win the award against nominees Maia Bouchier, Sophia Dunkley and Mady Villiers

Somerset completed the double as their captain Luff also won the player-voted for award and becomes the first winner of the Toyota PCA Women's Player of the Year since Eve Jones won it in 2021 to not have played international cricket.

Impressing for her county all season and in The Hundred, which she won with Trent Rockets, Luff was also selected in the Metro Bank PCA Women's Team of the Year.

"It's super special people have voted for me after the performances and impact they feel I've had this year. It means that I'm doing things in the right way, and people think highly of you," said the 32-year-old, who scored more than 1,000 runs this summer.

"I've always been a leader that wants to lead from the front, but I think people are seeing that play out in games now. I think this year I've just showcased what I'm capable of."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sonny Baker became the first player to take five wickets in the final of the Vitality Blast Men as Hampshire fought back against Northamptonshire

The Toyota PCA Men's Young Player of the Year award went to Hampshire and England's Sonny Baker who was rewarded with a Test match debut, playing against New Zealand at the Kia Oval.

The 21-year-old took 10 international wickets, showing his prowess with six in IT20s and remarkably becomes the first Hampshire player to win this award since it was introduced in 1990.

Left-arm spinner Tilly Corteen-Coleman enjoyed a year which saw her earn IT20 and ODI debuts for England, whilst impressing for Surrey and Southern Brave in The Hundred as she claimed the Toyota PCA Women's Young Player of the Year award.

Former England captain Heather Knight was announced as the PCA Outstanding Contribution Award winner for her incredible dedication to the game over a prolonged period.

Sports.title: Gill hits 223 not out as India chase down 406 to beat West Indies in second ODI
Sports.content:
A capacity crowd witnessed a host of batting records on Wednesday, Shubman Gill leading the way with 223 not out off 133 balls as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in their second ODI.

Gill notched his best ODI score and a record-high individual tally in an ODI run-chase. It was his 11th hundred in the format, one of five on the day, as India amassed 406-2 in 43.3 overs to take a winning 2-0 lead in the three-match series.

Opening partner Rohit Sharma made 101 as the duo put on 255 off 158 balls - the second-highest opening stand for India in ODIs.

It was the second successful 400-plus run-chase in ODI history, after South Africa's record 438-9 against Australia in 2006.

Sports.title: Man City sponsor Etihad Airways considering legal action against PL
Sports.content:
Manchester City's principal sponsor, Etihad Airways, has said it is considering taking legal action against the Premier League.

City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

The independent commission found that between 2009/10 and 2017/18, City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol answers your questions after Manchester City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches

The club continue to deny the breaches, with chief executive Ferran Soriano calling the process a "Premier League conspiracy theory" in a video message to players and staff.

And now the Abu Dhabi state airline Etihad Airways, which has sponsored City since 2009, says it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

In a statement, they say the Premier League did not engage with them and they were not given a chance to provide relevant information.

They are now seeking legal advice to protect their interests.

Etihad were not named in Tuesday's published judgment but say it has "created damaging implications" for them.

Sky Sports News has contacted the Premier League for comment.

Meanwhile, several Man City sponsors are standing by the club in the wake of the guilty verdict.

Lucozade, Kellogg's and Revolut have all told Sky Sports News they are not commenting on the independent commission's findings while the process remains ongoing.

Majestic Wines have refused to comment on whether they will continue their commercial partnership with Manchester City.

Sky Sports News is still awaiting responses from Sure, Durex, EA Sports, CP Company, Britvic, SilentNight, OKX, Gaucho and Champneys.

Etihad Airways statement in full

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dave Reed takes a look the independent commission's key findings on the 'Disguised Funding Scheme' used by Manchester City. The club continue to deny the breaches

A statement said: "Etihad Airways has reviewed the Premier League commission's published opinion relating to the disciplinary proceedings involving Manchester City, together with the Premier League's public communication of its findings.

"Etihad categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements.

"The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings.

"At no time did the Premier League reach out to or engage with Etihad in the process associated with the commission's opinion. Etihad was therefore never given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon in reaching conclusions that may now be interpreted as reflecting adversely on the airline.

"Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly. The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision. The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented.

"Etihad is immensely proud of its longstanding relationship with Manchester City. The Etihad name has been proudly carried by the club and its stadium for many years, as part of a partnership that has connected us with millions of supporters around the world. Our commitment to Manchester City, its supporters and our shared partnership remains strong.

"We stand with the club, its supporters and our wider Etihad community as Manchester City challenges the commission's conclusions through the processes available to it.

"Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests."

The Etihad statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

'Etihad statement shows how Man City will fight back'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News senior reporter Rob Dorsett outlines the possible punishment that could be handed to Man City

Sky Sports News' chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:

"In 2011, Etihad Airways signed a 10-year deal which was worth £400 million, which they have since extended.

"They have released a very strongly worded statement, and in it they say they are seeking legal advice to protect their interests.

"Now, why would they be doing that? The reason behind it is that the judgment from the independent commission on Tuesday said that Manchester City's owners had been inflating their sponsorship income, and that some of City's sponsorship deals were 'sham' deals that weren't real contracts.

"They acknowledged that they weren't named in the published decision, but they say it has 'created damaging implications for Etihad Airways'.

"This just proves that Manchester City are not going to take this lying down. They are absolutely convinced that they have done nothing wrong.

"They don't believe that this has been a fair and impartial process, and we've got the situation now where their principal sponsor has come out and threatened the Premier League with legal action and said that what the commission have done and the published decision yesterday has very damaging implications for them.

"Etihad Airways are a big airline and a big business. They're one of the biggest airlines in the world, worth around £4 billion

"I think this is a very big development as it gives you a sense of how City are going to be fighting back."

What did the independent commission find?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher says he's 'not surprised' that Man City have been found guilty

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven.

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

City: Process was not impartial

A Manchester City statement released on Tuesday read: "Manchester City is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Sports.title: Ronaldo walks out of Portugal camp and vows to reveal 'the truth'
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal's camp in Denmark and vowed to reveal "the truth" behind his departure in due course.

Reports of a rift between Ronaldo and Portugal's new head coach Jorge Jesus emerged after the six-time Ballon d'Or winner was left as an unused substitute in Sunday's Nations League win over Norway.

Jesus, who was Ronaldo's coach at Al Nassr, insisted "there was no incident whatsoever" in his press conference on Wednesday, claiming the star was set to return to training with his team-mates ahead of Thursday's Nations League game against Denmark in Copenhagen.

However, Ronaldo announced he had walked out on Portugal's camp later on Wednesday in a cryptic post on Instagram.

The 41-year-old wrote: "Following the national team manager's press conference, and after a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I decided to leave the national team's training camp.

"In due course, I will tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons behind my departure from the national team, to which I have always been dedicated.

"Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

Spanish ​outlet Marca reported earlier on Wednesday that Ronaldo, who is Portugal's record goalscorer and most-capped player of all time, took a private ‌jet to Madrid.

Ronaldo has not participated in Portugal training since Sunday's Norway win, which saw his replacement, Goncalo Ramos, score.

Image: Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo reacts to a missed chance during the UEFA Nations League, League A match at the Jose Alvalade Stadium in Lisbon

The Al Nassr forward started in Portugal's Nations League-opening home win over Wales last Thursday on a frustrating night for Ronaldo.

He missed a slew of chances and had a second-half effort ruled out by a VAR intervention before being taken off in the 67th minute.

His appearance against Wales was cap number 234 for Portugal, but his decision to leave the camp ahead of Thursday's Denmark game raises huge doubts over whether he will add to that tally in the future.

Ronaldo admitted during this camp with Portugal that he considered international retirement after his disappointing World Cup performance drew widespread criticism.

Across a 23-year international career, Ronaldo has scored 146 times in 234 appearances for Portugal. He has made no secret of wanting to reach 1,000 career goals - his current tally is 979 - but may have to achieve that feat in club football.

Analysis: Ronaldo's latest move leaves 'bad taste'

Sky Sports News chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:

"Another day, another big Cristiano Ronaldo story. He is a man who has been making headlines for 23 years with Portugal. This latest story, though, leaves a bit of a bad taste in the mouth.

"Ronaldo was a substitue in Portugal's game against Norway on Sunday night, which they won 2-1, and he was expecting to come on as a substitute.

"But the Portugal manager Jorge Jesus decided not to use him. He said, 'I planned to use him, but the circumstances weren't right for him to be introduced during that game'.

"Ronaldo appears not to have taken this snub very well because he has not trained with his teammates since that game, he had been training in the gym, and he has now confirmed he has left the camp."

Sports.title: Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball
Sports.content:
“Do you know the question that you are asking me? Today, do you honestly think it is my job to make this kind of question happen …” Cut to the long, painful pause. Chuck in a deep, shaming stare, eyes that have suddenly become death rays of betrayal and disgust and Pep Guardiola himself transformed from a man cheerfully toasting his own FA Cup final victory to a grizzled chief detective addressing a room full of convicted perverts.

Guardiola had the wind entirely at his back at this point, sitting in the Wembley press room an hour after Manchester City’s 6-0 defeat of Watford in May 2019. Success drowns out every other noise in football. To be good is also to be good, noble, virtuous. History is written by the domestic treble winners. Right up until the moment it isn’t.

The question in question was asked by Rob Harris of the Associated Press. It was basically this: information is now in the public domain that suggests Roberto Mancini received a second salary from Abu Dhabi when he was City manager. Mancini was one of Guardiola’s immediate predecessors. So had he, Pep, ever received two salaries?

Even as Harris was asking this he was interrupted by City’s press officer, saying: “We’re not going here, we’re really just not going there.” A simple “no” would have done the job. Instead the exchange ended with another beautifully executed mad-dog stare from Guardiola; not angry, just sad and disappointed. But also, let’s be honest, really angry as well.

Fast forward to this week and a clip has been doing the rounds of the same Rob Harris, now of Sky News, and still the same perky, questing figure. Harris is approaching Ferran Soriano this time, Pep’s key man through that era, and asking the same entirely legitimate things, with a very different outcome. “The Premier League maintains you cheated for nearly a decade … is all this success, as the Premier League says, based on sham contracts?”

There is no glare in return now, no outrage, no flushed moral high ground. “Thank you, thank you,” Soriano mutters, with the look of a man caught shoplifting a Twix at the local primary school fete, followed by a mute, fumbling exit.

Sunlight. Scrutiny. Awkward questions from awkward people. It turns out these are still the best disinfectant. Just as it turns out “the question” was the only one worth asking in that room in 2019. Not that anyone agreed at the time. Predictably enough the comments on social media were about scum, bias, the press as a national embarrassment. Even other journalists held a perfumed kerchief to their noses, suggesting this was all a non-issue because, er, the club had just won a treble.

It turns out the exact opposite was true. It was entirely the right moment to ask this question. That Cup final win came at the end of the main period of shammery. It was in many ways its unholy coronation. There was an industrial-scale embarrassment in that room. But it wasn’t the person asking the questions.

View image in fullscreen The sports correspondent Rob Harris confronts Manchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, in Copenhagen. Photograph: Sky News

There is an obvious problem with the City story at this stage. It’s just too big. There is too much to say, an entire Dickensian multiverse interlayered with oddities and moments of jaw-drop. This is not, repeat not, a media story. And yet it kind of is a media story. After all, it was media scrutiny and the efforts of the hacker Rui Pinto that first winkled it out. As such, Harris deserves his moment of grace, living proof that it’s culturally vital to keep on asking questions, the same Rob Harris I have seen grilling Vladimir Putin about corruption on the hoof in Zurich, and also walking into a pillar at the World Cup in São Paulo while running off with his laptop to ask someone else something else, a man so deeply locked into the news cycle even reinforced stadium infrastructure doesn’t register.

It is also worth mentioning at moments like this Nick Harris, AKA Sporting Intelligence, who has kept going at this story relentlessly despite an unusual degree of abuse, harassment and threats, and who has every right to feel vindicated, part of a world where we can still hold power to account, where a cat can look at a king. But for now the real object of interest in this exchange is, of course, the person on the other end of it. Welcome to the stage once again Pep Guardiola, the public face of the club for the past decade.

What did Pep know? This is more than just football legacy chat. It relates to pretty much everything here, the true nature of the club, of elite football itself, and more basic things like truth, spectacle and human nature. Is believing the assurances of others any kind of defence, given Guardiola was in the perfect position to ask questions of his own? Is any kind of deniability plausible here?

The other significant statement from Guardiola in that time came after City’s two-year ban from the Champions League for a serious breach of Uefa’s financial fair play rules was overturned by the court of arbitration for sport. “We didn’t break the rules. We played the same rules as all the clubs in the Premier League,” was Guardiola’s conclusion, which seemed pretty silly at the time, given time-barring of offences was key to that decision. How does it look now?

To this day Guardiola’s stance remains slavish adherence to the promises of his paymasters, as evidenced by his first statement on the matter on Wednesday. Guardiola says he will be getting through the current unpleasantness with the club and its fans, sticking together as always. But were you together, really? Because City’s fans have some urgent questions of their own now. The majority believed what they were told, and put their faith in the “irrefutable body of evidence” schtick. That ring binder of truth really is going to have to do a lot of instant high-speed kung fu when it finally comes screeching into the appeal room on its trail bike. Not to mention explaining where it’s been over the past three years of information exchange.

Guardiola will face his own questions too, and on a level that will hurt him. The coach who only stays for three or four years stretched this out to a full decade at a club where 80% of that time was spent under a cloud of sham contracts and casual hubris. Through all this he had a deeply personal relationship with his chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. The pair of them are seen whispering tenderly in the recent Prime documentary, in which Guardiola is presented as the most genuine and heartfelt of truth-seekers, a lone castaway on Integrity Island, Jedi-like in a tailored hoodie, eyes brimming with tears as he talks feelings and eternal truths, like a dad in the pub on Christmas Eve.

View image in fullscreen Kevin De Bruyne joined Manchester City from Wolfsburg for £51m in 2015. Photograph: Ash Allen/EPA

In his farewell hagiographies, Guardiola was routinely described as the greatest modern manager. He invented the Messi role for Messi. He reimagined the basic texture of the sport in this country. If this guy isn’t good, nobody’s good. On the other hand, the only logical conclusion on the facts as they stand is that all his City trophies were won with the benefit of concerted macro-cheating.

During the period embraced by the charges, City’s net spend on transfers was, according to Transfermarkt, almost £400m more than Manchester United in second place, and five times as much as Liverpool and Arsenal. From 2016 to 2018, the key period in building the Pep supremacy, they massively outspent every other team. After which they won the league on the final day or by a single point three times. There were little things throughout, like digging out an extra £25m for Kevin De Bruyne, stretching those fine details in your direction. How is it possible not to see that success as unrelated to stolen margins? This is an era that will now be defined by sham-ball, trophies hoisted with a hand behind your back and a thumb on the scale.

Pep can only double down now and ride this to the end. His life’s work, his vast and all-consuming reputation is at stake. “We will get through this together,” he says in Wednesday’s statement. Well, you have no choice now, Pep. Wherever that destination might be.

There are others who must now enter the matrix of who knew what. Soriano, subject of the second Harris grilling, is utterly bound up in this. He’s there right at the start, speaking to us in the leaked emails published by Der Spiegel. “We will need to fight this,” Soriano writes in one leaked memo, “and do it in a way that is not visible.” Hmm. How’s that part working out?

Soriano’s own pre-City past has already been sliced and diced by those who wish to see a pattern. For the record, and as a basic statement of fact, he was at Barcelona during the period when the alleged, unproved, time-barred refereeing scandal happened, but not implicated or punished. He was at Air Spain when it collapsed, but cleared of any wrongdoing. And now he’s been at City in the period of inflated income that has, in effect, left the club dangling over the edge of a cliff. It is certainly an unfortunate chain of coincidence.

Others who will be asked what they knew, or not asked because he’s not going to speak to you, include the owner, Sheikh Mansour. This has an added element. It speaks to the ultimate test, some way down the line, of fitness to run a football club. How is it possible to spend so much family money on this thing, to dole out what are in effect government contracts, and not know the actual process here?

But let’s face it, we all knew really. Weren’t the sham dealings obvious? It was there even in the absence of furious statements of support from the independent directors at First Abu Dhabi Bank, Etihad Airways, Experience Abu Dhabi, Emirates Palace Hotel in Abu Dhabi, Aldar Properties of Abu Dhabi, Masdar Energy of Abu Dhabi, e& telecoms of Abu Dhabi. Come on, chaps. Stand up for the investment. No word either from Dude Wipes, the club’s official male-oriented toilet-paper partner. Although who knows, we may now be entering full Dude Wipes territory.

We knew about the sportswashing aspect, knew that City was a soft-power vehicle for the state of Abu Dhabi, which has a record of alleged – and of course denied – human rights abuses and so on. And of course City’s fans must have known this too, or felt it on some level. It was there cooked into the blueprint, the sense of something brutally high-end but strangely cold.

JG Ballard coined the phrase “the death of affect” to describe the institutionalising of public feeling, rage and triumph commodified as a spectator event. Some champion teams have a strut. City’s basic vibe was always closer to an unceasing V-sign. Perhaps there was even a buried unease here. No one really enjoys being treated as a glove puppet, even when it is done gently and with a hand held discreetly under the desk. On which note, Pep? Any other questions now? Is this a good time?

Sports.title: Rival clubs feel relegating Manchester City to Championship would not be enough
Sports.content:
The Premier League will face pressure from Manchester City’s rivals to push for a sanction that will result in a prolonged absence from the top flight after the club were found guilty of more than 100 charges of financial rule-breaking.

Executives at a number of Premier League clubs have told the Guardian that a points deduction that would relegate City to the Championship for a single season would be insufficient given the scale of what an independent commission described as the club’s “disguised funding scheme” and “sham commercial deals”, which enabled them to artificially inflate their income by £900m between 2009 and 2018.

While the clubs have no involvement in the sanctioning process, the extent of their ill-feeling towards City illustrates the difficulties facing the Premier League as it seeks to conclude a case it began investigating almost eight years ago.

The same independent commission that found City guilty of the vast majority of 115 rule breaches will determine their fate at a sanctions hearing pending the outcome of the club’s appeal, which will be heard by a newly convened independent panel.

Under new Premier League rules introduced this season, the appeal hearing must be concluded within 12 weeks of the deadline on Friday for it to be submitted, with the panel given a further 30 days to deliver its judgment, meaning a decision should be reached by the end of January next year.

While not confirmed, the sanctions hearing could take place concurrently during the same time period, although it will not be published pending the outcome of the appeal. City could also subsequently appeal against the sanctions imposed by the commission.

It is also possible that the club could delay the process further by arguing that the Premier League’s new expedited timescales should not apply given they were only introduced this season, whereas the charges against them are historic.

The club has already succeeded in delaying the publication of the commission’s “core decision”, which was finally released on Tuesday following an appeal procedure.

As prosecutor, the Premier League is permitted to petition for its preferred punishment at the sanctions hearing, with City also pleading their case, before a decision is taken by the commission.

The Premier League’s position on sanctioning will be taken independently of the clubs by the board of directors comprising the chair, Alison Brittain, the chief executive, Richard Masters, and three independent non-executive directors: Mai Fyfield, Dharmash Mistry and Matthew Ryder KC.

View image in fullscreen Sheikh Mansour (centre) and Khaldoon al-Mubarak (right) have been Manchester City’s owner and chair respectively for the whole period covered by the rule breaches. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The commission has a wide range of sanctions at its disposal including points deductions, transfer embargos and expulsion from the Premier League. Given the scale of City’s offences, according to the independent panel, there are no comparable precedents. City say they are “innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case”.

In the first successful profitability and sustainability rules prosecution, of Everton three years ago for a £19.5m overspend, the Premier League pushed for the club to be docked 12 points in the sanctioning hearing, with the independent commission ultimately docking them 10 points, which was reduced to six on appeal.
