World.title: Liberia: President Boakai’s Name Drags In Courtroom Record In Saudi Rice Trial
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s name entered the courtroom record Monday as former General Services Agency (GSA) Director-General Mary T. Broh testified in the Saudi-donated rice trial, linking a letter from Boakai’s transition activities to a request for rice for young people working on a national cleanup campaign.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Broh, a subpoenaed defense witness for former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and other defendants, told Criminal Court “C” that Kemayah’s intervention in the rice matter was intended to “rescue the rice” and described the indictment against her and other officials as “character assassination.”



Her testimony offered a different account from the prosecution’s theory that the movement and distribution of the Saudi-donated rice formed part of an unlawful scheme.

The remaining defendants face charges including theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy.

The Saudi donation consisted of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice intended for disaster victims and vulnerable communities. Prosecutors allege that 25,054 bags, valued at approximately US$425,918, were unlawfully diverted or could not be accounted for.

Boakai’s Name Enters the Record

One of the most significant portions of Broh’s testimony concerned President Boakai’s transition activities.

Broh testified that John-Charuk Siafa, now Monrovia City Mayor, approached her while coordinating a cleanup campaign associated with Boakai’s inauguration.

According to Broh, Siafa told her he had been appointed by then-President-elect Boakai to coordinate the campaign and showed her his appointment letter.

She said the letter directed Siafa to contact her because she was considered a source of assistance for mobilization.

Broh testified that she later became concerned when young people participating in the cleanup complained that they had nothing to eat. She said she contacted Siafa and instructed him to write the Ministry of Internal Affairs requesting rice.

According to Broh, Siafa subsequently wrote then-Internal Affairs Minister Varney Sirleaf, after which rice was made available.

Broh’s testimony did not establish that President Boakai personally ordered the distribution of the Saudi rice. Rather, her account placed the transition-related cleanup campaign and Siafa’s appointment at the beginning of a chain of events through which rice was requested for “hungry cleanup campaign workers.”

‘Kemayah Was Rescuing the Rice’

Broh also challenged the prosecution’s characterization of Kemayah’s involvement.

She testified that Kemayah contacted her about the Saudi-funded rice and that a meeting was subsequently held at the GSA involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Internal Affairs, the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) and GSA.

Because of Kemayah’s official engagements and travel, Broh said he designated Deputy Foreign Minister Thelma Duncan Sawyer to participate in his place.

According to Broh, the institutions agreed to work together and minutes were taken during the meeting.

She characterized Kemayah’s intervention as an effort to “rescue” the rice.

Broh said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs became involved because the donation was connected to Liberia’s bilateral relationship with Saudi Arabia.

She maintained that the participation of Foreign Affairs, Internal Affairs, NDMA and GSA was part of an institutional effort to secure and manage the humanitarian commodity.

GSA Transfer Defended

Broh also defended the transfer of 13,895 bags of rice from NDMA to GSA, a movement that prosecutors have placed at the center of their case.

She testified that it was agreed through an interagency mandate that the remaining Saudi rice be moved to GSA for storage until further notice.

She also argued that GSA had a statutory responsibility to serve as custodian of government property and maintained warehouses for commodities and emergency supplies.

Had she known about the rice earlier, Broh testified, she would have recommended that it be stored at GSA because NDMA lacked adequate facilities for such a large quantity.

According to her, this has been the practice with several previous donations to the government. She cited, as an example, 60,000 bags of rice donated by the Government of the People’s Republic of China, which she said were stored by the GSA and subsequently distributed to beneficiaries.

She said the rice was inventoried upon arrival at GSA and that subsequent releases were subject to documentation and a gate-pass system.

According to Broh, requesting organizations were required to provide supporting documents, while information about trucks, including drivers’ names, telephone numbers and license plates, was recorded before rice could leave the warehouse.

She further testified that she and Sawyer used personal resources to facilitate the transfer, including securing trucks from the Liberia Electricity Corporation, and that no government funds were used for transportation.

‘The Indictment Is Character Assassination’

Broh stood by her earlier description of the indictment as “character assassination.”

“I sincerely mean what I said,” she told the court.

She maintained that officials were acting within their respective mandates to receive and distribute commodities based on requests.

She also pointed to documents she said she provided to investigators, questioning why she would voluntarily turn over records that could help trace the rice if she intended to steal it.

The 1,050-Bag Dispute

Broh also addressed allegations involving approximately 1,050 bags of rice, connecting the quantity to the Boakai transition cleanup campaign.

She testified that young people working long hours on the campaign complained about a lack of food. According to her, Siafa approached her for assistance after being appointed to coordinate the cleanup.

Broh said she helped facilitate communication with government institutions, after which a request was made to Internal Affairs and rice was released.

Her testimony sought to place the disputed quantity within a government-related request rather than a personal diversion.

Johnson Challenges Prosecution’s Accounting

For his part, former Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Momolu Johnson testified Tuesday, challenging aspects of the prosecution’s accounting of the rice.

Johnson questioned how certain quantities were treated in the government’s case, including 720 bags that he argued had not been properly exhibited to support the stealing allegation.

He also cited figures he said were presented to the defense, including 12,095 bags under relevant control and 2,281 bags remaining at GSA.

His testimony formed part of the defense effort to challenge both the prosecution’s calculations and its theory of criminal intent.

The competing figures have emerged as a central issue in the trial.

The indictment states that the original donation consisted of 29,412 bags. Prosecution evidence has placed 11,200 bags at GSA initially and another 13,895 bags transferred from NDMA, producing a reported 25,095 bags in GSA custody.

The prosecution has alleged that 25,054 bags were diverted or could not be accounted for, while defense witnesses have introduced additional figures involving distributions, pre-positioned rice and quantities remaining in storage.

The defense is using those discrepancies to challenge the prosecution’s accounting and argue that the movement of the rice through government institutions does not, by itself, establish criminal intent.

The defendants have pleaded not guilty and remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

The trial continues today, Wednesday, September 30, with the continuation of defendant Johnson’s testimony.

World.title: Liberia: Support the Women of the Lofa Women Weaving Center
World.content:
Illustration: Women weave Lofa Cloth from local cotton into blankets, bags and garments.

A short video from James Dorbor Jallah, Commissioner General of the Liberia Revenue Authority, made my day.

By Axel M. Addy

It showed the Lofa Women Weaving Center open again. The center started as an idea while I was Minister of Commerce and Industry. For years after 2018, it stood idle. Now the Government of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has brought it back. I thank the President and every official, community leader and weaver who kept pushing for this day.



For me, this is personal. I know the women, the land and the promise behind that building.

One question

The project began with one question. How can Liberia turn a product we treasure into a steady income for rural women?

Lofa has woven country cloth for generations. Families wear it and keep it. Yet the women who made it earned little from their skill. We wanted to change that. We wanted a Liberian brand called Lofa Cloth, with quality standards, legal protection and buyers at home and abroad.

Help from Japan

The answer started in Tokyo.

The Government of Japan invited me on an official visit. I met members of the Diet, Japan’s parliament, and made the case for Liberia’s small businesses. Our Japanese friends listened, and they acted.

In 2014, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry established the Liberia Innovation Fund for Entrepreneurship, the LIFE Fund, under a grant from the Government of Japan. Japan signed the Note Verbale on April 22, 2014. The fund had an approved budget of US$665,000. It supported three initiatives: the E-Plus youth entrepreneurship program, the Liberian Marketplace at the Nancy Doe Market, and the Lofa Women Weaving Center.

The road to Kolahun

After Japan, my team and I travelled to Kolahun. The Superintendent hosted us. We sat with weavers, producers and community leaders. We asked how much cloth they made, what they needed and where a center could stand.

The elders of Lofa answered with a gift. They donated land from a 25-acre site for the center. The people of Bolahun and Kolahun, in Liberia’s cotton belt, worked together to make it possible. That cooperation showed the community owned this project from the first day.

We also gave the women a challenge. We asked them to create two or three new colour patterns. We asked them to make blankets, throws and placemats for the national MSME Conference.

They exceeded every expectation. At the MSME Conference, their products won a US$5,000 prize. At the Made in Liberia Trade Fair, their work sold out.

I learned a lesson in Kolahun that still guides me. Liberia does not lack talent. We lack organized production, design support, finance, market access and steady follow-through.

Munah Pelham’s vision

The late Hon. Munah Pelham saw this early. As a designer and model, she brought Liberian designers together for a country cloth fashion show at the 2014 MSME Conference. Designers made handbags, garments and accessories from the cloth. The show proved a traditional fabric could compete in modern fashion and remain Liberian. I remember her energy with gratitude.

What we built

The center was part of the Rural Industrial Promotion Program for Economic Empowerment (RIPE). Its goal was to organize rural women into cooperatives of 50 to 150 members. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry provided US$231,000 for construction through the LIFE Fund, under the Japanese grant.

The design included:

A showroom for sales and exhibitions

A tailoring hall for at least 10 tailors

A weaving hall for at least 30 weavers

A cotton receiving and processing hall for at least 5 machines

Apprenticeship training for young weavers

The building went up. After 2018, it lacked the management, funding and market support it needed. The plan also relied on several ministries. The Ministry of Agriculture would support cotton farming. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry would connect the center to industrial policy, design and markets. When that coordination stopped, the center stopped too.

The next task: build the market

Phase one built the center. Phase two must build demand.

Liberia needs a national strategy for Lofa Cloth. It should cover cotton supply, weaving capacity, quality standards, modern design, cooperative management and reliable markets.

The Buy Liberian, Build Liberia agenda gives us a platform. The Wear Your Pride campaign gives us a simple action. If government officials wear Liberian-made clothing every Friday, weavers, tailors and designers gain regular customers. Citizens see that national pride includes buying Liberian.

Government can go further. Use Lofa Cloth for national gifts, official delegations and state events. Ask our embassies and diaspora groups to promote it abroad. Encourage hotels, airlines, universities and large firms to buy it.

The industry also needs investment in cotton processing, modern and manual looms, training, packaging, quality certification, e-commerce, trade fairs and geographical indication protection.

At a WTO Public Forum, I met a group from Burkina Faso that builds manual looms and trains women across Africa. Liberia should partner with African producers like them. Appropriate tools can multiply what our weavers produce.

Every Liberian has a role

The center can employ hundreds of women. It can create work for cotton farmers, transporters, designers, tailors, traders, photographers and exporters.

Government must lead with policy and resources. Businesses must invest and buy. Designers must innovate. The diaspora must promote and purchase. Development partners must support export readiness. Consumers must choose Liberian.

Lofa Cloth carries the history and skill of Liberian women. With steady support, it can travel from Kolahun to Monrovia, to the region and to the world.

So I ask every Liberian: Wear Your Pride. When you buy Lofa Cloth, you support a woman at her loom in Kolahun. You support a farmer, a tailor and a designer. You Buy Liberian, and you help Build Liberia.

World.title: Why the War in Ukraine Is Making Rice More Expensive in Liberia
World.content:
When we hear about the war in Ukraine, it can feel distant – something happening far away that doesn’t touch our lives in Liberia. It is tempting to view it as a political dispute between foreign nations that has little to do with the daily realities in Monrovia, Gbarnga, or Harper. But in today’s deeply interconnected global economy, no nation is an island. What happens in the Black Sea directly affects market stalls, kitchen tables, and family budgets here in Liberia.

By Zoltan Szalai, contributing writer

Before the war, Ukraine was known as the “breadbasket of the world.” It supplied 15 percent of the world’s corn, 10 percent of its wheat, and half of all sunflower oil. These are not just numbers; they are the ingredients in the food we eat every day. But now, Russian attacks are destroying Ukrainian ports, farms, and grain storage facilities. Ships carrying food cannot move freely. Millions of tonnes of grain sit trapped, at risk of spoiling. Farmers who cannot sell their crops this year may not have the money to plant next year’s harvest. If this continues, food shortages and high prices could stretch well into 2027.



For Liberia, this is a serious problem. While Liberian farmers grow rice, they do not produce enough to feed everyone. Here in Liberia, we rely on imports for rice, wheat, cooking oil, and even fuel. When global food supplies shrink, prices rise – and those higher costs are passed to us consumers. That means the bag of rice you buy at the market costs more. The loaf of bread for your children’s breakfast is pricier. The cooking oil you need for every meal becomes harder to afford. For families already struggling with rising living costs, this is not just an inconvenience – it is a crisis.

The impact goes beyond food. When shipping and fuel prices increase, everything becomes more expensive. The cost of farming goes up. The price of transporting goods rises. Inflation stretches household budgets even thinner. Globally, over 645 million people now face hunger. Liberia, like many import-dependent nations, remains highly exposed to these disruptions. At stake is not merely the challenge is not just fighting against high prices; it is a fight for one’s ability to survive.

Food should never be used as a weapon. Yet right now, attacks on Ukraine’s food infrastructure are doing exactly that – using hunger as leverage in a war. The European Union has created alternative routes, called “Solidarity Lanes,” to help move Ukraine’s food by land and river. But these cannot replace the Black Sea, which normally handles 90 percent of Ukraine’s exports. Without safe shipping lanes, the world’s food supply remains at risk.

Liberia cannot afford to ignore this. The international community must take urgent action. First, the attacks on grain facilities and commercial ships must stop. These are not military targets; they are the sources of food for millions of people. Second, there must be guarantees for safe passage for civilian cargo vessels carrying essential supplies. Third, and most importantly, the only real solution is a lasting ceasefire and peace. Until then, families in Liberia and across the world will continue to pay the price.

This is not just Ukraine’s war – it is a crisis that touches us all. When The European Union demands an end to attacks on food supplies, we are not just standing up for Ukraine; we are protecting our own ability to feed our families. No parent should have to choose between putting food on the table and paying for their children’s school fees. No child should go to bed hungry because of a war they had no part in.

The world is connected, and our struggles are connected. What happens in Ukraine affects the price of rice in Monrovia, the cost of bread in Gbarnga, and the availability of cooking oil in Harper. The time to act is now – before more families are pushed to the brink. We may be thousands of miles away, but this fight is ours too.

About the author

Zoltan Szalai serves as the Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of the Delegation of the European Union to the Republic of Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: MODA Distances Itself from Agriculture Minister Nuetah, Says He Is Not and Has Never Been a Member
World.content:
According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

GBARNGA, Bong County – The Movement for Democratic Alliance (MODA) has clarified that the Minister of Agriculture, Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah, is not a member of the organization. It also rejected claims that his support for a youth training initiative in Bong County signals a political alliance or an effort to form a political party.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

In a press statement issued Tuesday in Gbarnga, MODA said it had taken note of recent public discussions and media reports that sought to link the Minister to the Movement and to present his backing of a youth skills-development program as evidence of political collaboration.



“MODA considers it important to place the facts on record and to correct any misunderstanding surrounding the matter,” said Acting Chairman Lawrence N. Yallah, who signed the statement.

“Not a Political Party”

MODA first clarified its own status, stating that it is “not a political party” but a “political movement.” It then addressed Minister Nuetah’s relationship with the group directly.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

The Movement said it therefore “rejects any representation suggesting that the Minister is a member, official, political leader, financier, or representative” of MODA.

Describing itself as a people-centered movement founded on democratic participation, integrity, unity, equity, inclusion, public service and sustainable development, MODA said it remains open to working with individuals, institutions, organizations and public officials when such engagement serves the legitimate interests of the Liberian people. However, it cautioned that cooperation on a specific development project should not be read as political membership, affiliation or endorsement.

Origin of the Excavator Training Slots

The statement traced the controversy to July 14, 2026, when Minister Nuetah made five excavator-training slots available for young people from Bong County. MODA said this followed an appeal from its Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Jomah B. Dolo, for more opportunities for the county’s youth.

The Movement described the slots as an initial contribution toward skills development.

The five slots reportedly drew 252 applicants, who then went through an independent vetting and selection process.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process

MODA stressed that the Minister did not personally select the five beneficiaries and did not set up any political recruitment process through the Movement.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process.

The Movement added that it was “even more excited” that all five selected individuals turned out to be supporters of the Unity Party, even though party affiliation was not a requirement for applying.

The five young people are expected to begin their excavator training at For Life Zoe in the coming days. MODA said it regards the initiative “strictly” as an opportunity for young Liberians to acquire practical skills that can improve their employment prospects and economic participation.

It noted that the Ministry of Agriculture has itself publicly emphasized youth empowerment, agricultural mechanization and practical skills development as part of its broader agenda.

MODA Dismisses New Party Speculation

The Movement also responded to commentary suggesting that the Minister’s support for the training slots through MODA means he has established a political party to challenge President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s potential bid for a second term.

MODA dismissed the suggestion in strong terms, describing it as “blatant mendacity coming from the mouth of back-door politicians who are afraid of youth progression.”

The Movement called on individuals, commentators, political actors and media practitioners to distinguish between a development initiative and political affiliation.

“A public official providing opportunities for young people does not, by itself, establish membership in MODA or demonstrate an intention to form or lead a political party,” the statement said.

MODA further stated that Minister Nuetah’s political affiliation and future decisions are matters that should be addressed through his own public statements and actions, not attributed to the Movement.

“For the avoidance of doubt, MODA does not claim Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah as a member of the Movement, and the Movement has no authority to speak on his behalf regarding his political affiliation or future political plans,” the statement said. It added that the group has known the Minister only as a people-centered leader, not through “the opinions of agent provocateurs.”

Outlining its position, MODA said the country’s political and development environment should allow people and institutions to cooperate on matters of national and community interest without every act of cooperation being treated as partisan politics. It encouraged public discussion to remain grounded in facts, particularly where individuals, political organizations, public officials and opportunities for young people are concerned.

The Movement also urged everyone discussing the excavator-training initiative to respect the integrity of the 252 applicants and the five young people chosen. “Their opportunity should not be reduced to political speculation,” the statement said.

MODA reaffirmed its commitment to its stated principles and to engaging anyone prepared to support initiatives that advance the interests of the Liberian people, noting again that such engagement does not automatically create political membership or affiliation.

It pledged to continue supporting efforts that expand opportunities for young Liberians, promote skills development, encourage transparency and contribute to national development.

World.title: Liberia: Beyond Survival: WONGOSOL Gives FGM Survivors Dignity Today and Livelihoods for Tomorrow
World.content:
MONROVIA — For women and girls who have survived female genital mutilation (FGM) and other forms of gender-based violence, the road to recovery often extends far beyond the immediate trauma.

By Patience M. Jones

It can mean having access to basic hygiene supplies, clothing and personal-care items while receiving support—and, for some survivors, having the means to earn an income and rebuild their lives.



That is the focus of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, implemented by the Women NGOs Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL) with support from the United Nations Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women.

As part of the project’s third consignment of support, WONGOSOL is distributing more than 600 dignity kits to FGM and gender-based violence (GBV) survivors through one-stop centers across six counties, while also preparing livelihood assistance for 365 women trained in vocational skills, business management and Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) approaches.

Speaking to journalists on Friday, WONGOSOL Executive Director Esther S. David Yango said the initiative is designed to address both the immediate needs of survivors and the economic challenges that can leave women vulnerable.

“The FGM project connects immediate survivor support with long-term economic empowerment, providing dignity today while helping women and communities build safer, more resilient and sustainable futures,” Yango said.

A Kit Designed to Restore Dignity

The dignity packages are intended to provide practical assistance to survivors during periods of vulnerability.

According to the project team, the packages include toothpaste and toothbrushes, sanitary pads, towels, grease, slippers, bath soap and lappa.

Separate packages are being prepared for younger survivors, with additional items such as snacks and toys intended to make their experience at one-stop centers less distressing.

Clothing, including blouses and dresses, will also be provided to survivors.

Jeneba M. Vessellie, Project Officer of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, explained that the materials are meant to respond to survivors’ immediate needs while they access health, psychosocial, legal and protection services.

The intervention, officials said, recognizes that recovery is not only about medical or legal assistance, but also about helping survivors maintain dignity during a difficult period.

From Training to Economic Independence

While the dignity kits address immediate needs, the livelihood component is intended to provide a longer-term pathway toward economic independence.

The project has trained 365 women in livelihood and vocational skills, business management and VSLA approaches. The beneficiaries include FGM practitioners, FGM survivors, single mothers, youth and women leaders.

Livelihood support will include materials for activities such as soap making, tailoring, pastry and baking, among other income-generating activities.

The project team said the assistance is intended to help trained women put their skills into practice, establish or strengthen businesses and build economic resilience after the project ends.

For women involved in agriculture, support will also include farm materials and tools.

The program team cited women survivors involved in agriculture in Bong County as among those expected to receive agricultural support.

The project also links livelihood support to savings.

Officials said beneficiaries trained in savings and loan approaches will be able to save from the income generated through their activities, helping them sustain their businesses beyond the life of the project.

Reaching Communities Across Six Counties

The Liberia Fight FGM Project is being implemented in 38 communities across Bomi, Bong, Gbarpolu, Grand Cape Mount, Margibi and Montserrado Counties, in partnership with local organizations.

The project has also established 40 community coalitions comprising 600 members who have been trained to advocate for the protection of women and girls against harmful practices, including FGM and sexual and gender-based violence.

The coalitions are also supporting advocacy for the passage of the Women and Girls Protection Act.

The implementing partners include Women Care Initiative (WOCI) in Bomi; Community Women Peace Initiative (CWPI) in Bong; Paramount Young Women Initiative (PAYWO) in Gbarpolu; Sister Hands Liberia (SHL) in Grand Cape Mount; Women Education and Development Organization of Liberia (WEDOL) in Margibi; and WEPS and INSURED in Montserrado.

Two Needs, One Intervention

For WONGOSOL, the distribution represents two connected sides of survivor support.

The dignity kits respond to immediate needs, helping survivors meet basic personal-care and hygiene needs and restore a measure of dignity during vulnerable periods.

The livelihood assistance, meanwhile, addresses longer-term economic vulnerability by helping women transform training into sustainable economic opportunities.

Together, the interventions form what WONGOSOL describes as an integrated approach to prevention, protection and women’s economic empowerment.

The project, which began in October 2023, was initially scheduled to end in September 2026. A five-month no-cost extension has now extended implementation through February 28, 2027.

For the women at the center of the intervention, the assistance is therefore about more than receiving a package or business materials.

It is about having something to meet a need today and, through skills and economic opportunities, something to build on tomorrow.

World.title: Mwanza Demands ECZ Account For Suspended Vote Count And Stolen Mandevu Ballots
World.content:
Democratic Progressive Party president Antonio Mwanza has demanded that the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) publish a detailed report on why it suspended the counting and announcement of results during the general election. He said the credibility of the process will stay in question until the commission accounts for what happened in those missing hours.

Mr Mwanza said he had no doubt that President Hakainde Hichilema won the election and would always have crossed the 50 per cent plus one threshold. His quarrel, he said, was not with the winner but with the way the contest was run, and with an electoral body he believes cannot act independently because of how it is set up.

“The outcome of the election was never in doubt,” he said. “But the election itself raised very critical issues that we must address going forward.”

The first of those issues was the suspension of counting on what the commission described as security grounds. He said the ECZ had never told the public how widespread those concerns were, nor what took place between the moment counting stopped and the moment it resumed.

“The Electoral Commission of Zambia did not give us a detailed account of what happened between this period,” Mr Mwanza said.

He then turned to Mandevu constituency, where no election was held after the commission said ballot papers and other electoral materials had been stolen. Weeks after the polls, he said, the public still did not know whether anyone had been apprehended for the theft.

He also raised the death of a Socialist Party election agent. He said neither the commission nor the Zambia Police had explained what happened to him, and warned that the same failures would return at the next national vote unless all three matters were answered.

“If we don’t get to the bottom of this and to the extent of how widespread it was and to what extent it affected the outcome of the elections, we will have a repeat of this in 2031,” he said.

Mr Mwanza was careful to separate the question of who won from the question of how the result was produced. He pointed to the Christian Churches Monitoring Group (CCMG), whose members include the Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection, the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Council of Churches in Zambia and the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia. He said he respected its finding that the President won.

“There’s no doubt about him winning the election,” he said. “We’re talking about the credibility of the process.”

For the opposition leader, the root of the problem lies in how commissioners are appointed. ECZ commissioners are appointed by the President, who is also a candidate in the same election the commission is meant to referee, and he said that placed the body in an impossible position.

“It is extremely difficult for the Electoral Commission of Zambia to act in an independent, impartial manner when they are appointed by a President who also happens to be part of the election process,” he said.

His party is proposing that commissioners be selected by an independent and impartial body through an accountable and transparent process, with their appointments ratified by Parliament. Only then, he said, would the commission have the confidence to enforce the rules against everyone, including the governing party.

He said the conflict showed most plainly in the commission’s failure to enforce the Electoral Code of Conduct on media coverage. The code requires public media to give equal, fair and balanced coverage to all contestants. Yet in his view every state outlet, from ZNBC to ZANIS, Times of Zambia and Zambia Daily Mail, leaned towards the ruling party.

“It is not the first time,” Mr Mwanza said. “It has always been like this from time immemorial. And this must change.”

He blamed the editorial policies of publicly owned media houses, which he said left their journalists no room to give the opposition fair and balanced airtime or space.

The second structural failure, he said, was the campaign timetable. Mr Mwanza said he accepted its purpose, which is to keep rival presidential candidates apart and prevent clashes. The problem was that the sitting President, who is also a candidate, is exempt from it.

“The President is given a free will to campaign and to be anywhere he wants,” he said. “That disadvantages the other candidates who don’t have that free will.”

He said opposition candidates were at times turned away from areas because their timetables placed them elsewhere. In a campaign of about 90 days, where every hour counts, he described enforcement of the electoral code as “extremely selective”.

“He cannot be a candidate but is given preferential treatment by virtue of him being the President,” he said. “The election must be free, must be fair, and everybody must be on an equal footing.”

Mr Mwanza made three proposals. First, the ECZ must publish its report on the suspended count and the scale of the threats it cited. Second, commissioners must be appointed by an independent body and confirmed by Parliament. Third, the timetable must bind every presidential candidate, including the incumbent, and public media must be compelled to give all contestants fair coverage.

He added that the commission was also under-resourced, lacking the money and staff to carry out voter education across the country. Reform of its governing law, he said, must come with the funding to match.

The Democratic Progressive Party did not field candidates in the general election. Mr Mwanza said registering the party took more than a year, leaving it too little time, manpower and money to mount a credible challenge against the United Party for National Development (UPND).

The party has instead begun preparing for 2031, and Mr Mwanza said electoral reform would be central to that effort. His demand for a full report now sits with a commission that has yet to publicly account for the suspended count, the stolen Mandevu materials or the death of the Socialist Party agent.

World.title: Zambia keeps changing drivers and never fixes the car
World.content:
Zambia keeps changing drivers and never fixes the car

In April 2017, police broke into the Lusaka home of the country’s main opposition leader in the dead of night, fired tear gas and carried him away on a charge of treason. His offence was that his motorcade had failed to give way to the presidential convoy on a road in Western Province. Hakainde Hichilema spent more than four months in custody before the State quietly dropped the case.

Nine years later, that same man is President, freshly returned for a second term. And the runner-up in the election he has just won, Brian Mundubile, sits in custody on a treason charge, with a sedition charge added for good measure. The State says it is still gathering evidence.

If there is a single image that captures what has gone wrong in Zambian politics, it is this one. The faces change. The furniture stays exactly where it was.

Antonio Mwanza, the Democratic Progressive Party leader who sat out the polls, put it bluntly in a long radio interview this week. There are no good men when it comes to power, he said, only good institutions or bad ones. It is the most useful sentence any Zambian politician has spoken since the results were declared, and it should be read as an indictment of every party that has ever held State House, including the one Mr Mwanza once served.

Consider the record. Kenneth Kaunda built the University of Zambia and the University Teaching Hospital, and then built a one-party state to protect himself. Frederick Chiluba rode to power on the promise of multiparty freedom and then tried to buy himself a third term, until churches, lawyers and students stopped him in 2001. The Patriotic Front turned the Public Order Act into a padlock on opposition rallies. The UPND spent a decade on the receiving end of that padlock and promised, loudly, never to use it.

Now look at what has happened since polling day.

On polling night, the Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended counting and the announcement of results on security grounds. Counting later resumed, and a clear winner was declared. Nobody seriously disputes that President Hichilema won. Church monitors said so. Mr Mwanza says so. This column says so.

But nobody has explained what happened in the hours when the count stood still. Nobody has told the voters of Mandevu, who did not vote at all because ballot papers were stolen, whether a single thief has been caught. And on 24 August, the last day on which any losing candidate could file a petition challenging the result, the courts of the Republic were shut on “security reasons” that have never been set out in public.

The Law Association of Zambia said it best: the right of access to the courts is meaningless if the courts can simply be closed at the precise moment citizens most need them. That is not a partisan complaint. It is a description of a door slammed in the face of the law itself.

Then came the arrests. Opposition leaders, former Members of Parliament and campaign figures have been picked up, some in circumstances their lawyers and families only learned of later. Where the law requires an appearance before a court within 48 hours, detainees have waited. Where public figures with fixed addresses could have been served a simple call-out, the police have preferred the drama of a night arrest.

The Government says it had been investigating some of the accused for three years. Yet the prosecutions chief has been quoted as saying the State is still collecting evidence. Both statements cannot comfortably be true. If the evidence exists, put it before a judge. If it does not, open the cell door. There is no third option in a constitutional democracy.

And now, as if on cue, comes the oldest song in the Zambian hymn book. A ruling party Member of Parliament has floated the removal of presidential term limits. Cadres have taken up the chorus. The line, as always, is that it is not the President asking. It is “the people”. When that fails to persuade, the line becomes “let Parliament decide”, which is another way of saying “let us decide, because we have the numbers”.

Zambians have been here before. They were asked about term limits by the Mung’omba Constitution Review Commission and said two terms. They said it again in 2001, in the streets, in green ribbons. They have said it at every review since. A people who have answered the same question the same way for a quarter of a century are not confused. They are being ignored.

To his credit, President Hichilema has said on more than one platform that nobody deserves a third term. He should say it again, now, from the podium, in words that leave no room for interpretation. Silence from the Head of State is not neutrality. In this country, silence has always been read as permission.

What makes all of this so dispiriting is not that the UPND has turned out to be wicked. It is that it has turned out to be ordinary. It has inherited a presidency with the power to appoint judges, electoral commissioners, ambassadors, police chiefs and almost every head of a public institution, and, like every party before it, it has found that power far too comfortable to surrender.

The ECZ is appointed by the President, who is also a candidate. The prosecutions office answers to a system the President heads. The public broadcaster, funded by every taxpayer, tilts towards whoever holds State House, as it has done since independence. The courts can be closed with a notice and a phrase. None of these arrangements was invented by the current Government. All of them have been used by it.

That is the real crisis. Zambia keeps changing the driver and leaving the car exactly as it is: faulty brakes, a steering wheel that pulls to one side and a speedometer the driver is allowed to reset. Each new driver swears he will fix it. Each one discovers that the faulty car suits him perfectly well while he is the one behind the wheel.

The cadres understand this better than anyone. Mr Mwanza tells of friends who walked Lusaka’s streets with him five years ago and are now building blocks of flats in Silverest and posing with pigs and fish ponds. We have seen this before too. The MMD had its instant businessmen. The PF had its instant businessmen. Where are they now? Their fortunes lasted exactly as long as their party did.

There is a lesson in that for the UPND, and it is not a moral lesson. It is a practical one. Every law passed for comfort in power becomes a weapon in the hands of the next Government. The treason charge that held Mr Hichilema in 2017 is the same instrument now holding Mr Mundubile. The cyber laws the UPND once denounced are now turned on its own detractors. A Constitution amended to suit one President will one day serve a President the UPND fears.

So what should be done?

First, take the appointment of electoral commissioners away from the President and give it to an independent panel, with confirmation by Parliament. Second, bind every presidential candidate, the incumbent included, to the same campaign timetable and the same rules on public media. Third, give the judiciary financial independence so that no administrator can lock its doors on a deadline day. Fourth, require the prosecution to have a case before it takes a liberty. And fifth, leave Article 106 exactly where it is.

None of this requires the UPND to lose power. It only requires the party to govern as though it one day will.

President Hichilema has five years left. He knows, better than any President before him, what it feels like to sit in a cell on a charge the State cannot prove. He can be the leader who finally fixes the car. Or he can be the next name on a long list of men who were certain the rules would always favour them.

Zambia has already seen how that list ends.

By Kingsley Mwila

World.title: Zambia, UK to enhance trade relations
World.content:
Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane, says Government is open to more trade and investment between the United Kingdom and Zambia.

Dr Musokotwane says the United Kingdom and the Zambian government have long standing cooperation with the UK having several investments in the country.

He said this when British Trade Commissioner, Alastair Long and British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon paid a courtesy call on him at his office where they had a cordial discussion to enhance cooperation and open investment opportunities for Zambia.

Dr Musokotwane said the discussion was centered on specific investment areas adding that Britain has expertise and capital to invest in Zambia.

He stated that various proposals have been put across to the British High Commission delegation.

“This comes at a time when the focus in Zambia is how to get the economy to grow so that young people can get jobs as well as business opportunities for Zambians,” he said.

Dr Musokotwane added that the British business community can take advantage of some of the targets on the Grow Zambia Agenda that include beef, mining, sugar and forestry.

And British Trade Commissioner, Alastair Long, said the United Kingdom is committed to investing and contributing to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Long noted that Zambia has great potential to grow with the coming of the Grow Zambia Agenda being spearheaded by President Hakainde Hichilema.

He further said Zambia has taken some significant steps to stabilize the economy and prepare itself for a bright future.

“The UK is really proud of our relationship, we are also incredibly proud of the investment relationship,” Mr Long said.

And British High Commissioner to Zambia, Rebecca Terzeon said UK will continue to invest in Zambia saying British international investments in the country date back to many decades ago.

World.title: Farmers advised to prepare for anticipated El Nino
World.content:
The Ministry of Agriculture has called on farmers in Northern Province to urgently start implementing mitigation strategies in anticipation for the forecast El Nino weather pattern for the 2026/2027 farming season.

Seed Control and Certification Institute Senior Seeds Officer, Zombe Sikazwe has warned that the expected El Niño conditions could bring prolonged dry spells and erratic rainfall, posing a threat to crop yields and national food security.

Ms Sikazwe said the Ministry of Agriculture has already begun rolling out awareness campaigns and technical support programmes to encourage farmers to start growing climate resilient crops as a mitigating factor.

“We are urging all farmers to take proactive steps now and this includes adopting drought-tolerant seed varieties, practicing conservation farming, and ensuring efficient water management,” she said.

She urged farmers to work closely with extension officers who are being deployed to their areas to provide guidance on soil moisture conservation, early planting, and crop diversification.

Ms Sikazwe stated that the meteorological forecasts are indicating a high likelihood of reduced rainfall in several regions, which could impact maize, groundnut, and soybeans production if no preventive measures are taken.

“Our goal is to safeguard livelihoods and ensure that Zambia remains food secure despite the challenges posed by climate change, officers are in your areas heed to their advice on soil moisture, conservation and early planting practices,” she said.

Ms Sikazwe also encouraged farmers to work closely with local agricultural offices for timely weather updates and technical advice as they are preparing their fields.

And James Bukankala, a farmer from Mulanshi Agricultural Camp in Kasama District has commended the Seed Control and Certification Institute for its timely call to prepare for the anticipated El Nino condition.

Mr Bukankala said the call for agricultural producers to adopt mitigation measures is important as it aims at safeguarding crop yields and livestock health in the face of potential droughts and erratic rainfall patterns.

He expressed appreciation to the Ministry of Agriculture for the proactive stance, noting that early guidance allows them to plan ahead.

“This advice is a lifeline for us, we can now invest in drought-resistant seed varieties, improve water storage, and adjust planting schedules before the rains,” he said.

He appealed to other farmers to support programmes being initiated by experts, such as access to weather forecasts and promotion of planting verified seeds, which is being rolled out to help them adapt.

World.title: Kanyangala Pri. School implements Presidential Irrigation Initiative
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has expressed satisfaction with the progress made at Kanyangala Primary School in Chienge District under the Presidential Irrigation Initiative (PII).

Ministry of Education Directorate of National Science Centre Training Officer, Moses Phiri, says the school had made good progress, particularly in fencing and land clearing, with the remaining works expected to be completed by the end of this week to pave the way for maize planting.

“We are impressed with the progress that has been made so far, particularly in terms of fencing and land clearing. The remaining works are expected to be completed by the end of this week so that the school can proceed with maize planting,” Mr Phiri said.

Mr Phiri, who is one of two officers monitoring the programme in Luapula Province, said the nearly flat terrain at the school was suitable for precision farming and the installation of drip irrigation systems.

He urged the school management, teachers and learners to accelerate the remaining works so that planting could commence as planned.

Kanyangala Primary School Headteacher, Idah Nkandu, said the school was on course to complete all the works and plant maize by this week.

Mrs Nkandu said the project would provide learners with practical agricultural skills that they could apply even after completing their education.

“This project will give our learners practical agricultural skills which they can use even after completing their education,” she said.

She said Kanyangala Primary School and Lambwe Chomba 2 Secondary School were the two pilot schools selected for the initiative in Chienge District.

And Chienge District Commissioner, Rosemary Chikonde has called for greater involvement of Agricultural Science teachers in the project to ensure that learners gain practical farming skills.

Ms Chikonde said the irrigation field should be used as a practical learning environment where pupils could learn land preparation, planting, crop management and maintenance.

“The irrigation field should be used as a practical learning environment where pupils can learn land preparation, planting, crop management and maintenance,” Ms Chikonde said.

She urged pupils to take both the project and their education seriously, saying the knowledge and skills acquired would help prepare them for future careers and leadership.

“The knowledge and skills you acquire through this project will help prepare you for your future careers and leadership. Therefore, I urge you to take both the project and your education seriously,” she said.

World.title: Chief Kashiba calls for promotion of free education policy
World.content:
Chief Kashiba of the Lunda people of Mwense District has called on elected leaders and other stakeholders to help promote the Free-education policy during their tenure of office.

Chief Kashiba says promoting the policy will encourage more girls and boys to acquire education thereby reducing the high illiteracy levels in the district.

Chief Kashiba pledged to take a leading role to ensure that youths in Mwense District utilise government empowerment initiatives in order for them to secure their future.

“I will also ensure that girls and boys in my chiefdom and district at large acquire education through the free-education policy and utilise the various empowerment programmes that opportunity has been provided by government,” Chief Kashiba said.

Chief Kashiba has since appealed to government to employ more civil servants across various government departments to enhance public service delivery in the district.

The traditional leader particularly called for the deployment of more teachers to improve the teacher to pupil ratio in view of a surge in enrolment levels following the introduction of the free education.

Meanwhile, Chief Kashiba has implored the local authority to expedite road network expansion works using the earth moving equipment that was procured using the CDF.

“Most of our areas in the district are not accessible. Iam happy that the council recently managed to buy equipment but this equipment should now work to construct roads in the district to make areas accessible,” Chief Kashiba said.

He observed that with improved road network, the district is poised to open up more potential economic activities especially in the agricultural and mining sectors.

Chief Kashiba hoped to see growth in the mining sector in Mwense saying mining activities have the potential to transform the socio-economic status of the district through job creation which will also result in a multiplier effect on other income generating activities.

World.title: Police detain Stepfather for suspected murder of three -year- ld girl
World.content:
Police in Lundazi have picked up a Malawian national suspected to have murdered his three year old step daughter.

Eastern Province Police Commissioner, Robertson Mweemba, confirmed the incident to the media which occurred yesterday, September 29, 2026 between 06:00 hours and 09:00 hours at Mutelela Village in Mphamba chiefdom of Lundazi district.

Mr Mweemba said both the suspect Nelson Chisomo Banda and his 26 year old wife Ephelida Phiri, are farm workers for a Zambian farmer.

“A Malawian national, Nelson Chisomo Banda allegedly murdered his step daughter Sofeliti Banda aged 3, while his wife was working on the farm,” he said.

It is alleged that both the suspect and the mother of the deceased left the child at home as they went to work at their employer’s farm.

“Shortly after, a female neighbour to the couple spotted the suspect walking back alone to the house. The suspect was seen entering the house and minutes later, the neighbour heard him call the name of the child twice and was seen leaving the house back to the farm where he had left his wife,” he explained.

Mr Mwemba said the suspect’s wife said when her husband went back to the farm where she had remained working, he told her to return home and check on the child whom he claimed had messed herself.

Upon returning to the house, the mother found her daughter lifeless and the husband failed to give proper explanation as to what had really transpired.

Mr Mweemba said physical inspection of the child’s body showed blood coming out from the child’s mouth and nose as well as faecal matter coming out from the child’s anal opening.

The body of the deceased has since been deposited at Lundazi District Hospital mortuary awaiting a possible postmortem examination.

Police have detained the suspect to help with investigations in the suspected murder case.

World.title: Catholic Bishops Question Credibility of 2026 Elections as CCZ Demands Kafwaya Probe
World.content:
Catholic and Protestant Churches Close Ranks on Rule of Law, Demand Dialogue and End to Arbitrary Arrests

Zambia’s two largest church bodies have issued separate but closely aligned statements warning that the rule of law, public confidence in institutions and national unity are under strain in the aftermath of the 2026 general election. The Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops (ZCCB) raised concern over the credibility and transparency of the elections, arrests of opposition figures and the presence of military personnel in civilian spaces. It also pointed to reports of excessive or unlawful force, including the loss of civilian lives. The Council of Churches in Zambia (CCZ) called for an independent investigation into the death of former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was killed in August during a State security operation. Both bodies called for sustained national dialogue and an end to detention without due process.

The Catholic bishops’ pastoral statement followed an extraordinary plenary meeting of eight bishops on September 29. The bishops said they had listened to the concerns, fears and hopes of citizens before reflecting on the situation in the light of the Gospel and the social teaching of the Church. They said their intervention was not intended to deepen political divisions or take sides in partisan struggles. Instead, they said, it was meant to protect human dignity, justice, truth, peace and national unity. The bishops said the moment called for action, not silence.

“The present moment requires not silence or resignation, but responsible action directed towards peace, justice, reconciliation and the common good,” the bishops said.

The bishops warned that increasing political polarisation was weakening dialogue and making it difficult for citizens to put the common good above partisan interests. They expressed concern over the manipulation of ethnic identities and tribal sentiment for political purposes, warning that it threatened the spirit of ‘One Zambia, One Nation’. Many citizens, they said, were living in fear over their personal security, freedom of expression and employment, and over the consequences of voicing political opinions. They also pointed to a narrowing of space for independent media, civil society and dissenting voices.

The ZCCB questioned the credibility and transparency of electoral processes, particularly concerns over the conduct and management of the 2026 General Elections. The bishops said public confidence in elections was essential to the legitimacy and stability of democratic institutions. They raised concern over restrictions affecting access to justice and perceptions that the independence of governance institutions was being weakened. They also flagged debates around the constitutional provisions on presidential terms of office, where such debates raise anxiety about constitutional safeguards and democratic continuity. On opposition politics, the bishops cited reports of harassment, restrictions and arrests, and they defended the right of rival voices to take part.

“Democracy requires space for alternative political voices and peaceful political participation,” the bishops said.

The bishops’ gravest concern was the use of force. They cited reports of arbitrary arrests and detention, the presence of military personnel in civilian spaces and reports of excessive or unlawful use of force, including the loss of civilian lives. The statement did not name any individual case. The bishops said such developments risked eroding trust between citizens and institutions, and they spoke plainly on the value of life.

“Every human life is sacred and must be protected,” the bishops said.

The CCZ was more direct on the one death that has come to define the post-election period. In a communique issued after a Heads of Churches meeting at the University of Zambia Chapel, CCZ president Reverend Ackson Banda called for a thorough, independent, impartial and transparent investigation into Mr Kafwaya’s death. He said the facts must be established and accountability must follow wherever wrongdoing is found. Mr Kafwaya was killed in Lusaka’s Kabulonga area during what police described as an intelligence-led operation by a joint task force. Police said officers came under gunfire and returned fire. That account has been contested by the opposition, and a complaint over the death has since been lodged with the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

The CCZ also raised concern over people being arrested and held without being promptly brought before a competent court. It stressed that every citizen’s constitutional rights must be respected regardless of political affiliation, religious standing or social status. The council called for urgent investigations into allegations of organised groups or militias operating outside established security structures, without saying which groups it meant. Rev. Banda said the moment called for wisdom rather than political triumphalism, restraint rather than provocation, and justice rather than the selective application of the law.

Beyond their concerns, both bodies set out remedies, and these largely overlap. The ZCCB proposed a sustained process of national dialogue, reconciliation and healing across political, ethnic, religious and social lines. It also called for stronger democratic institutions and a review of electoral processes so that citizens can trust their votes are protected. The CCZ urged the Government, opposition parties and civil society to commit to national dialogue, saying reconciliation must be shown through justice, forgiveness and rebuilding trust rather than declarations and ceremonies. The bishops also called for civic and constitutional education for young people, protection for journalists and civil society, and legal and humanitarian support for families affected by violence or arbitrary detention.

“Public institutions must be instruments of justice and service rather than sources of fear,” the bishops said.

The two statements part ways on the economy. The CCZ acknowledged progress in debt restructuring, key economic indicators and free education, while noting that many Zambians still struggle with the high cost of living, unemployment, food insecurity and energy challenges. The ZCCB kept its focus on governance, rights and the conduct of the elections. The CCZ urged leaders to keep constitutional reforms inclusive and people-driven, and said the Church would maintain its independence from partisan political interests.

The statements come in the same week that the Catholic Archbishop of Lusaka, Dr Alick Banda, was released on bail after a night in custody on a charge of possessing a vehicle allegedly obtained unlawfully from the Zambia Revenue Authority. ZCCB president Archbishop Ignatius Chama had earlier accused the ruling party of seeking to silence the Church. The ruling UPND has rejected that charge, describing the Catholic Church as an important voice in matters of governance. The bishops’ pastoral statement did not refer directly to the Archbishop’s case.

The Catholic statement was issued at Kapingila House on the memorial of St Jerome. It was signed by Archbishop Chama, vice-president Bishop Charles Kasonde, Bishop George Lungu, Bishop Clement Mulenga, Bishop Patrick Chisanga, Bishop Edwin Mulandu, Bishop Raphael Mweempwa and Auxiliary Bishop Gabriel Msipu Phiri. The bishops declared October a special month of Holy Rosary prayers for peace in Zambia. They closed with an appeal to the nation.

“We call upon all people of good will to work together so that Zambia may remain a home for all her children, a nation in which human dignity is respected, justice is accessible, differences can be expressed peacefully, and power is exercised as service,” the bishops said.
