Raids, arrests and asset seizures

Kövesi said European delegated prosecutors would have the same investigative powers as domestic prosecutors, including ordering investigative measures, conducting searches, requesting arrests, bringing charges and freezing or seizing assets. The EPPO’s cross-border structure could be particularly significant when allegedly misappropriated money or assets are moved abroad.

The chief prosecutor cited property purchases elsewhere in Europe as an example, arguing that a national authority can face difficulties tracing and securing assets outside its jurisdiction. The EPPO already operates as an independent European prosecution service, conducting investigations and bringing cases before national courts in participating countries.

Stay up-to-date: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention

‘It is time for them to take back their country’

Kövesi believes some investigations could produce results within a year or two, depending partly on Hungary’s legislative framework and the independence and quality of the prosecutors appointed. She also offered a broader assessment of Hungary’s recent political history, saying: “It is time for them to take back their country,” and arguing that police, prosecutors and judges must be able to perform their duties independently.

Asked about cooperation with Viktor Orbán’s governments, Kövesi said there had been cooperation in some VAT cases, but claimed cooperation became more difficult when investigations involved people close to politicians. The EPPO already has a cooperation agreement with Hungary’s prosecution service dating from 2021, but until now Hungary has remained outside the office’s full operational structure.

World.title: BudapestGO receives useful new update to make metro journeys easier
World.content:
Should you board at the front, in the middle or towards the end of the train? The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has added a new feature to BudapestGO that will now help passengers make this choice.

When planning a metro journey, the app shows passengers exactly which carriage they should board to reach the exit at their destination as quickly as possible, or to make a simpler transfer to another metro line. The new feature will be rolled out gradually and will be available to all users within a few days.

BudapestGO gains another useful feature

BKK is continuously developing BudapestGO to ensure that the app can provide assistance with more and more aspects of everyday travel. One of the key new features in the update released on 29 September – which will become available to all users within a few days – is that, when planning a journey, the app now also shows passengers which part of the metro train they should board.

The new feature can be particularly useful on journeys where passengers have little time to make a connection or are less familiar with the metro station concerned. At the same time, it can also help regular passengers travelling along the same route to reach their exit more directly, avoiding a few unnecessary minutes or detours.

The new feature also plans step-free routes without any additional settings

The new feature works automatically, without requiring any additional settings. If a route recommended by BudapestGO includes a metro journey, the app indicates which carriage passengers should board to reach their destination exit more quickly or make a faster transfer between metro lines.

The app also takes accessibility into account when planning a journey. In such cases, it recommends the carriage closest to the exit with a lift and will only plan routes that are accessible without steps.

World.title: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention
World.content:
Two former ministers from Viktor Orbán’s governments have been caught up in a major corruption investigation, with one ordered into pre-trial detention and prosecutors seeking the detention of another.

The cases involving former national development minister Miklós Seszták and former culture minister Balázs Hankó concern alleged misuse of public funds and bribery. Both politicians deny wrongdoing.

Court orders Seszták detention

A Budapest court on Wednesday ordered Seszták, a Christian Democratic Party (Kereszténydemokrata Néppárt, KDNP, the junior partner of Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz) MP and former national development minister, to be held in custody for 30 days.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal, NVVH) suspects Seszták of accepting bribes and committing other offences. The court said it found no grounds to doubt the reasonable suspicion of corruption offences and ruled that detention was necessary to protect the integrity of the investigation.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Seszták was involved in the so-called Volánbusz case

According to prosecutors, Seszták allegedly accepted bribes worth hundreds of millions or even billions of forints from construction companies during his time as minister between 2014 and 2018. Investigators also allege that Seszták and Norbert Szivek, then chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company, obtained around HUF 11 billion (more than EUR 30 million) in illicit benefits.

The investigation also concerns alleged losses linked to Volánbusz procurements. Authorities suspect that more than 600 second-hand buses were purchased at inflated prices between 2015 and 2018, causing around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.3 million) in damage.

Investigators also allege that the purchase of a Volán company headquarters in Kecskemét was overpriced, resulting in losses of at least HUF 550 million (more than EUR 1.5 million). Seszták has pleaded not guilty. His detention order is not yet final and his defence has appealed.

Miklós Seszták (L). Photo: Facebook/Dr. Seszták Miklós

Stay up-to-date: Former Fidesz minister Seszták gives interview before being detained over EUR 34 million bribery scheme

Prosecutors seek Hankó’s detention

Meanwhile, prosecutors in Bács-Kiskun County have requested the detention of Balázs Hankó and another suspect in a separate investigation into alleged mismanagement. Hankó, who served as culture minister, is accused of helping divert funding administered by Hungary’s National Cultural Fund (NKA) away from its legally designated purposes.

Prosecutors allege that a parallel decision-making system was used to distribute funds according to political considerations. Authorities say that 1,079 grants were improperly allocated between 3 September 2025 and 30 March 2026, allegedly causing HUF 17.3 billion (more than EUR 47.25 million) in financial damage to the central budget.

According to Telex’s report, prosecutors cited the seriousness of the alleged offences and the suspects’ extensive networks as reasons for seeking detention, arguing that there was a risk of flight and interference with the investigation.

Former minister Balázs Hankó. Photo: MTI

More on the NVVH: Former Slovak police chief warns Hungary’s asset recovery office as he claims ‘2 years should be enough for accountability’. Also, questions arose whether one of the weakest candidates has been installed at the helm of the all-but-omnipotent NVVH.

He claims a political campaign is ongoing against him

Hankó was questioned for around five hours after being detained and transported to Kecskemét. He denied the allegations and filed complaints against both his detention and the suspicion against him. He has described the proceedings as a political campaign against him and said they were intended to marginalise nationally minded politicians and artists.

The Kecskemét court is due to decide on the prosecutors’ request for Hankó’s detention on 1 October. The legal processes of the Volánbusz case started as Hungary’s newly established NVVH took over several major investigations into alleged corruption and misuse of public assets, while Hankó’s detention was requested by Bács-Kiskun County’s prosecution. Authorities have indicated that further investigative measures are expected in the cases.

World.title: Orbán’s friend Mészáros remains Hungary’s richest as Forbes publishes first-ever top 100 list
World.content:
Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain by far the wealthiest Hungarians, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion (EUR 4.87 billion), according to the Forbes Hungary 2026 rich list. This year’s ranking is the magazine’s first to feature the 100 richest Hungarians rather than 50, and is published as Hungary’s political and business landscape undergoes major changes.

Mészáros remains firmly at the top

Forbes Hungary has published its 2026 list of the country’s wealthiest people, expanding the ranking from 50 to 100 individuals and families for the first time. Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain at the top, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion.

The combined estimated wealth of the 100 people on the list is now approaching HUF 13,000 billion (EUR 35.5 billion), according to Forbes.

The ranking is based on financial reports from the most recently completed business year. As a result, Forbes notes that the list does not yet fully reflect the effects of the political changes that followed the April election.

The magazine says reviews, criminal proceedings, falling share prices and the establishment of a state asset recovery office are already pointing towards a new period in Hungary’s business world.

Have you read this? Legal threats fly as PM Magyar confronts Orbán-linked billionaire over motorway deal

Csányi, Felcsuti, Veres and Szíjj complete the top five

The five wealthiest Hungarians on the 2026 Forbes list are:

Lőrinc Mészáros and family – HUF 1,785.7 billion Sándor Csányi – HUF 649.7 billion Zsolt Felcsuti – HUF 587.6 billion Tibor Veres – HUF 567.7 billion László Szíjj – HUF 530.6 billion

Mészáros has therefore retained the top position, although Forbes says his estimated wealth increased by only HUF 39 billion this year – the smallest increase relative to his total fortune since he first appeared at the top of the list.

Last year, Forbes estimated his wealth at HUF 1,749.1 billion.

Jellinek ranks seventh, while Garancsi and Jászai remain in the top 15

Dániel Jellinek, owner of Indotek Group, ranks seventh with an estimated fortune of HUF 314.1 billion.

Jellinek was detained and subsequently placed under arrest in September in connection with a criminal investigation. The Forbes ranking, however, is based on the financial data and company valuations underlying its 2026 methodology.

His former wife, Kamilla Hermann, ranks 60th with an estimated HUF 59.8 billion.

István Garancsi, owner of Market Építő and Las Vegas Casino, ranks 10th with an estimated HUF 271.9 billion, while Gellért Jászai, head of 4iG, is 11th with HUF 254 billion.

István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, ranks 13th with an estimated HUF 185.6 billion.

The expansion to 100 names has also brought several figures onto the Forbes list for the first time. Árpád Habony ranks 52nd, while Mária Schmidt is 62nd and former defence minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky is 74th.

What could the political changes mean for Hungary’s billionaires?

Forbes describes this year’s ranking as a snapshot taken at the end of an era in which several business groups grew substantially through state-linked contracts and concessions.

The magazine says that the future of long-term state concessions could become a major issue for businesses closely associated with the previous system. It also raises questions about how companies that expanded in sectors heavily dependent on state contracts will perform in a more competitive environment.

Forbes further notes that businesses which previously benefited from preferential state financing, bond programmes or major public contracts are unlikely to be able to rely on the same conditions under the new government.

However, the 2026 ranking largely reflects the previous business year, meaning the longer-term impact of the political transition is not yet visible in full.

How does Forbes calculate the fortunes?

Forbes Hungary uses a methodology based on that of the US Forbes. Where possible, companies are valued using EBITDA – earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – multiplied by an industry-specific valuation multiple.

Since its 2023 list, Forbes has used the average EBITDA of the previous three years rather than the latest figure alone. The magazine says this better reflects how companies have recently been valued in the Hungarian market.

For non-production businesses such as property developers, the calculation is primarily based on the value of the assets minus liabilities. Start-ups are assessed partly on the basis of investment received, while investment management companies are valued using their after-tax profit and an industry multiple.

Forbes also applies a standard 10% liquidity discount to private companies. Businesses heavily dependent on state contracts or holding state concessions are assessed on an asset basis with a significant discount, where their state exposure is considered substantial.

The magazine says its calculations were supported by data from company information providers Opten and Dun & Bradstreet, as well as Ingatlan.com, while valuation practices and exceptional cases were discussed with M&A advisers.

World.title: Romania’s Crisis Spirals as Parliament Rejects PM-Designate’s Govt
World.content:
Romania’s parliament on Wednesday rejected the programme and proposed cabinet of Siegfried Muresan, a Member of the European Parliament, adding to the country’s political crisis.

The Prime Minister-designate needed 233 votes for his government to be approved. He received only 182.

“The parties that triggered the political crisis have voted to prolong it … We are now waiting to see what position the President … will take,” Muresan said after the result was announced.

His proposed cabinet was backed by the centre-right National Liberals, PNL, and two smaller former coalition partners, but the Social Democrats, PSD, the biggest party in parliament, rejected it.

The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians, AUR, the second-largest party in parliament, also declined to endorse Mureșan. Party leader George Simion said the AUR would not vote for any government until the far-right politician Calin Georgescu “is freed from prison”.

A court on Tuesday ordered 30 days’ detention for former presidential candidate Georgescu, who is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than 1 million euros.

President Nicusor Dan must now nominate another Prime Minister-designate, who will have ten days to put together a cabinet and seek parliament’s approval.

Under the law, the President may dissolve parliament and call an early election if two prime ministers-designate fail to secure parliamentary backing within 60 days. However, Dan has ruled out an early election, arguing that it would likely fail to produce a strong parliamentary majority.

Since May 5, Romania has been operating under an interim government, following the collapse of the previous cabinet. During this period, Dan has made two previous nominations for prime minister, both of whom failed to secure parliamentary support.

In June, independent Eugen Tomac, the first of them, withdrew before even facing a parliamentary vote. Three weeks later, parliament rejected the proposed programme and cabinet of liberal politician Adrian Vestea.

Romania’s political crisis stems from deep tensions among the parties that previously formed the pro-European governing coalition.

The coalition, formed in June 2025, brought together the centre-left PSD, the centre-right National Liberal Party, PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. One of its main objectives was to curb the rise of the far-right AUR.

Its mandate included stabilising the economy, which is burdened by the largest budget deficit in the European Union, securing access to 11 billion euros in EU recovery funds and safeguarding Romania’s investment-grade credit rating.

But unpopular austerity measures introduced to cut the budget deficit placed growing strain on the coalition, particularly with the Social Democrats, who withdrew support in May.

World.title: In Serbia, ‘Fictitious’ Corruption Campaign Becomes Tool of Distraction
World.content:
Over the same period, Serbia has slid 11 places on Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perception Index, published in February. It now stands in 116th place out of 182 countries, the worst ranking of any country in the Western Balkans.

Last year, Transparency Serbia published a report showing that for the first time since the fall of Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in October 2000, the Serbian public considers corruption the biggest issue in the country.

“Vucic came to power in 2012 on, among other things, a campaign of ‘zero tolerance for corruption’,” said Draskovic. “That zero tolerance has turned into absolute tolerance of corruption.”

Nemanja Nenadic, programme director of Transparency, questioned the very notion of an ‘anti-corruption campaign’, given fighting corruption is the day-to-day remit of special corruption departments within the public prosecution service.

“Based on what has been announced, it can be concluded that a large number of arrests presented as part of this campaign essentially have nothing to do with corruption, but with other criminal offences,” Nenadic told BIRN.

“For example, cases in which owners of private companies engage in schemes to avoid paying taxes, not in collusion with tax officials, but with other private business owners.”

“In 2025, the number of reported corruption cases and indictments did increase compared with the previous year. For four major criminal offences, the number of indictments was 52 per cent higher than a year earlier, but there were only nine per cent more first-instance judgments.”

Arrests are the least important indicators of success, Nenadic said.

“More important indicators include how quickly reports submitted by citizens are examined, which can encourage more people to report cases; the amount of benefit obtained through corruption offences or the level of damage caused to public property or the public interest; the number and seniority of those indicted; the speed of court decisions; and, finally, the value of unlawfully obtained assets that are confiscated.”

Draskovic said that long-running proceedings without final judgments risk weakening public confidence.

“It sends a signal that it is not worth fighting corruption,” he told BIRN.

World.title: Three Kosovo Serbs Plead Not Guilty Over 2022 Unrest in North
World.content:
Barricades set up by Kosovo Serbs on a road in Rudare leading to the Jarinje border crossing with Serbia, December 2022. Photo: Adelina Ahmeti/BIRN.

Three Kosovo Serbs, Dusan Maksimovic, Nemanja Jolovic and Srdjan Vucinic, pleaded not guilty at the Pristina Basic Court on Wednesday to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of the country in December 2022.

A fourth defendant, Nenad Orlovic, was not present in court. Judge Rrahman Beqiri said that “every effort has been made to secure his presence in the criminal proceedings but it appears that he is not in Kosovo”.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo set up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a spontaneous outpouring of popular anger after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

Two Kosovo Serbs have already been convicted over the case. Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively on August 31, 2026, after pleading guilty to charges.

Dobrac was convicted of acts breaching the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six people – Maksimovic, Drobac, Radosavljevic, Jolovic, Orlovic and Vucinic – with staging violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

The police discovered a Viber group named “Barricades December 2022” on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They obtained the phone in September 2023 after Maksimovic was arrested over the armed attack on police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian police officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident.

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included: “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and, “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors said the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs spontaneously set up the barricades.

World.title: Kosovo’s Kurti Pushes for Deal on President to Avoid Elections
World.content:
Photos of Kosovo’s presidents. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja

With a court deadline to elect a new President approaching, Prime Minister Albin Kurti on Wednesday called on opposition leaders to take urgent steps to address the issue, which risks triggering another legislative election only five months after the last one.

Last week, the Constitutional Court ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

“The Constitutional Court verdict … has put us in an urgent situation,” Kurti said. “The election of a new President is possible, and subsequently new repeat, unnecessary and costly elections, with heavy consequences, are [then] avoidable,” he added.

Kurti, who was re-elected Prime Minister less than three weeks ago, wants an agreement to be implemented that has already been reached with the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK. This would see Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, take the post of president.

But Sejdiu withdrew from consideration on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

“We have Bekim Sejdiu as a candidate who withdrew because six LDK MPs did not agree with the deal. But from Vetevendosje’s point of view, we have a political agreement and we respect it. We don’t have a new name,” Kurti said on Wednesday when pressed on a possible new agreement with the opposition on a fresh candidate.

For a vote electing a President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect a President – but at least 80 of them still need to be in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Kurti’s Vetevendosje party is serving as Acting President.

While the deal with the LDK hangs in the balance, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK is meanwhile urging parliament to support amendments to the law on the Specialist Chambers, approved in 2015, which would limit the scope of this court before considering any discussion on a President. This comes after the Hague-based court found four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, guilty of war crimes.

On Wednesday, PDK MPs boycotted the work of parliamentary committees in order to press Vetevendosje to proceed with the law change. “Six laws have been brought to the committee today but the Law on the Specialist Chambers is being dragged out because they say it needs expertise. We won’t participate in the committees without proceeding with this law,” Blerta Deliu Kodra, a PDK MP, warned.

World.title: Bosnia Mourns Wartime Co-Inventor of Limb-Saving Medical Device
World.content:
Enes Baralic, who co-created a revolutionary external medical fixator that prevented thousands of limb amputations during the siege of Sarajevo, has died aged 84.

During the 1992–1995 Bosnian war, the city endured a 1,425-day siege by Bosnian Serb forces. Amid relentless shelling, local hospitals faced an overwhelming influx of casualties, with nearly 70 per cent suffering severe limb trauma caused by bullets and shrapnel.

As imported medical supplies were rapidly exhausted under a total humanitarian blockade, two orthopedic surgeons, Dr Sukrija Djozic and Dr Raib Salihefendic, designed a modification for an external fracture fixator.

To manufacture it from raw industrial materials, they partnered with Baralic, a mechanical engineer and factory director at the state-owned industrial conglomerate Energoinvest. The resulting device, named the Sarajevo Wartime Fixator, or “Sarafix”, became a crucial tool for saving shattered limbs from amputation.

More than 4,000 fixators were manufactured inside the besieged city at the Energoinvest facility. As equipment was scarce, devices were routinely recycled and re-sterilized to treat subsequent waves of wounded citizens. The fixators were transported to frontline hospitals via underground tunnels and even by bicycles under sniper fire.

“Enes Baralic was an exceptionally creative man, a massive patriot, and an outstanding friend,” Dr Djozic told BIRN. “Within just ten to 20 days of receiving our initial concepts, he developed the prototype within his factory division. He was tireless, organising the production and ensuring these devices reached trapped enclaves like Srebrenica, Mostar, and Gorazde through the wartime tunnel. He left a profound mark on our history.”

The “Sarafix” earned international acclaim, winning gold medals at global innovation fairs in Brussels and Geneva in 1995 and 1996.

The city administration officially honoured the three co-creators with the high-profile Sixth of April Award in 2001 for their outstanding contributions to science and humanitarian technology.

Dr Djozic said that the legacy of their joint innovation remains permanently preserved across borders.

“I donated one of the original wartime fixators alongside our medals to the Historical Museum in Sarajevo,” he noted.

“Furthermore, a British colleague who volunteered with us later donated another original ‘Sarafix’ to a museum in London, where it remains on display today as a symbol of human ingenuity in the face of total isolation.”

Media reported that Baralic died n Sarajevo on Monday. His funeral was due to be held on Wednesday at the Vlakovo city cemetery in Sarajevo.

World.title: Turkey Freezes Former Minister’s Assets in Market Manipulation Probe
World.content:
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said on Tuesday that it had asked Turkish institutions to freeze all assets belonging to former Family and Social Policies Minister Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, as part of an investment fund investigation.

“As part of the fund investigation conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office’s Terrorism Financing and Money Laundering Crimes Investigation Bureau, relevant institutions have been instructed regarding the freezing of all assets belonging to Ilyas Kaya and his wife, Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya,” it said.

The investigation into dubious capital market transactions has resulted in 51 people being remanded in custody. Turkish authorities previously ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. Turkish television channel CNBC-e estimates the total at about 17.4 billion euros and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya, Turkey’s family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

Following a cabinet meeting, Erdogan said the government would act against wrongdoing in the markets. “We neither violate people’s rights nor turn a blind eye when the rights of our citizens are violated,” he said on Tuesday.

Liquidation of funds does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

Opposition politicians allege that the couple invested around 2.9 million euros in shares of shipbuilder Ozata Denizcilik in April and later sold the shares for about 39.5 million euros. The figures have not been published by the authorities.

Media reported on Monday that the couple subsequently transferred around 39.5 million euros to an account designated by the Treasury and Finance Ministry. The reported payment has also not been publicly confirmed.

Kaya comes from a family with extensive experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Tracing Illicit Cigarette Flows over Mountainous Bosnia-Montenegro Borderland
World.content:
To cross between the municipalities of Gacko and Pluzine, in Bosnia and Montenegro respectively, most local residents must drive at least 100 kilometres, crossing at the Deleusa-Vracenovici border crossing.

Not so for the cigarette smugglers.

They use an asphalt road linking the Gacko village of Lipnik with Ravno in Pluzine. It’s a distance of some 10 kilometres.

“It’s exclusively a smuggling road,” a security source in Bosnia told BIRN on condition of anonymity.

The terrain around the road is too steep for farming, and the road sees almost no other traffic.

According to the case files seen by BIRN, police believe the gangs smuggled the cigarettes from Montenegro into Bosnia via mountain passes and stashed them in and around Avtovac and Lipnik.

“Given that the territory of the municipality of Gacko borders Montenegro, specifically the municipality of Pluzine, it is possible to transport excise goods to stash locations in the areas of Avtovac and Lipnik within a short period of time,” one document states.

With Zirojevic and Miletic allegedly in charge, other members of the group monitored the movement of police or drove ahead of the contraband as reconnaissance, according to the documents. The files name 14 other individuals as involved, all from Gacko and neighbouring municipalities.

They used at least nine different vehicles and often switched licence plates.

“They drive like crazy,” said a source familiar with the police investigation. “They can be over the border and back in ten minutes.” Police nicknamed one of the drivers ‘Phantom’.

“He drives so fast that nobody can catch him in a police chase,” said the source.

The smugglers often targeted an evening gap in patrols when shifts change between 6 and 7 p.m.

According to sources familiar with the investigation, rather than rotating officers directly along the road, border police shift changes take place at fixed points further away, leaving the unofficial mountain crossing unmonitored for about an hour every day.

“And while the shift happens, they have done the job,” a source said.

From Lipnik and Avtovac, the cigarettes are transported deeper into Bosnia for sale through street vendors. This reporter found smuggled cigarettes for sale on the streets of Sarajevo for 4.5 Bosnian marks, or 2.25 euros. The price of the cheapest legally sold pack of cigarettes is 6.2 Bosnian marks, or 3.10 euros.

Overlapping crimes

World.title: Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević: We Won’t Pay Workers for Their Strike
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević has stated that the workers who went on strike from both ZET and Zagreb Holding won’t be paid.

After three days, the strike by ZET and Zagreb Holding workers has ended. Trams and buses are running again, and Čistoća has resumed regular waste collection. The County Court in Zagreb today declared the strikes at ZET and Holding illegal and ordered them to stop.

The unions then suspended the strike and announced they would appeal the rulings. Index reports that ZET has announced that from today onwards, all tram and bus traffic will again run according to the regular timetable.

what you need to know…

Mayor Tomislav Tomašević has stated that none of the workers who went on strike will be paid for the time they spent striking. A ZET union lawyer has stated that he received two drastically different rulings. Municipal workers and ZET workers have now formally ended the strike after the court banned the ZET workers’ strike and the municipal workers’ strike.

After three days, the strike of ZET and Zagreb Holding workers has ended. Trams and buses are running again, and Čistoća has continued regular waste collection. The County Court in Zagreb today declared the strikes at ZET and Holding illegal and ordered their termination. The unions then suspended the strike and announced appeals against the rulings. Mayor Tomislav Tomašević stated that workers will not be paid for the days spent on strike. ZET published that from tomorrow all tram and bus traffic will again operate according to the regular schedule.

The strike had caused significant disruption in Zagreb for three days, with no trams, buses or regular waste collection.

World.title: Butković: We’re Signing Largest Contract in History of Croatian Railways
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – Transport Minister Oleg Butković has stated that today the signing of the largest contract in the history of Croatian Railways will be signed.

Minister of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Oleg Butković announced the signing of a contract for the reconstruction and upgrading of the Dugo Selo – Novska railway line, worth almost 900 million euros. Index reports that this is the largest contract in the history of Croatian Railways.

The Dugo Selo – Novska line is part of one of the main corridors that runs through Croatia towards the east of the country. “This is truly the largest contract in the history of Croatian Railways – almost 900 million euros for 83 kilometres of track reconstruction and the construction of a second track. We’ve been working on this project for a long time, preparing it, a public tender was carried out and now the procedures are complete,” said Butković.

first cooperation with an indian company

After the realisation of this project, he added, the Okučani – Vinkovci section will still remain. “Then we will have a fully reconstructed and built railway line from the Slovenian border, because Savski Marof – Zagreb has been reconstructed, that is, from Zagreb to the border with Serbia,” the minister said. Butković confirmed that this is the first time a company from India has won a job in such a tender. “As far as we have inquired and according to the documentation they submitted, they have very good references. They have worked on one of the largest projects in India and the world, so I believe everything will be as it should,” he said.

The minister is aware that large projects also bring challenges. “Some things today you cannot predict and you cannot influence them. I hope there will be as few of them as possible,” he said. The start of works is planned for the first quarter of 2027 and they should last five and a half years. Butković expressed the hope that there will be no new major crises in the world that could, like previous ones, cause disruptions and price increases.

the lowland railway project

The minister also spoke about the lowland railway, a project that has been in preparation for a long time. “We have started with the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section. As for the reconstruction of the lines around Zagreb, mostly everything has been reconstructed: towards the west, towards Zagorje and towards Bjelovar. By the end of the year we are finishing Dugo Selo – Križevci, which is actually almost done, and Križevci – Koprivnica – Hungarian border,” he said.

He emphasised that it is now important to move towards Rijeka, where the most expensive section from Karlovac to Rijeka remains, whose value is estimated at more than 2.5 billion euros. “There has been an increase in prices due to all the disruptions I spoke about, but we have accelerated the entire project.

A tender for technical assistance is currently underway. We would go for the so-called Alliance model, in which design, obtaining building permits and execution of works would be in one package,” he explained. Under that model, the selected contractor would lead all procedures, which would shorten public procurement and appeal procedures, and the deadline for construction of the line would be five to six years.

another decade before any real change

Asked when passengers will feel real progress and get fast trains, Butković replied that passenger transport around Zagreb is already functioning well. “We’ve more than 70 new trains in passenger transport. Of those, 42 trains have been procured in the last four years. Contracts are constantly being signed and funds secured. This was also shown these days during the strike, when the trains helped a lot, especially in the suburban area,” he emphasised.

Nevertheless, the complete reconstruction of the railway network will still take time. “I always say that we have to be patient for another ten years or so. In those ten years we would manage to mostly reconstruct and build everything on the main corridors and reconstruct a large part of the regional lines. We have already spent around 900 million euros on the reconstruction of local and regional lines across Croatia,” he said.

the continuation of motorway construction

The minister also commented on motorway construction. He announced that the Istrian Y will be completed by the end of the year or the beginning of 2027. “We’re strongly and decisively going ahead with the construction of the Adriatic-Ionian Corridor, Križišće – Žuta Lokva. Two contracts have been signed there. Today we received the building permit for the first section and we are starting the works. That is around 400 million euros,” he said.

Bids have also been opened for the first section of the motorway towards Dubrovnik. Although the new bids are also above the estimated value, the tender will not be cancelled again. “We would not have cancelled the first one either if there had not been really large differences in price compared to the estimated values. The bids that arrived in the new tender are around 40 to 50 million euros lower compared to the previous tender,” Butković concluded. He said that they are decisively proceeding with the completion of the Adriatic-Ionian Corridor, that is, the motorway towards Dubrovnik and the Križišće – Žuta Lokva section.

World.title: Record Revenue from Foreign Tourists in Croatia in 1st 6 Months of 2026
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – Record revenue from foreign tourists in Croatia during the first 6 months of 2026 has amounted to incredible sums, amounting to well over 3 billion euros.

In the first six months of this year, 2.5 billion euros more revenue was generated than in the same period of 2016, said Tonči Glavina. As Novi list reports, according to the latest data from the Croatian National Bank (HNB), in the second quarter of 2026 revenues from foreign tourists amounted to 3 billion and 641.7 million euros, which represents growth of almost 4 percent compared to the same period in 2025, or 132.7 million euros more.

Overall, in the first half of 2026, revenues from foreign tourists amounted to 4 billion and 587 million euros, which represents growth of almost 5 percent compared to the same period in 2025, or 212.4 million euros more. In addition, strong growth in domestic tourism also contributed to the positive results of the tourist year.

In the first six months of 2026, a record 1.5 million arrivals and 4.2 million overnight stays by domestic tourists were recorded, which is 7 percent more arrivals and 6 percent more overnight stays than a year earlier.

“The excellent indicators in the pre-season are the result of strong strategic and promotional activities that we adapted to changes in the market, thereby continuing the positive trends of Croatian tourism even in this extremely challenging year. If we compare these financial results with those recorded back in 2016, revenues from foreign tourists have risen by 120 percent, both in the second quarter and in the first half of the year.

In the first six months of this year, 2.5 billion euros more revenue was generated than in the same period of 2016, while in the second quarter revenue was higher by two billion euros compared to the same period ten years ago. In line with all our strategic goals, we’re permanently changing Croatian tourism for the better in all segments,” emphasised Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina.

World.title: St. Jerome Exhibition Awaits Passengers at Split Airport
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – A brand new St. Jerome exhibition now awaits passengers coming and going from Split Airport.

The new exhibition brings together works by 24 prominent Croatian painters and sculptors created at the St. Jerome Art Colony on Marjan. Morski reports that the exhibition was officially opened by Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban.

“On the occasion of the feast of Saint Jerome and Split-Dalmatia County Day, we organised an exhibition of our most eminent painters and sculptors, not only from our county but from the whole of the Republic of Croatia, who took part in the art colony on Marjan. We are presenting the exhibition for the third time, after the University Gallery and the National and University Library in Zagreb,” said Boban. He added that the exhibition at the Airport also opens the possibility for the story of Saint Jerome, Marjan and contemporary Croatian fine art to travel beyond Croatia’s borders.

“I’d like to thank all the artists and the director of Split Airport, and I congratulate him and all the staff on 60 years of very high-quality work by Saint Jerome Airport,” the Prefect said.

This year’s presentation of the exhibition has additional symbolism because Split Airport is marking the 60th anniversary of its founding. Its director Josip Čorić expressed satisfaction that such a cultural event is being held for the first time in the Airport premises.

The exhibition brings together works by Goran Balić, Duje Botteri, Nikola Džaja, Kažimir Hraste, Petar Jakelić, Kuzma Kovačić, Đani Martinić, Duje Matetić, Matko Mijić, Dijana Iva Sesartić, Ana Marija Botteri, Josip Botteri Dini, Željko Bubalo, Alma Čače, Vladimir Davidenko, Lili Gluić, Karin Grenc, Ivan Listeš, Zvonimir Mihanović, Tea Morić Šitum, Hrvoje Marko Peruzović, Vice Tomasović, Marko Gugić and Frane Šitum. The works were created at the St. Jerome Art Colony, held on the 22nd and 23rd of September 2023 on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of Split-Dalmatia County, organised by Split-Dalmatia County, the University of Split and the Parish of the Holy Cross, Veli Varoš.

World.title: HVARMONY, Celebrating Wellbeing on Croatia’s Premier Island
World.content:
September 30, 2026 – Famous for its sun, beaches, heritage and nightlife, a new initiative celebrates another of its gems – wellbeing. Meet HVARMONY.

Soon after I moved to the island of Hvar back in 2003, an island whose existence I had only become aware of two days before I bought my house, I realised that it was a very distinct island of two halves. The most famous, of course, was the tourism side, with its world famous beaches filled with tourists all over the world, as they also enjoyed the fine gastronomy, culture and endless sun.

But there was another side to Hvar, and one that I liked much better – the off-season. No longer warm enough to swim (although some did), devoid of tourists, most businesses closed for the season, but what a fantastic slice of nature to enjoy in peace and quiet. If Croatia made me realise that quality of life, lifestyle and wellbeing were the shortcut to happiness, it was the winters in Jelsa that first pointed the way.

Olive groves, vineyards, growing their own food, while loudly discussing olives and Hajduk Split over timeless coffees, I had never come across a place so contented with itself. And I quickly learned that I was not alone. All over the island, there were Austrians, Norwegians, Americans, Germans living in the hills or smaller villages, some with yoga studios, but all thrilled that they had found such a gem off the radar.

The digital nomad revolution came to Croatia in 2020, enabling a new breed of tourist to spend an extended period in Croatia. One of the first was an American couple who moved to Jelsa and did a great documentary for national tv on why life on a Dalmatian island in January was perfect. Some locals might have thought they were nuts, but I understood perfectly.

And as look around Hvar these days, in addition to the tourism, there is another undercurrent bubbling away – wellbeing. Yoga, pilates, energy healing, retreats – they are all increasing in number and diversity. It is for me an essential part of the Hvar DNA – this is, of course, the island that was nicknamed the Austrian Madeira for its temperate and healing climate, which resulted in it becoming the birthplace of organised tourism in Europe with the founding of the Hvar Health Society in 1868.

But there has been precious little official recognition of this wellbeing aspect. Until now.

Meet HVARMONY, an excellent initiative from the Hvar Tourist Board, which will take place for the first time from October 15-18. And before we get to the concept and programmes, the locations of the event set the tone – the oldest public theatre in Europe, the impressive Arsenal on the corner of the main square, the 1930s colonnade, Bonj les Bains, and the 5-star Maslina Resort, whose slogan is Mindful Luxury.

So what exactly is HVARMONY? An explanation from the dedicated website:

HVARMONY is a four-day gathering built around one simple question: how can we live better, longer and more fulfilling lives?

From 15 to 18 October in Hvar, talks, conversations, workshops and shared experiences will explore what wellbeing really means today, why we seem to need it more than ever, and whether somewhere along the way it has become yet another industry selling us health, happiness and longevity.

Over the four-day event, some 23 Croatian and international speakers will put on an excellent and diverse programme exploring key themes on health, happiness and longevity, with plenty of yoga, pilates and other energy food for the body. You can see the whole programme here.

I really like the direction that Hvar tourism is going these days, it is a much more pleasant experience, and I applaud the organisers of this initiative, which will not only bring together motivated like-minded people, but also showcase some of the magic I first discovered a quarter of a century ago.

Entrance and participation for events is free of charge (with the exception of a few sessions which are paid), although registration is required. You can do this on the official HVARMONY website.

World.title: Uber CEO Comes to Zagreb and Tries Out Rimac’s Robotaxi
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi arrived in Zagreb and tried out Mate Rimac’s famed robotaxi without a safety driver.

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi visited Verne and the Rimac Campus in Zagreb yesterday and rode in a robotaxi without a safety driver, Mate Rimac announced. “Uber is an investor and strategic partner in Verne. Dara tried out the robotaxi without a safety driver in Zagreb and was delighted with the experience. We talked about further cooperation and expanding Verne beyond Croatia with the ‘final’ Verne car without a steering wheel and pedals,” Rimac wrote on Facebook.

Index reports that Uber and Verne have otherwise been cooperating for months now on an autonomous taxi project. Back in March, Verne, China’s Pony.ai and Uber announced a strategic partnership to launch a robotaxi service in Europe, starting in Zagreb. Uber also announced an investment in Verne at that time.

driverless rides are already being tested out in zagreb

At the beginning of September, Verne and Pony.ai began testing rides with passengers in Zagreb without a safety driver or other staff in the vehicle. The tests are taking place on a 22-kilometre route connecting Verne’s headquarters with the area of Zagreb Airport. However, these are vehicles from the Chinese manufacturer BAIC with Pony.ai autonomous driving technology, not the final Verne vehicle without a steering wheel and pedals that Rimac mentions in today’s post. Since August, Uber has also enabled the ordering of autonomous rides via its app in Zagreb. In that phase a licensed operator was still behind the wheel, while fully driverless rides were introduced as separate tests.

the final report for the eu-funded project has been submitted

Mate Rimac’s announcement comes on the same day that Project 3 Mobility, the company developing Verne, submitted its final report to SAFU on the last day of the deadline for the robotaxi project financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. According to what remains unofficial information, the company is not requesting recognition of the remaining part of the already paid advance in the final documentation. Verne had 179.5 million euros in non-repayable EU funds approved for the project, and back in July 2023 it received an advance of 89.75 million euros. SAFU earlier confirmed to Index that of that amount around 8.77 million euros had been justified so far, while around 80.98 million euros had not been justified.

The project formally ended on the 30th of August, after which a 30-day deadline for submitting the final documentation began. SAFU now has 60 days to check the reported costs and documentation, and during the procedure it may also request additional information. Only after the check is completed will it be known how much of the paid advance will be recognised and how much money, if any, Verne will have to return.

the primary contracted goal was not completed in time

The key problem of the EU-funded project remains the fact that by the deadline it was not confirmed that a fully autonomous Level 5 vehicle had been produced and homologated, which was one of the main contracted results of the project. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said after the deadline expired that the project had not received final homologation from the competent institution in Germany and that it had not been completed by the end of August.

At the beginning of September, Verne revealed that it was ready to return the funds if the final evaluation showed that the contracted obligations had not been fully met. At the same time the company claimed that during the project test prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles had been confirmed and appropriate tests carried out. Mate Rimac’s meeting with Uber’s Dara Khosrowshahi therefore concerns the continuation of Verne’s commercial development and cooperation with Uber, while the final evaluation procedure for the EU-funded project continues separately.

World.title: EU Raises Retirement Age, Here’s What Awaits Croatia
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – As the EU raises its retirement age and multiple countries now expect their work forces to work for longer, what exactly awaits Croatia?

Working life across the European Union is lengthening significantly, and for younger generations the difference could be as much as ten years. Croatia is not currently going to raise its retirement age above 65. The retirement age is rising across Europe, and for some of today’s younger workers a working life could last until the age of 70 or even longer. The OECD estimates that the average retirement age will increase further in the future as life expectancy rises, while numerous countries have already legally adopted gradual increases.

Denmark stands out the most. There it has already been decided that the statutory retirement age will rise to 70 by 2040, while the OECD projects an even higher threshold for generations that have only just entered the labour market if the current method of linking the pension age to life expectancy continues. According to the latest edition of the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance report, the average normal retirement age for people who retired in 2024 is around 64.7 years for men and 63.9 years for women.

For those who have only just entered the labour market, the OECD expects a significantly longer working life. The average future retirement age is estimated at 66.4 years for men and 65.9 years for women.

denmark is taking it the furthest

Denmark is at the top of the European ranking. The current normal retirement age there is 67, and parliament has already adopted an increase to 70 years from 2040. The OECD projects that if the current formula linked to life expectancy continues to be applied, the future retirement age in Denmark could rise as high as 74 years. It is important to emphasise, however, that 74 is not a legally set limit for a specific year, but a projection that depends on whether Denmark continues to link the pension age to increases in life expectancy. The country is already discussing possible easing of that formula after 2040.

High future thresholds are also expected in other European countries. Estonia could reach 71 years, while the OECD projects a normal retirement age of around 70 for Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden. Under current rules, Finland could reach around 68 years and Slovakia around 69, while in a number of other countries the future normal retirement age is approaching 67.

many countries are adopting reforms

The changes are no longer just projections. In several European countries reforms have already been adopted that gradually increase the retirement age or link its future movement to life expectancy.

Belgium will reach a retirement age of 67 years, while the United Kingdom has planned a further increase towards 68. The Czech Republic has also adopted a gradual increase of the statutory age to 67. Slovenia has reformed its pension system and raised the statutory age, but in international comparisons the possibility of full retirement with a sufficient number of contribution years must also be taken into account. The main reason for such reforms is demographics. Europeans are living longer, while at the same time in many countries the share of the working-age population that finances pension systems is shrinking.

Countries are therefore trying to achieve a balance between longer life expectancy, the number of years spent in retirement and the financial sustainability of the system.

men and women are moving towards the same threshold

Differences in retirement age between men and women are gradually narrowing. In most European countries men and women already have the same statutory retirement age, while differences have been retained only in some countries. Some countries where the difference still exists have already decided on its gradual abolition, so the number of systems in which women can take full retirement earlier than men will decrease further.

where does croatia fall here?

Croatia is currently among the countries that do not have a legally determined increase in the regular retirement age above 65. Men in Croatia acquire the right to an old-age pension at the age of 65 with at least 15 years of pensionable service. For women a transitional period is still underway. In 2026 a woman can acquire the right to an old-age pension at 64 years of age and at least 15 years of service.

The threshold for women then increases by three months each year. In 2027 it will be 64 years and three months, in 2028 64 years and six months, and in 2029 64 years and nine months. From the 1st of January 2030, the conditions will be equalised, so both men and women in Croatia will acquire a regular old-age pension at the age of 65. There are also special rules for long-term insured persons. A person who has 60 years of age and 41 years of insurance service in effective duration can acquire the right to an old-age pension for a long-term insured person.

For early old-age pension the general rule is 60 years of age and 35 years of service. For women a transitional period is still underway, so in 2026 they can acquire the right at 59 years of age and 34 years of pensionable service.

will people in croatia have to work for longer?

So far no decision has been taken according to which the regular retirement age in Croatia would be increased above 65. This currently distinguishes Croatia from countries that have already legally linked the retirement age to life expectancy or adopted increases towards 67, 68 or 70 years. Nevertheless, the demographic pressure that is driving reforms in other European countries is also present in Croatia. The population is ageing, and the ratio of the number of employed people to pension beneficiaries is one of the key factors in the sustainability of the system.

That is why the question of how long future generations will have to work before retiring will remain one of the more important topics of European, and also Croatian, social policy. The difference between today’s and future generations can be large. While in a large part of Europe today’s normal retirement age is around 65, in some countries those who are only just starting work could, under current rules, retire only after the age of 70.

World.title: Wellovar – Bjelovar Geothermal Complex Now Open
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Wellovar, the much anticipated Bjelovar geothermal complex is now open, with the ceremony attended by approximately 600 guests.

The ceremony was attended by around 600 guests, and alongside Mayor Dario Hrebak and Bjelovar-Bilogora County Prefect Marko Marušić, the highest-ranking state guests included Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Gordan Jandroković and Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina.

Poslovni reports that after years of planning, preparation and 23 months of intensive construction, Wellovar opened its doors today. The ceremony was held as part of the celebrations of Bjelovar’s 270th birthday, and the new complex in Veliko Korenovo was presented as the largest project in the city’s history.

The way Wellovar was opened was particularly symbolic. Instead of the classic ribbon-cutting, 18 Bjelovar residents of different generations jumped into the Olympic pool. The youngest was a kindergarten-age girl, and among the participants were also well-known Bjelovar athletes, swimmers and pensioners. This “Generational Jump” was meant to symbolise the decades during which the people of Bjelovar had waited for an indoor Olympic pool, as well as the fact that the project is intended for the generations to come.

Wellovar was built as a geothermal sports and recreational complex and contains a total of 10 pools – five indoor and five outdoor. The complex also has four saunas, a gym, sports and recreational facilities and a restaurant. The outdoor pools will be presented to the public next spring.

Terme Bjelovar Director Zvonimir Žarec emphasised that behind the project were 23 months of intensive work, numerous challenges, but also a large team that in recent months prepared the complex for its first guests. Terme currently employs 47 people, and the number of employees will continue to grow. For Bjelovar, the opening of Wellovar also marks the beginning of a new tourism and economic story. With the project, the city aims to position itself as a destination for geothermal, sports and health tourism, and the new complex should also attract visitors from outside Bjelovar.

World.title: Defense Forces critical of 2-member ambulance crews plan
World.content:
The Ministry of Social Affairs' plan to reduce ambulance crews from three members to two would make it more difficult to ensure emergency medical services capacity in a crisis or wartime situation, the EDF finds.

The Estonian Defense Forces disagrees with plans under the ambulance reform to make some ambulance crews two-person teams and reduce the number of crews.

In a response to an information request from Tartu Ambulance (Tartu Kiirabi), the Defense Forces said that, from a national defense perspective, an effectively functioning emergency medical service is a critical necessity in a crisis or wartime situation. It also noted that the ambulance development guidelines through 2035, approved by the social affairs minister, themselves cite having a personnel reserve for crises as one of the advantages of three-person crews.

The current ambulance training model, implemented in cooperation with the Defense Forces, has also been based on three-person crews.

"Experience to date, both in exercises and in real-life situations, has shown that a three-person crew is the minimum needed to effectively deal with a seriously injured patient or begin initial procedures in a mass-casualty situation. The math also weighs against two-person crews. With three-person crews, calling an additional ambulance crew to the scene increased the number of medical personnel there by three, while with two-person crews the corresponding increase is two (3+3 vs. 2+2). This, in turn, results in a shortage of personnel at the scene, which could begin to affect patient care," the Defense Forces wrote.

The Defense Forces added that three-person crews provide a personnel reserve in a crisis, noting that the war between Ukraine and Russia has shown that in a crisis or wartime situation, when the need for medical assistance increases, not all additional personnel called in will necessarily report for duty.

The Ministry of Social Affairs is planning an ambulance reform in Estonia by 2028 that would expand the existing network of ambulance bases, change the locations of physician-led crews, reduce their number, make some ambulance crews two-person teams and reduce the number of crews operating at night.

"In such a situation, three-person crews can, if necessary, be quickly reorganized into two-person crews, meaning the necessary personnel reserve is available. If there is a broad shift to two-person crews, that reserve will no longer exist," the Defense Forces said.

"In a crisis affecting the entire healthcare system — and, more broadly, society as a whole — replacing employees is difficult or may even be impossible for a certain period. The personnel reserve provided by three-person crews makes it possible, at least temporarily, to cover potential staff shortages. If two-person crews predominate, that capacity does not exist, which in turn reduces or eliminates the resilience of emergency medical services in a crisis," the letter added.

Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller said in August, responding to criticism of the reform plan, that the reform would improve the quality of emergency medical services.

"The plan is also to change crew composition where possible and necessary, but this certainly will not have any negative impact on the quality of the care provided. On the contrary, quality will be monitored more closely than before. Ambulance bases will be located closer to people, meaning ambulances should also be able to reach people more quickly," Joller said.

According to the Ministry of Social Affairs, the reform is based on prior analysis and related modeling.

World.title: Tartu Folk festival returns November 12–15
World.content:
The 11th international folklore festival Tartu Folk will take place in Tartu, bringing together folklore communities from Estonia and from the Baltic and Nordic countries.

Tartu Folk brings together the folklore communities of Tartumaa and Europe to create new friendships, share knowledge and keep alive the song, dance and instrumental music heritage and folk‑costume traditions of different regions. The festival focuses on interaction between people, making music together, dancing and sharing tradition with both participants and the audience.

This year's most distant guests arrive from 1,900 kilometres away, from the Faroe Islands. The youth association Ung í Dansi belongs under the folk‑dance organisation Sláið Ring and deals with keeping old circle dances alive, accompanied by fairy‑tale‑like ballads.

From Lithuania, the youth group Dolija of Vilnius Žvėrynas Gymnasium arrives at the festival; it stands out for strong awareness of tradition in both music and dance and has participated in Tartu Folk before. Latvia is represented by one of the country's oldest folklore communities, Skandinieki, led by the musician Julgī Stalte, who has Livonian roots.

The festival also introduces the cultural landscape of Estonia's islands. This year the festival includes the Muhu folklore group Uijee, awarded the title of folklore group of the year. The folklore club Maatasa, the organiser of the festival, performs traditional songs, dances and instrumental tunes of South Estonia.

The festival begins on Thursday, late in the evening of 12 November, with folk songs on the bank of the Emajõgi River.

On Friday, 13 November, community parties take place in Tartu and Tartumaa, where the festival's guest groups and local traditional‑culture collectives perform. At the Tartu community party, young traditional musicians from Tartu and South Estonia meet this year.

On Saturday, 14 November, the main day of Tartu Folk takes place at the Vanemuine Concert Hall. At the gala concert, the festival's guest groups perform, with presentations inspired by the traditional songs, dances and instrumental tunes of their home regions.

While folklore communities present their tradition as authentically as possible, the folk‑dance groups participating in the gala show how tradition has inspired contemporary choreographers and musicians. The choreographers' works are performed by the folk‑dance ensemble Tarbatu of the Estonian University of Life Sciences, the folk‑dance group Vassakule of the Defense Forces Academy, and the folk‑dance group Pistandi of the Tartu Applied Health Sciences University.

After the gala concert, an international dance club follows, where it is possible to learn traditional dances of the Faroe Islands, Lithuania, Latvia, and Muhu and South Estonia according to the instructions of the main performers. Communities from across Estonia are also visiting, and one can dance, for example, to the Näppepildurid from Tapa or to the Tartu Udmurt ensemble Jumšan Gur; dances of the northern coast are introduced by the dance society Pikne.

At the café stage, small ensembles of traditional musicians can be heard at the same time, among them Susanna Viktoria and Tuvimärulihärrad. The evening ends with an ethno‑disco, led this year by Eveliina and Mitja Pilke from Finland.

On Sunday, 15 November, the festival's final concert takes place under the bridge area of the Estonian National Museum. Performing are the festival's main guests Ung í Dansi from the Faroe Islands, Skandinieki from Latvia, Dolija from Lithuania, Uijee from Muhu and Maatasa from Tartu.

The theme of this year's final concert is mythological beings, through whom the supernatural characters of different peoples and the stories connected with them are introduced. The concert is hosted by Tuule Pihlap and Kaarel Pogga.

World.title: Marti Soosaar: A green exit from the deadlock in Estonian politics
World.content:
Sensible people in Estonia and elsewhere in the world are looking with concern at the triumph and proliferation of conservative populism. The closer elections come, the more people's faces sour after a look at the polling results.

In Estonia, too, the main question seems to be whether the next prime minister will be named Mihhail or Urmas (Center Party head Mihhail Kõlvart or Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu – ed.). Behind them, an increasingly vociferous Martin Helme [EKRE] smells an opportunity to return to the post of minister and "make heads roll." Listening to talk of reversing marriage equality, burning oil shale and the like is about as unpleasant as sitting next to an aggressively ranting non-citizen on the tram.

Who will deliver us from this mess? The Parempoolsed?

Let us do some ratings calculations. EKRE, Isamaa and Center have 50 sets, Reform and SDE 40 and Parempoolsed 11. If the latter become the kingmaker in parliament, which is entirely possible, we will find ourselves in a situation where the government will be ensuring the timber sector's "security of supply," or in the words of timber industrialist Jaak Nigul, harvesting another billion euros from Estonian forests. A few bank accounts would grow, while most people would be left with nothing but tree stumps to look at.

The Greens stand opposed to such developments. Selling a kidney so you could continue binge-drinking with your friends for another week might seem like a good idea through the haze of a hangover after a months-long bender, but it is generally advisable to sober up completely before making decisions of this magnitude. We will have need of our world's best living environment.

We're talking about economic growth as if it could make us happy. Growth is good, but who draws real happiness from it? Let us, instead, center debate around happy people, a brilliant living environment, good mental and physical health. These are the things we should be talking about, instead of spending our days wondering why the economy grew by 2 percent and not 3.

What will improve if Eesti 200 and Greens join forces? The idea that Eesti 200 could be a far greener party is nothing new. Züleyxa Izmailova, a former member of both Eesti 200 and the Greens, fought toward that goal with some success. Eesti 200 was at a crossroads then and made what we believe was the wrong choice, but the measure of a good politician is not whether they make mistakes, it's whether they learn from them.

The Greens have been widely criticized for both ignoring other important topics in society and talking about them. In a sense, we've painted ourselves into a green corner and are pondering how to get out. Clearly, we, too, need major change to move forward. We need to correct our own mistakes and once again take part in the public debate.

Eesti 200 talked about having a long plan ahead of the 2023 elections. But a single election cycle is not a long plan. Mistakes were clearly made when the long plan started and a price has been paid in the polls.

However, any truly long-term plan is also a green plan. That said, green topics tend to be a nice-to-have for people. Everyone is green in words, but making ends meet and security always comes before the environment.

The new party must take this into account because the party and its politics are, after all, for the people of Estonia and no one else. We protect nature because people cannot survive without it and because no other party will do it. Our task is to show how a good life and environmental protection are inextricably linked and that green solutions exist for all the problems that matter to people.

We invite people to join us who want individual freedoms to be protected in Estonia and want us to remain free. Free not only from Russian troops, but free in our thinking as well. People who understand that without protecting our living environment, our future is bleak. Those who want Estonians to be enterprising and prosperous and to fulfill their talents for their own benefit and that of society, but who do not want that prosperity to come at the expense of our living environment.

There are a million other ways to do business than cutting down every tree. We welcome everyone who sees Estonia's future as free and green.

World.title: Ülle Madise has broad public backing as Estonia's next president
World.content:
Nearly two-thirds of Estonia's residents support electing Ülle Madise as Estonia's president, a new Emor survey shows.

Almost one-third (31 percent) of respondents fully support her, and the same share (32 percent) somewhat support her.

21 percent do not support electing Madise: 11 percent do not support it at all and ten percent somewhat do not support it. 17 percent were undecided.

There is considerable support in society for Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president, Emor research director Aivar Voog said.

She has been visible to the public for years as chancellor of justice and is therefore familiar to most residents. The result shows that broad political support in the Riigikogu is accompanied by fairly strong public support.

Support for electing Madise is somewhat higher among people age thirty-five and older. Among residents of other nationalities, a significant share (35 percent compared with 13 percent among Estonians) are unable to give an assessment.

Looking at support by party preference, the new president is strongly backed by supporters of the Social Democratic Party (86 percent), Reform Party (83 percent), Eesti 200 (83 percent), Parempoolsed (80 percent) and Isamaa (68 percent).

Supporters of the Estonian Center Party are more hesitant (23 percent undecided and 34 percent supportive), while opposition dominates among EKRE supporters (67 percent do not support).

The Riigikogu elected Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president on September 2 with 71 votes in favor.

The data is based on Emor's nationwide representative online survey conducted September 17–24, 2026. A total of 1,114 Estonian residents age sixteen and older were interviewed.

World.title: Justice chancellor challenges Keila's infrastructure fee in Supreme Court
World.content:
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise is asking the Supreme Court to invalidate a regulation under which the City of Keila has imposed a general infrastructure fee on developers, which Madise says has no legal basis.

Madise this week filed an application with Supreme Court Chief Justice Villu Kõve, asking the Supreme Court to invalidate a 2023 regulation adopted by the Keila City Council that the chancellor of justice says has no legal basis.

Madise approached the Keila City Council in May this year and proposed bringing the regulation into line with the Constitution. Although the council said in its response that it agreed on the need to link agreements on covering costs to the circumstances of a specific detailed plan and to base any obligations imposed on a legal basis and justified considerations, the regulation has yet to be amended.

The City of Keila told Madise that the regulation needed to be reviewed and, if necessary, amended, but deferred taking a final position.

The regulation imposed a public-law fee, or infrastructure fee, on parties seeking a detailed plan, payable to the city within one year of the plan's adoption. The fee is €4,000 per residential unit — a detached house, apartment or terraced-house unit — for a detailed plan that complies with the comprehensive plan and €10,000 per residential unit for a detailed plan that amends the comprehensive plan.

Under the regulation, the fee applies to developments planning at least four residential units. If a developer refuses to enter into an agreement on paying the infrastructure fee, the city may terminate the detailed planning process and decline to adopt the detailed plan. If a developer fails to pay the infrastructure fee, the city may refuse to issue building and/or occupancy permits for the building or buildings envisaged by the detailed plan, according to the regulation.

Madise noted that the city has no statutory authority to impose an infrastructure fee in this form because it has assumed broader powers than the law allows. While the city has established a general fee through the regulation, the Planning Act only addresses the costs of constructing a specific facility.

"The infrastructure fee can be regarded as a public-law financial obligation whose amount is not determined by assessing the circumstances of an individual case. Such a fee resembles a tax, which likewise requires a legal basis under the Constitution. Regardless of precisely how the infrastructure fee is classified, imposing by regulation such a financial obligation that restricts fundamental rights requires a legal basis. There is currently no such legal basis," Madise wrote in her letter to Kõve.

Requiring a party seeking a detailed plan to meet financial obligations imposed by the city but not provided for by law restricts that person's fundamental right to property, as well as the freedom to conduct business, without a legal basis, the chancellor of justice added.

In May this year, Madise also approached Tallinn over the same issue, saying that a Tallinn regulation used to collect money from real estate developers to finance the construction of public facilities conflicted with the law in several respects.
