World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Japan Times 1926: Meiji Shrine baseball park opens
World.content:
100 YEARS AGO

Sunday, Oct. 24, 1926

The Meiji Jingu (Shrine) baseball park, which is one of the finest in the Orient and capable of seating over 30,000 spectators, was formally opened Saturday afternoon by His Imperial Highness the Prince Regent before a capacity crowd which filled to overflowing the spacious stands on all sides of the field. Field Marshal H.I.H. Prince Kan-in was also present and took part in the ceremonies; Prince Tokugawa, representing the Meiji Shrine Hosenkai, and (Osachi) Hamaguchi, the home minister, representing the government, likewise helped in the formalities while Professor (Isoo) Abe of Waseda, the father of Japanese baseball, spoke on behalf of the ball players.

World.title: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, Israel says, after co-pilot stabs pilot
World.content:
Passengers on a flydubai flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after customers and crew foiled a co-pilot’s attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, in a struggle that began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.

Passengers and crew entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and enabled a second pair of flydubai pilots who were aboard the flight to land the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, Israeli officials said.

More than 10 hours later, the passengers arrived at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport aboard a flydubai replacement aircraft, with several describing the episode as a miracle and recounting a frantic struggle to prevent a catastrophe.

World.title: U.K. accuses China of using academics to spy on AI and other tech research
World.content:
Britain’s MI5 spy agency issued an unprecedented alert on Wednesday to warn that a Chinese organization was involved in funding academic research into topics such as AI on behalf of Beijing’s state security service.

In its “Espionage Alert,” MI5 said more than 100 U.K.-based academics had contributed to projects funded by the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), which had “very strong ties” to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), Beijing’s civilian intelligence service.

“MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage,” the alert said.

World.title: Japan officially overhauls permanent residency rules
World.content:
Japan has officially revised its guidelines for permanent residency requirements, the government announced, including adding stricter income and pension standards, as well as Japanese-language requirements, with some revisions effective as of Thursday.

Most of the new criteria will apply to applications filed from April 2027, while revisions to criteria regarding minimum income requirements will apply to applications filed as far back as April of this year.

Under the revised guidelines, applicants will be assessed on whether their income has continuously exceeded the average income of Japanese households of a comparable size.

World.title: Komeito selects former party policy chief Okamoto as new leader
World.content:
Opposition party Komeito decided Wednesday to appoint former party policy chief Mitsunari Okamoto as its new leader.

Okamoto, 61, will assume the post at a party convention on Saturday, in line with the expiration of the term of the current leader, Toshiko Takeya, 57.

Last week, House of Representatives lawmakers who had transferred from Komeito to the Centrist Reform Alliance returned to Komeito after the CRA decided to disband.

Komeito is rushing to rebuild its organization ahead of an extraordinary Diet session beginning next week and unified local elections set for next spring.

Okamoto told members of the media, “I will make all-out efforts to create a new party.”

On the possibility of Komeito collaborating with other parties, he said that his party aims to cooperate with lawmakers who share its values in policy planning, including members of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.

Still, he denied the possibility of Komeito returning to the LDP-led coalition government.

World.title: Emperor and empress visit quake-hit Kumamoto Prefecture
World.content:
Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako visited Kumamoto Prefecture on Wednesday to comfort people affected by a powerful earthquake that struck the prefecture in late July and to thank those engaged in relief efforts and support activities.

The Imperial couple left Haneda Airport on a special flight in the morning and arrived at Kumamoto Airport around 11:30 a.m. They transferred to a Self-Defense Forces helicopter, which carried the couple to a temporary heliport on a riverbank in the city of Yatsushiro in the afternoon.

Soon after getting off the helicopter, they bowed silently toward areas heavily damaged by the July 28 quake, including Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro plant, where a chimney collapsed and killed nine people.

According to Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura, who accompanied the couple, the emperor and the empress received explanations aboard the helicopter about the Nippon Paper plant and the Aeon Mall Kumamoto shopping facility in the town of Kashima, where an explosion that occurred shortly after the quake killed seven people.

The couple then visited a facility in Yatsushiro which is used as a shelter. At the facility, which currently accommodates about 80 evacuees, the imperial couple listened to some of them and expressed sympathies for the difficulties they experienced.

The emperor and the empress also visited the town of Hikawa.

According to aides, Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako had shown their intentions to console affected people in person as they are saddened by the severe damage from the latest quake, which occurred while reconstruction work following the April 2016 massive earthquakes were still underway.

The July earthquake registered the maximum seismic intensity level of 7 on the Japanese scale in Hikawa and the city of Uki.

The death toll from the quake, including indirectly caused fatalities, has reached 38, according to the Kumamoto Prefectural Government.

As of Tuesday, the number of homes damaged by the quake stood at about 72,000, including some 9,700 that were destroyed or heavily damaged. About 1,400 people were staying in evacuation centers.

Wednesday’s visit marked the imperial couple’s first trip to a disaster-hit area not long after disasters since December 2024, when they visited the city of Wajima, Ishikawa Prefecture, after torrential rains that hit the region in September the same year.

World.title: New internal affairs minister Fujii vows to revamp local government systems
World.content:
Japan needs to strengthen local government systems to address labor shortages, new internal affairs minister Hisayuki Fujii said in an interview on Wednesday.

Small local governments are particularly affected by labor shortages, said Fujii, who took office on Sept. 17 as part of a Cabinet reshuffle by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

“It’s important to expedite the review of administrative procedures and role allocations to allow local governments to focus on creative administrative tasks,” he said.

Fujii acknowledged that the furusato nōzei hometown tax donation program is “very significant” in addressing regional challenges. Noting that local governments seek a reduction in the fees they pay to dedicated portal site operators, he said the central government will discuss the matter as part of an annual tax system review later this year.

He said that he will ask social media platform operators to take voluntary actions to mitigate negative impacts on elections from false information before the new law that requires them to do so takes effect.

Elections are “fundamental to democracy” and combating misinformation about them and defamation of candidates is a “critical challenge,” he said.

Asked about economic security, Fujii emphasized the importance of submarine cables, which cover 99% of the country’s international communications. He outlined plans to secure supply capacity, support cable laying and implement multi-routing to reduce disruption risks, and enhance cable protection.

The minister suggested that Osaka was not the primary choice for a secondary capital candidate to serve as a backup for Tokyo. He said the focus is on “establishing a backup system in case of large-scale disasters and creating a multipolar decentralized economic zone.”

World.title: Japanese hospital performs world-first surgery using heart muscle stem cells
World.content:
A hospital in Japan has carried out the world’s first surgery using sheets of commercially available heart muscle stem cells after the ground-breaking therapy was approved this year, one of the surgeons said.

Sheets of muscle cells derived from regenerative products known as induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells, were transplanted into the heart of a woman in her 50s during the hourlong surgery performed on Tuesday.

It marked the first clinical use of the regenerative therapy since it received conditional government approval in March.

“Our hope is that this will improve the patient’s quality of life,” surgeon Yoshiki Sawa, the head of Osaka Keisatsu Hospital, told reporters after the surgery.

Trials of the regenerative therapy were conducted on eight patients suffering from ischemic heart disease — damage caused by narrowed heart arteries.

All eight experienced an easing of their symptoms, including four whose heart functions improved, Japanese media said.

Sawa developed the technology in collaboration with Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka, who won the Nobel Prize in 2012 for his research into iPS cells, which have the potential to develop into any cell in the body.

Sawa’s therapy is primarily designed for heart patients who have exhausted other treatment options.

It is expected to improve heart muscle function, resulting in improved cardiac performance and exercise tolerance.

His team plans to conduct similar operations on 75 patients by 2033 and to report on the treatment’s efficacy, media reports said.

The treatment would then be fully authorized after its benefits and safety are proved over the next seven years, the Asahi Shimbun said.

Japan also gave conditional approval in March for a Parkinson’s disease treatment that transplants iPS cells into a patient’s brain, following a successful clinical trial.

IPS cells are created by stimulating mature, already specialized cells back into a juvenile state — basically cloning without the need for an embryo.

World.title: Watch: Hong Kong holds ceremony and reception on China’s National Day
World.content: Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee and senior government officials are attending a ceremony and a National Day reception as the city celebrates the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.

World.title: Retailers expect ‘golden week’ sales growth, but trade groups warn of modest gains
World.content:
Some Hong Kong retailers are forecasting double-digit sales growth over the National Day “golden week” holiday, but industry leaders have warned that the expected influx of mainland Chinese visitors may deliver far smaller gains across the sector as tourists remain cautious about spending.

The cautious outlook came after authorities estimated that about 1.29 million mainland visitors were expected between October 1 and 7, with average daily arrivals projected to exceed last year’s figure by more than 5 per cent.

Businesses are offering discounts, shopping rewards and events to persuade visitors to spend more, while some hotels are counting on late bookings to fill their remaining rooms.

“The net effect is that total retail receipts may still increase, but the growth will be disproportionate to visitor arrivals,” said Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank.

World.title: How Hong Kong’s foreign carer scheme aims to get ahead of ageing city
World.content:
When I first heard about the Hong Kong government’s plans to allow the importation of specially qualified carers to look after the elderly, my mind turned to some colloquial English expressions. The first was “set the cat among the pigeons”, which basically means to say or do something that causes a good deal of trouble, alarm, anger or controversy in a peaceful situation.

The immediate trigger for this thinking was a brief reference in Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address to the government introducing a pilot scheme in which domestic helpers with more advanced training and experience could be brought in to take care of the elderly living at home.

Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han expanded on the idea in a subsequent press briefing. In short, carers possessing a suitable certificate of expertise and three years’ relevant experience could expect to be paid 10 to 20 per cent more than the normal helper salary. The minimum wage for domestic workers is currently HK$5,100 (US$650) per month.

The government will also strengthen its support for carers by regularising the pilot schemes on training for domestic helpers in elderly care and care for people with disabilities.

World.title: Taxi passengers take wheel after cabby faints while driving on Hong Kong highway
World.content:
Four taxi passengers escaped injury after their driver lost consciousness at the wheel on a Hong Kong highway, leaving them struggling to control the vehicle before it hit a road divider.

Dashcam footage circulating online on Monday captured the incident.

It showed the 66-year-old driver slumped unconscious behind the wheel as a male passenger in the front seat and three women in the back desperately try to rouse him.

The taxi was travelling eastbound on Ching Cheung Road near Nob Hill at about noon when the driver suddenly passed out.

World.title: Nearly 150 firms in Hong Kong cut packaging waste equal to weight of 900 buses
World.content:
Nearly 150 companies have reduced packaging material equivalent to the weight of about 900 double-decker buses over the past year after taking part in a government charter on waste reduction launched in Hong Kong in 2025.

A-1 Bakery, Watsons Water and SF Express Hong Kong were among 75 firms recognised for their efforts at an award ceremony on Wednesday, following an assessment by the Environmental Protection Department on five criteria, including packaging recyclability and promoting the use of less packaging materials.

Undersecretary for Environment and Ecology Diane Wong Shuk-han said at the ceremony that the city had striven to explore and promote cutting packaging waste according to “pragmatic and feasible principles”, while noting mandatory national standards launched in mainland China in July to restrict excessive packaging in delivery parcels.

“Environmental protection and economic development are never mutually exclusive. Rather, they complement each other,” Wong said.

World.title: Hong Kong’s Pansy Ho wins permanent injunction against woman who harassed her
World.content:
Pansy Ho Chiu-king, daughter of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun, has won a lawsuit to permanently bar a woman from contacting her after the defendant repeatedly harassed her and her companies with emails and hand-delivered letters containing false allegations.

The defendant was also ordered to pay Ho HK$1.8 million (US$229,000) in compensation for damages.

A judgment handed down by the High Court on Wednesday revealed that Ho, chairwoman and executive director of MGM China Holdings, had been harassed for a year by Steffi Chen Pan-yu, a former licensed broker, since March 2025.

Ho, one of the city’s richest women, is also the group executive chairwoman and managing director of Shun Tak Holdings.

World.title: ‘Who wants McDonald’s?’: mainland tourist shares HK$10,000 prize in Hong Kong
World.content:
A mainland Chinese tourist who won a HK$10,000 (US$1,275) McDonald’s voucher in Hong Kong has turned her last 24 hours in the city into a whirlwind giveaway to the elderly, cleaners and the homeless.

The woman, who shared her spree on Chinese social media platform RedNote, said she won the “Hong Kong McDonald’s HK$10,000 subsidy” through Alipay on Saturday.

According to a screenshot of her post, the voucher was valid for only one week and allowed up to 10 transactions, each capped at HK$1,000 and was restricted to McDonald’s stores in Hong Kong.

With only a day left before returning to the mainland and in-store gift cards sold out, the woman decided to treat strangers as a way of sharing her good fortune around the city.

World.title: China’s Tiangong space station camera captures its first images of Hong Kong
World.content:
A remote-sensing camera aboard China’s Tiangong space station that was developed by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology has released its first images of the city ahead of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.

The university published a series of videos and photos on Wednesday captured by the Musico camera, saying they showcased the major achievements of the Hong Kong research team’s participation in the national space programme.

Professor Zhang Limin, who jointly led the camera project, said the photos were a “special gift” to China, including Hong Kong, ahead of National Day on Thursday.

“It not only marks the successful deployment of a Hong Kong-developed scientific payload aboard the Tiangong space station, but also demonstrates Hong Kong’s growing contribution to the nation’s space endeavours,” said Zhang, who is also head of the university’s department of civil and environmental engineering.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.title: The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.content:
This summer, “All Wishes Come True!” took in more than 1.8 billion yuan ($268 million) at the Chinese box office, becoming the latest in a string of hit animated films inspired by traditional Chinese myths and legends. The movie reimagines the Eight Immortals, a group of legendary figures in Chinese mythology and Taoism, as ordinary mortals who pose as immortals and venture into the celestial realm of Penglai. There, the mismatched group finds itself caught up in a conflict involving powerful gods, including the warrior deity Erlang Shen.

Despite the film’s widespread acclaim, some Taoist friends of mine were far from impressed. They believe it trivializes important figures in Taoist tradition, completely reimagining their stories while simply borrowing the names of Chinese immortals as a gimmick. But how fixed are the stories of the Eight Immortals in the first place?

Firstly, what makes the Eight Immortals — one of the best-known groups of immortals in Chinese culture — so special? And how exactly are they understood within Taoism?

Let’s start with why there are eight. In traditional Chinese culture, the number eight has long been associated with completeness and balance. The “Zhou Yi” (or “Book of Changes”), for example, describes the eight trigrams; traditional cosmology divides space into eight directions; and ancient people worshipped eight agricultural deities collectively associated with the harvest.

Then there are the “immortals” themselves. The Chinese word xian, or “immortal,” has long been associated with hermits who withdraw into the mountains in pursuit of spiritual cultivation. In Taoism, immortals are distinct from shen, or deities, in that ordinary humans can attain immortality through cultivation. Immortals thus occupy a space between the human and sacred worlds, embodying the Tao in the human realm.

Before the Eight Immortals became established as a group, several individual members had already appeared in historical writings and paintings from the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) dynasties, each associated with their own supernatural feats.

Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin practiced neidan, a Taoist tradition of spiritual cultivation sometimes called “internal alchemy,” and frequently interacted with the influential Taoist priest Chen Tuan. Zhang Guolao once demonstrated various miraculous Taoist arts before Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Han Xiangzi could make flowers bloom instantly. Lan Caihe was a beggar who wore a shoe on one foot while leaving the other bare, often singing and dancing while intoxicated and carrying a large clapper.

Once they had formed into a group, however, the Eight Immortals did not simply retreat into the mountains or ascend to heaven. Instead, they remained closely connected to the human world. The most representative figure in this respect is Lü Dongbin, who chooses to remain among mortals and save them. He assumes various guises, including those of a fisherman, an ink and paper peddler, a sick beggar, and even a pregnant nun. Stories and images of Lü spread across China, with saving and enlightening ordinary people becoming a central theme in legends surrounding him.

The Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) mural “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” at Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, in northern China’s Shanxi province, shows that the Eight Immortals had by then become an established subject in Taoist art. But closer inspection reveals that the only female member of today’s group, He Xiangu, is missing. In her place is Xu Shenweng, a Taoist figure associated with the Northern Song period (960–1127) who once ranked among the Eight Immortals. In other words, the Eight Immortals were originally an all-male group.

So, when did He Xiangu become one of the Eight Immortals? One early appearance of her as part of the group comes in the Yuan dynasty drama “Chen Jiqing Mistakenly Boards a Bamboo Leaf Boat” by Fan Kang. By the time Wu Yuantai wrote the mythological novel “Journey to the East” during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), she had become a permanent member of the group.

This change came amid the flourishing of women’s literary and religious activity during the mid-to-late Ming. Like male scholars, educated women participated in religious and intellectual life and produced literary works of their own. In “Journey to the East,” He Xiangu’s defining supernatural ability is her power to foresee good and bad fortune. Born into a family that ran an herbal medicine shop, she possesses medical knowledge and uses encounters with people seeking treatment as opportunities to encourage them to do good.

With the addition of He Xiangu, the lineup familiar today became fixed and increasingly popular. The Eight Immortals eventually became influential enough to attract the attention of European missionaries studying Chinese religion and folklore. French Jesuit Henri Doré (1859–1931), for example, compiled stories about them in “Researches into Chinese Superstitions,” his multivolume study of Chinese popular religion, folklore, and customs.

The Chinese Jesuit priest Pierre Hoang (1830–1909), also known as Huang Bolu, meanwhile, described the Eight Immortals as representing a cross-section of society: the old and young, men and women, the rich and poor, the noble and lowly. In another interpretation, Zhang Guolao represents old age; Lan Caihe and Han Xiangzi, youth; Zhongli Quan, the military; Lü Dongbin, the scholar; Cao Guojiu, the nobility; Li Tieguai, the sick; and He Xiangu, women.

The Eight Immortals thus came to encompass a broad range of social identities and experiences. They had, collectively, seen many sides of the human world, allowing people from different backgrounds to recognize something of themselves in the group. Their differences also created a kind of balance, recalling a passage in Chapter 2 of the “Tao Te Ching,” which states: “Thus existence and non-existence produce each other; the difficult and the easy bring about each other; the long and the short impart form to each other; the high and the low comply [or change places] with each other; sounds and voices harmonize with each other; priority and sequence alternate with each other.”

From the mid-to-late Ming dynasty onward, the Eight Immortals also became a popular decorative motif on ceramics produced in both imperial and private kilns. They often appeared more subtly on everyday objects, including furniture, utensils, clothing, and architectural decorations. Rather than depicting the immortals themselves, artisans represented them through eight objects associated with the group: Li Tieguai’s gourd, Zhongli Quan’s fan, Zhang Guolao’s fish drum, Lan Caihe’s flower basket, Cao Guojiu’s jade tablet, Han Xiangzi’s flute, He Xiangu’s lotus, and Lü Dongbin’s sword. Craftsmen combined these symbols with scrollwork, bats, clouds, and waves to create decorative compositions that also conveyed wishes for longevity, good fortune, and wealth.

Stories about the Eight Immortals were similarly adaptable. Among commoners, plays such as “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” and “The Eight Immortals Assembly Celebrate Longevity” were widely performed. By the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns (1736–1820) of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), such stories were increasingly associated with birthday celebrations, with gatherings of the Eight Immortals symbolizing longevity, joy, and good fortune.

Among intellectuals, meanwhile, the Eight Immortals served as a source of creative inspiration. One example is “The Record of Handan,” the last of the “Four Dreams of Linchuan” by the great Ming playwright Tang Xianzu. Rather than focusing on reunion, the play uses Lü Dongbin to explore the illusory nature of worldly ambition.

In the play, Lü meets a poor scholar obsessed with achieving fame and gives him a porcelain pillow. After putting on a pot of rice to boil, the scholar falls asleep and dreams that he marries, places first in the imperial examinations, and spends decades navigating political machinations before becoming a powerful and honored official, only to eventually die from overindulgence. Waking to find his pot of rice still cooking, the scholar realizes his entire lifetime of ambition was merely a brief dream. Lü then begins the process of enlightening him, introducing him to the other immortals, who appear one by one to admonish him until he finally awakens to the emptiness of his desires.

All this shows just how adaptable the stories of the Eight Immortals have always been. Taoist traditions and popular folklore have continually shaped and reshaped one another, producing new versions of the group for different audiences and eras.

In that sense, what is happening to the Eight Immortals today is nothing new.

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: An Eight Immortals room screen at a museum in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.title: She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.content:
Editor’s note: After Mu Qianwen hit the headlines in 2024 as one of Porsche’s top sales consultants worldwide, she became the target of toxic online abuse, including sexually explicit AI-generated videos. For this 35-year-old mother in Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, the harassment got so bad that she even contemplated suicide. Rather than give in, she decided to fight back through the courts. Here, Mu shares her ordeal in her own words.

I first started attracting attention online in early 2024. I’d already been “sales champion of the month” at my dealership more than 20 times, but on the last day of 2023, our sales manager presented me with a crystal trophy. I had sold 170 cars that year.

When I posted about the achievement on Xiaohongshu (the lifestyle platform known globally as RedNote), it soon became a trending topic, and more than a dozen media outlets asked me for interviews.

But there was also a huge backlash, with some questioning how I could have sold so many cars and suggesting that the dealership must have inflated my sales figures. Our general manager issued a statement to refute any talk of deception, but the allegations kept coming.

A woman selling luxury cars seems like an easy formula for a viral story. Some people claimed I was making 3 million yuan ($447,000) a year. Porsche pays its salespeople about 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in commission for every car sold. We can earn several hundred thousand yuan a year, but exceeding 1 million is extremely difficult. I make enough to give my family a comfortable life, and I do own an entry-level Porsche, but I’ve never made anything close to that amount.

Rumors also began circulating that I treat my customers to lavish dinners, which is pure innuendo. In reality, I work such long hours that I barely have time to eat, let alone entertain. I’ve never dated a customer or had any kind of inappropriate relationship. More than 60% of my buyers are women.

After people claimed that the dealership had exaggerated my sales figures, I set myself a goal: In 2024, I would sell another 170 cars, no matter what. On Dec. 31, I was still one car short of the target. But then a female customer walked in. I told her about my goal and offered her an attractive price on a model. It was win-win. A little after 3 p.m., she placed an order.

In 2025, I sold even more cars — 192. At this point, I felt I’d answered all my critics. But the online abuse had only gotten worse. Early that year, I discovered that someone had spread a sexually explicit rumor about me using an overseas social media platform. They claimed that I slept with customers, and posted as “proof” a fabricated video and audio recording using a different woman, whose face was concealed throughout.

I tried to brush it off and told myself not to take it too seriously, that this was just the price of publicity. But my friends urged me to report it to the police, so I ultimately filed a report.

At first, the explicit material mainly circulated on overseas websites and social media, so the impact was limited. But last October, things escalated. Someone shared a misleading video via (the instant-messaging platform) WeChat that combined one of my sales-promotion posters with footage of a woman with a completely different body shape to me undressing in a hotel room. There were also some demeaning AI-generated videos.

This time, the content spread incredibly fast among my circle. Friends, colleagues, and customers all started asking me what was going on. I felt like my world was collapsing. I again reported the videos to the police.

My phone number was also leaked, and I began receiving harassing calls, sometimes at one or two in the morning. A man in Qingdao called out of the blue to ask me to “come over and spend the night with him.” I recorded the conversation and sent it to the police, who issued the man a warning.

My WeChat was blowing up, too. I didn’t know whether a new friend request was from someone looking to buy a car or for something else. Some people would start by talking about cars and then steer the conversation toward asking me out. Others were more covert, asking me to record a video showing the “backseat legroom.” I knew what they really wanted. One person messaged, “I know it’s not you in those videos, but I fantasize that it is. Can you provide me with services?”

Social media is an important source of customers for me, so I couldn’t just ignore it. I still had to livestream. But when I was on camera introducing cars, I’d always see inappropriate comments pop up, like “I saw that video” or “You’re so hot.”

I even overheard some customers in the showroom talking about me. That hit me hard. I could no longer pretend that this online smear campaign wasn’t affecting me.

By now, the enthusiasm and confidence I used to have with customers was gone. I feared talking with people, paranoid that they must be gossiping about me.

At my lowest point, I briefly considered jumping from a building. I felt there was no point in being alive, that the world had become dark. It seemed everyone looked at me differently.

I told my supervisor that I had reached breaking point and needed time off. I was given three days, so I took my son back to my hometown, Yantai (about a three-hour drive from Qingdao), where we stayed at a beautiful guesthouse. I told myself that I had to keep living for my child and be responsible for my family. I had to clear my name.

When I returned to work, I was so anxious I couldn’t walk straight; my muscles were so tense I unconsciously leaned to one side. I wore a neck brace because even the slightest jolt during a test drive would send sharp pains up my back. I developed insomnia and tinnitus. At one point, I even struggled to speak.

Zero to hero

I started in auto sales in 2013, initially selling Audi and Lincoln cars in Beijing. I joined the Porsche dealership in downtown Qingdao in 2018. At first, my performance was so poor that I nearly lost my job.

Most of the salespeople had years of experience, and I was the youngest. Social media wasn’t the powerful tool it is today; business depended largely on walk-ins and referrals. For the first six months, I barely sold anything. At our 2019 New Year’s meeting, the sales manager asked everyone to share their goals for the year ahead. I said, “I want to survive at Porsche.”

I didn’t know the different models or specifications well enough. If a knowledgeable customer asked me a question, I felt intimidated and out of my depth. I started getting up at 6 a.m. to memorize technical information. I’d stand near colleagues and listen as they explained different cars. I studied the way they talked.

One colleague said I needed to dress better, so I started wearing tailored shirts and paying more attention to the cut and quality of everything I wore. In sales, it’s appearance, not skill, that makes the first impression. When I applied makeup, I felt more confident. Even though I had only four days off a month, I scheduled manicures and eyelash extensions, and sometimes skin booster injections.

I was a core consultant by my second year, became one of the dealership’s top performers in 2020, and was closing 17 deals a month in 2021.

Demand for foreign luxury cars has declined in the past two years, but my sales have continued to increase, largely because of social media. Of my 170 customers in 2023, 15% found me through social media. In 2025, it was 41%.

I also run a Porsche owners’ WeChat group with several hundred members. I organize monthly group events, such as camping trips, yacht outings, and nature walks. If I stop talking to someone as soon as a deal is done, they’ll always be just a customer. But if we spend time together, we can become friends. Referrals are an important part of my sales.

My typical workday runs from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. I’ve hardly taken any annual leave in all these years. If I go on vacation, customers disappear. I’m competitive by nature. I crave deals, performance figures, the feeling of being number one. I’m currently leading Porsche’s global sales rankings for September 2026, but someone could still overtake me.

The hardest word

When selling cars, effort usually pays off. But clearing a damaged reputation? That’s different.

Someone can casually share something about me online, and suddenly I have to spend money, time, and energy to respond. I have to pay lawyers and gather evidence. I filed 31 complaints to Douyin (China’s version of TikTok) alone between October 2025 and April this year about abusive messages, videos that used my image without permission, and people cloning my voice to promote get-rich-quick books.

I hand the most egregious messages directly to the police. One man I reported was initially very cocky. He seemed to think I was bluffing and wouldn’t be able to track him down. The authorities eventually found him, and he sent me an apology.

A 20-something Porsche owner in Qingdao forwarded some offensive material about me in a group chat and was given five days of administrative detention. I later accepted his apology, too, but then his family called my dealership’s customer service line to complain — they couldn’t understand why he still needed to be detained. I had no say in his punishment, but they obviously never stopped to think about how his actions might have affected me.

Even the outcomes of such cases haven’t halted the spread of false allegations; I still encounter vitriol during livestreams and on social media.

In July this year, the police gave me details of a 30-something man in the eastern Fujian province who’d been behind one of the AI-generated videos. I’d never met him. He was given 10 days of administrative detention in last October, but he never contacted me to apologize.

I think receiving punishment is not the same as saying sorry. This man was punished for spreading rumors, but what about the harm he caused? So I decided to file a civil lawsuit against him. All I want is for him to apologize and say explicitly that the woman in that video is not me.

Some friends urged me to press criminal charges, but I don’t want him to bear the consequences for the rest of his life. As a mother, I think about what would happen to his child if he were prosecuted. My lawyer says that if the civil case goes to trial, it could take up to two years. No matter how long it takes, I need to see it through.

Now I’m facing claims that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt, that I’m dredging things up again. In reality, just because the story is no longer in the headlines, it doesn’t mean those negative voices have disappeared from my life.

My son is in kindergarten. He doesn’t have a phone, and he knows nothing about what’s going on. All he knows is that his mom is the top salesperson at Porsche Qingdao. When I asked him what he wanted to do when he grew up, he said he wanted to sell cars. He’s proud of his mom.

What happens when he grows up, gets a phone, and sees what people have said about his mother? What if his classmates use the rumors against him? Who takes responsibility for that? The same goes for my parents. I want to clear my name for my family’s sake.

I still like being number one, but after everything that’s happened, my ambition has waned. I want to focus more on family and my health.

My life used to be a straight line between work and home, but over the past two years, I’ve started leaving more time for myself — meals with colleagues and friends, live music bars, taking my son to the mountains or the beach.

I wonder whether the rumors will disappear once the lawsuit is over. If people keep talking, there might be nothing more I can do. I’ve done everything within my power. If I win the case, that will be the end of it for me.

Women have sent me long messages of support, telling me how brave I am. Many professional women have shared that they have been the targets of similar smear campaigns and felt completely helpless. They ask me what they should do. I don’t know what to tell them.

As told to reporter Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Mu Qianwen at her workplace in Qingdao, Shandong province, August 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.title: Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.content:
A northern Chinese village has announced it will spend 30 million yuan ($4.5 million) to recruit 100 character performers — known in China as NPCs, or non-playable characters — to interact with tourists. Successful hires will receive a range of salaries, with the highest reportedly reaching 10 million yuan a year.

Situ Town, a scenic spot located in Situ Village in the northern Shanxi province, will finance the recruitment partly through its publicity budget and partly from startup funds, Zhou Xiaoming, the village Party secretary, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper on Sunday.

Once a coal town, Situ Village’s coal was gradually depleted by the end of the 20th century. To address its lack of resources, in 2009, the village built an agricultural ecological park — an area that combines farming with ecological protection and tourism — on a slag heap, which later grew into a highly rated national attraction. The village is known for its “iron flower” performances — a folk art in which local blacksmiths hurl molten iron into the air.

Zhou announced the NPC recruitment on Sept. 19 in a video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. “No matter what your talent is, as long as you can make the tourists on stage have fun, and the audience below enjoy themselves, we’ll give you a platform — and 1 million, even 10 million (yuan),” he said in the video.

The plan quickly drew suspicion online, with some arguing that the money would be better spent investing in the scenic area itself, such as by adding amusement parks, building affordable guesthouses, improving green spaces, upgrading the “iron flower” show, or supporting local artists.

Previously, the scenic spot had announced a short video contest — also led by Zhou — in August in which 5 million yuan was offered to participants based on likes and views. Winning the top prize of 1 million yuan required 10 million likes and 300 million views.

Official data showed that in 2025, Situ Town received 2.2 million tourist visits, double the year prior, generating a total revenue of 350 million yuan. Meanwhile, tourism-related jobs grew from 500 to more than 1,000, the latter accounting for roughly a third of the village’s labor force.

Zhou noted, however, that the scenic spot has faced steep losses in recent years. “In 2023 we lost 500,000 yuan, in 2024 we lost 500,000 yuan, and in 2025 we lost money, but not much,” he said.

More than 7,000 people have applied for the NPC positions so far, with video interviews planned for over 50, Zhou said, adding that they have not yet set an application deadline. Zhou added that NPC salaries will range from 500,000 to 10 million yuan depending on the traffic they generate, the emotional value they bring to tourists, and tourists’ degree of satisfaction.

Recruiting NPCs is reportedly the scenic spot’s first step, with the goal of eventually cultivating its own homegrown talent. Its employees, Zhou said, are actually the biggest NPCs, but they need a good environment and role models to imitate — and those recruited with the 30 million yuan are meant to set an example.

Zeng Bowei, a professor at the Tourism College of Beijing Union University, told The Paper that the most important value of NPCs is transforming culture into something tourists can see and participate in.

“Although NPCs have been called ‘non-playable characters,’ their true value to scenic areas is precisely making each tourist into a player,” Zeng said, adding that with the right roles, stories, and cultural backing, NPCs can increase traffic in the long term.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019070/Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.title: Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019070/Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.content:
The hair business in Xuchang, in China’s central Henan province, has been growing since the 16th century. Starting from opera props, the city is now the “Wig Capital of the World.”

Roughly 60% of wigs on the global market come from Xuchang. According to the local commerce bureau, the industry’s total import-export value hit 11.56 billion yuan ($1.72 billion) in the first half of 2026, up by nearly 11% year on year.

The core of this pillar industry, Jian’an District, is home to 311 foreign trade enterprises shipping hair products — and business is booming. Yet life behind the sales figures isn’t so rosy.

Although cross-border e-commerce platforms have helped companies reach new markets, including North America and Europe, businesses here say the commissions they charge are making it difficult to turn a profit.

The industry is also facing a potential serious labor crisis, with high-than-average salaries failing to attract more talent, especially younger workers.

Long and short of it

According to local historical archives, people in Xuchang began collecting human hair as early as the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), using it to make theatrical props and fake beards.

It wasn’t until 1900, when Bai Xihe from the city’s Quandian Village collaborated with a German merchant to establish a hair trading depot, that a wider industry began to emerge. Soon, villagers were fanning out nationwide to find supplies, with the raw materials pooled in Jian’an.

By the 1930s, Xuchang had dozens of workshops making processed hair, or dangfa, which was shipped through ports in Qingdao in the eastern Shandong province and Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, to overseas markets including Japan and the Philippines.

Dangfa is a semi-finished product made from human hair that has been washed, straightened, sorted, and tied into bundles. It’s a key upstream raw material for wigs.

Many rural families opened small home-based operations, forming the embryo of a cottage industry. The men would travel around the nation collecting hair, while the women stayed home to sort and knot wigs strand by strand, an essential craft that takes at least six months to master.

“An industrial ecosystem doesn’t come together overnight,” says Tian Liangjun, vice president of the Xuchang Hair Products Association, established in 2004. “Our industry has more than a century of accumulated history. The raw materials, the talent, the technology, the market intelligence are all here — and so are the supporting accessories, equipment, printing, and packaging.”

By the time China began to open its economy in the late 1970s and early ’80s, Xuchang possessed the raw materials and manufacturing capacity, but companies from South Korea had control of the network channels to overseas markets. They purchased hair and semi-finished goods from Xuchang and sold finished products to beauty supply stores in the United States. Chinese enterprises were consigned to contract processing, with limited profits and little market leverage.

“In the past, more than 80% of the U.S. hair-product market was controlled by South Korean companies. They had us by the throat,” Tian says. “We depended on them, so when South Korean agents came to Xuchang to inspect the goods, they acted like they were above us. Some of us even had to bring them bowls of water to wash their hands at the end of their inspection.”

However, things changed in 1990, when entrepreneur Zheng Youquan founded the Xuchang Hair Products General Factory, which saw local businesses advance to producing finished wigs.
