World.title: Azerbaijan, Russia discuss military and military-technical cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. Meetings are being held as part of the 6th Azerbaijan International Defence Exhibition “ADEX-2026”, organized at the Baku Expo Center, to discuss issues related to the development of Azerbaijan’s military-technical cooperation with other countries.

This was stated in a report by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense.

According to the report, on September 30, Minister of Defense of the Republic of Azerbaijan Colonel General Zakir Hasanov met with a delegation from the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation headed by Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov.

The sides discussed the role of military and military-technical cooperation in ensuring peace and security in the region, as well as other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijani Defense Minister holds meetings with UK and Slovak counterparts (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. On September 30, a number of meetings were held as part of the 6th Azerbaijan International Defense Exhibition ADEX-2026, focusing on issues of Azerbaijan’s military-technical cooperation with other countries, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense reports.

According to the ministry, Azerbaijani Defense Minister Colonel General Zakir Hasanov held meetings with the defense ministers of the United Kingdom and Slovakia, who were participating in the international exhibition.

The Defense Minister emphasized that Azerbaijan is interested in cooperation with the United Kingdom and the Slovak Republic in all areas, particularly in defense and security, and expressed satisfaction with the current state of these relations.

The UK Minister of State for Defense, Lord Vernon Coaker, and Slovak Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defense Robert Kaliňák expressed their satisfaction with their visit to Azerbaijan and participation in the exhibition, noting that cooperation between the defense structures of the two countries in the areas of military education, military-technical innovations, as well as other fields, continues on a positive trajectory.

During the meetings, the ministers discussed future plans for cooperation in the areas of defence and security, military and military-technical fields, and held a broad exchange of views on matters of mutual interest.

World.title: Mother of men killed on Mexico surf trip asks for timely verdict at murder trial
World.content:
The mother of Jake and Callum Robinson has made a heartfelt plea at the Mexican murder trial into her sons' deaths for a timely verdict.

The bodies of Australian brothers and their American friend, Carter Rhoad, were found at the bottom of a well in Baja California, along Mexico's Pacific coast, after the men were reported missing from a surfing trip in 2024.

The prosecution has argued the trio were killed in a robbery gone wrong. However, the defence has claimed there is not enough evidence to prove this theory.

For the past four weeks, Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús have been on trial in Ensenada over charges of aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery, violent robbery and grand theft auto.

Today, a court heard the closing arguments in the case against the men would be held on October 8, local time with a verdict to be delivered some time afterwards.

Ángel Jesús has been in custody in a local jail. (Supplied)

Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", faces a possible sentence of 378 years. (Supplied: Mexican police handout)

Irineo Francisco has links to the Sinaloa cartel, according to court documents. (Supplied)

In response, the prosecution asked Judge Raul Hernandez Arellano if Debra Robinson could address the court. The request was immediately accepted.

Ms Robinson, who has appeared at court with her husband Martin almost every day since the start of the trial, began by expressing her gratitude at the time and attention Judge Hernandez Arellano had given to the case.

She then explained that she and Martin had booked flights back to Australia and needed to leave Mexico on October 9.

Ms Robinson requested the verdict be delivered before they returned home, adding that they would be "extremely grateful" if their plea was accepted.

"It would mean so much to us as Callum and Jake's parents to be here for the verdict," she told the judge, close to tears.

" We have travelled such a long way to seek justice for our sons and Carter. Thank you. "

The three men accused of killing the Robinson brothers were seated close to the Robinsons in court. Shackled in orange prison jumpsuits, they appeared to show no emotion as the request was heard.

The judge, who had listened intently to Ms Robinson's short plea, said he would take it into consideration. He later came back and said he had adjusted his schedule to accommodate the request.

He told the court he would hand down a verdict at 10am on October 9, less than 24 hours after closing arguments and shortly before the Robinsons were due to fly home.

The parents are also set to deliver a final statement in court after the verdict is delivered next week.

As today's court session ended, the judge stood up from his seat and came down to the floor to shake the hands of the Robinsons as well as the lawyers for the prosecution and defence. He did not shake the hands of the accused.

'We feel your love and your arms around us'

Today the defence was due to cross-examine two key witnesses who gave evidence at the beginning of the trial.

The mother and son, whose names have been withheld, are in witness protection.

The court was told the defence did not wish to question the two witnesses.

Debra and Martin Robinson delivered their plea for a quicker verdict at the murder trial. (AFP: Guillermo Arias)

Outside court, the Robinsons delivered a brief statement to waiting media, thanking everyone for their love and support.

"To everyone back home in Australia and around the world, we feel your love and your arms around us," Ms Robinson said.

"And it is giving us strength during some difficult days. As you know, we don't want to comment on the proceedings while the trial is going out of respect for the court. And its process.

"We will wait until the verdict before we speak any further."

Throughout the trial, Mr Robinson has worn a T-shirt supporting the Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation. The logo on the back reads: "Live bigger, shine brighter, love harder."

The case is set to resume next week.

World.title: Shock closure of school leaves parents of additional needs kids in a bind
World.content:
The sudden closure of a school in Melbourne's east has left parents and staff stunned, with families now scrambling to find their children new schools for the coming year.

In a letter sent to parents in early September, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools (MACS) said the decision to close St Philip's School at the conclusion of the coming term was made after a review into school's long-term sustainability.

The review found the Blackburn North school was "not sustainable in its current form" due to enrolments having been in "steady decline for many years", the letter said.

"Despite genuine effort to strengthen the school's position and some recent interest from prospective families for the 2027 prep intake, enrolments remain critically low at only 33 students for 2026," it said.

MACS attributed the closure in part to a low level of enrolments at the school for the coming year. (Facebook: St Philip's Parish Blackburn North)

The letter, signed by St Philip's principal Michelle Worcester and MACS regional general manager Marwin Austerberry, said neighbouring MACS schools would have sufficient capacity for displaced students and that it would support them with the transition process.

But several parents told the ABC they selected the school for the support provided to students with learning difficulties and neurodivergence, making suitable alternative schools difficult to find.

The ABC has contacted MACS and St Philip's for comment.

Anthony Navaretti said he and other parents were blindsided by the closure announcement in early September.

"There was no communication that this might be anywhere near a possibility," said Mr Navaretti, who has two sons enrolled at St Philip's School.

" They haven't asked for any fundraising or raised concerns or given any sort of deadlines, it just kind of came out of the blue. "

'33 lives' affected by closure

Mr Navaretti's eldest son lives with autism and has been able to attend the same school as his brother due to the support offered by St Philip's.

The sudden closure meant the two boys may need to split up, he said.

"There's not a lot of time to find a school. I know one school near us said their enrolments were already full," Mr Navaretti said.

He said he believes teachers and support staff were also notified on the same day as parents.

MACS said in a letter to parents it will work with students and families to support a transition into nearby Catholic schools. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Angi Hill was devastated by the news of the school's imminent closure.

"I can only speak for my own family, my son was very upset, there were tears," Ms Hill said.

"So there's a lot of processing to do, obviously for ourselves as parents, but also for the children as well."

Her son has been enrolled at the school since prep and she said his challenges would have made attending a mainstream school very difficult.

While she could understand the financial aspect of the closure, Ms Hill said the school meant so much more to the community than raw numbers suggested.

"If you were just looking at spreadsheet of numbers of kids in different schools under MACS, it's kind of no-brainer to say: 'Hey, 33 kids, let's just shut that down'," Ms Hill said.

"But it's not just 33 children, it's 33 lives.

"We have families in our community who have shopped around for schools for a long time, they might have been on to their sixth, seventh or eighth school."

Ms Hill worries the closure will send the wrong message to children that have struggled in mainstream schools.

"'What if the next school I go to is going to shut down? I better not even bother or make friends or try too hard," she said children might think.

"With these children who finally find a school that feels emotionally safe, for them to hear this school has closed down it only exacerbates the anxiety and their fears."

World.title: Teenager faces youth justice court over 'pro-Nazi' Instagram posts
World.content:
A Northern Territory teenager who allegedly posted "pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist" content on Instagram over the course of almost a year has faced court over a string of alleged Commonwealth offences.

The boy, who cannot be identified, faced the Youth Justice Court this week charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass or offend as well as accessing or possessing violent or extremist material online.

In January this year, according to a charge sheet obtained by the ABC, the boy allegedly accessed a video "featuring a tachometer amended to look like Adolf Hitler".

A tachometer measures the revolution of a spinning object and features on the dashboard of most cars.

The boy also accessed footage of a 2017 "white supremacist terrorist attack" in Charlottesville, Virginia in the United States, where white supremacist James Alex Fields Jr deliberately drove his car into a crowd of people, killing 32-year-old Heather Heyer and injuring more than two dozen others. Fields later pleaded guilty to 30 hate crimes over the attack.

Four days later, the boy allegedly "possessed or controlled" a video of a livestream of the 2019 New Zealand mass terror attack made by Brenton Tarrant, the Australian man who was later convicted of murdering 51 people at two Christchurch mosques.

The AFP's Paula Hudson says investigators "worked tirelessly to disrupt anyone who attempted to possess or distribute violent extremist material". (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The boy also stands charged with possessing or controlling a video of a livestream of another terrorist attack in New York state, in which Payton Gendron recorded himself killing 10 black people at a Buffalo supermarket in 2022.

Among a total of 14 charges, police allege the teenager possessed an "imitation firearm with silencer and magazine" in May.

In announcing the boy's arrest in May, Australian Federal Police Counter Terrorism Commander Paula Hudson said investigators "worked tirelessly to disrupt anyone who attempted to possess or distribute violent extremist material".

"Early intervention is key to ensuring individuals are disrupted and our community is kept safe," Commander Hudson said.

"Criminal behaviour or actions which advocate hatred, fear, violence and humiliation, and attempt to erode Australia's social fabric will not be tolerated.

"Those who engage in this unlawful activity will be investigated and brought before the courts."

The boy has been granted bail and will return to court on October 26.

World.title: This marsupial used to be 'abundant' — now, researchers can't find it
World.content:
For nearly a year, Ryan Sauermann has been scouring the Top End's Litchfield National Park in hopes of catching a glimpse of a northern quoll — but he's yet to spot one.

The University of Melbourne PhD student believes the once-common marsupial may now be locally extinct in the region.

Cane toads and feral cats are among the threats facing these small marsupials. (Supplied: Parks and Wildlife)

"We started out hoping to set up a captive breeding and rewilding colony, given how quickly their populations have declined," he said.

"Now the PhD project has turned more into [looking at] where are they, are they even still around, and if not, why?"

Northern Territory Parks and Wildlife ranger Darius Nasir has been helping Mr Sauermann with the research.

The senior park ranger used to spot the nocturnal northern quolls "almost every night", but said it's now been four or five years since he's seen one.

Ranger Darius Nasir says northern quolls were a lot more common in the area just a few years ago. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Around 2009, 2010, I used to see them all the time around my house … my dogs would be going off and it'd be quolls, quite abundant quolls back then," he said.

Mr Sauermann said the spread of cane toads was largely to blame for the decline in the native species.

"As the cane toad front moves through, we're losing 85 to 95 per cent [of the northern quoll population]," he said.

The species' decline is not restricted to the Top End — earlier this year, research in Queensland confirmed spotted-tail and northern quolls were "functionally" extinct in large parts of the state, where the introduced toads also pose an ecological threat.

Ryan Sauermann, alongside rangers and other researchers, has set up a number of cameras around the national park, in hopes of capturing footage of northern quolls. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Sauermann said changes to fire management and other feral species also posed major threats to northern quolls, which are listed as "endangered" nationally, and "critically endangered" in the Northern Territory.

"More frequent burns tend to be worse for the quolls as well," Mr Sauermann said.

"The introduction of feral predators — cats especially — are a big issue."

A range of methods

Mr Sauermann has set up more than 30 wildlife-tracking cameras throughout the national park.

Filming equipment has been set up in Litchfield National Park, but none of the cameras so far have captured a glimpse of the endangered northern quoll. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Food is used to attract animals to these "camera traps", with footage showing a variety of feral animals and other wildlife sniffing around the area.

"We've gotten quite a lot of buffalo and pigs, we've gotten a fair few cats, but no quolls at all so far," he said.

"It's been north of 4,000 nights of camera trapping, which means 30-plus cameras deployed for almost a year."

Loading...

Citizen science is also playing a big role in the study, with Mr Sauermann doing everything he can to raise awareness about the plight of the northern quoll.

"In Litchfield where we've got a lot of tourists, I've been putting up flyers around park that say, 'If you see a northern quoll, please give me a shout'," he said.

"I've reached out to a number of Facebook groups … but unfortunately, those have yielded very limited success so far."

A wanted poster, on display inside the national park, urges visitors to report any sightings of the northern quoll. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The search continues

Mr Sauermann has been flying from Melbourne to the Top End "every couple of months" since late last year — and said he will keep coming back, despite so far not locating any quolls.

"Just because we're not finding anything right now doesn't mean that they're not here, doesn't mean we should stop looking," he said.

The PhD candidate said, aside from dingoes, the carnivorous northern quoll is "probably one of the apex predators out here".

Researchers say feral cats and cane toads inside Litchfield National Park are threatening the species. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"They're the ones managing, not just insect populations, but also other rodent populations," he said.

" They're massively important for the ecosystem. "

Mr Nasir said keeping quolls in northern Australia was "greatly important", and he feared the possibility of an ecological snowball effect if the "quite cute" animals were wiped out.

Northern quolls used to be abundant in the NT, but the Litchfield-based research project has confirmed the population is declining. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"If we lose these quolls, we won't see them again — it'll be like the bloody thylacine," he said.

" We've got too many extinct animals around already as it is, let alone [adding] another one. "

Mr Sauermann urged pet-owners to keep dogs and cats away from wildlife, encouraging Territorians to do their bit in protecting the environment and trying to limit fire risk.

"There's so much more out there than I think people realise and just getting people interested would be a huge, huge win," he said.

World.title: Charges laid over shooting near Geraldton
World.content:
Police have charged a Geraldton man in relation to a shooting that left a man with a bullet wound to his leg in WA's Midwest.

The victim was shot in the early hours of Wednesday morning near Moonyoonooka, just east of Geraldton.

He was found with the gunshot wound just before 1am and is recovering in Geraldton Regional Hospital with serious injuries.

The WA Country Health Service confirmed the man had since been released from hospital.

Officers from the WA Police Tactical Response Group speak to a man in Utakarra after Monday's shooting near Geraldton. (Supplied)

The shooting sparked a major police operation with tactical response officers fanning out across Geraldton, eventually honing in on a property in the nearby suburb of Utakarra.

Stunned neighbours watched as heavily armed officers from the Tactical Response Group swarmed the house, with five people taken into custody.

A 30-year-old man from the suburb of Wonthella has since been charged with an unlawful act or omission endangering a person's life, health or safety, along with wilfully destroying evidence.

He is due to face the Geraldton Magistrates Court today.

An armed officer stands outside during a raid of the property. (Supplied)

Yesterday, Acting Superintendent Ben Huggett said some of the five people arrested were released, but would not confirm how many remained in custody.

He said three people were believed to be involved in the shooting, but it was early in the investigation, and details were still being firmed up.

Police have declined to reveal any details about the incident or what led to it, but confirmed the alleged shooter and victim are known to each other.

World.title: 100-million-year-old fossil reveals ancient outback bird
World.content:
An "extremely rare" fossil discovery in outback Queensland has revealed a new species of prehistoric bird that roamed Australia more than 100 million years ago.

While digging in the remains of an ancient inland sea near Richmond, about 500km inland from Townsville, Kevin Petersen uncovered a long, slender bone.

The then-curator of marine fossil museum Kronosaurus Korner sent a picture to University of New England palaeontologist Matt White, who drove to Richmond to have a look.

"I was first looking at bones that looked quite similar in China … over 20 years ago, so I knew exactly what they were," Dr White said.

Tenuicruris piscanexum is believed to have been roughly the size of a bush turkey. (Supplied: Artwork by Travis Tischler)

A week later, another bone was found.

"We usually find a lot of marine reptiles out at Richmond, but to find bird bones, it's extremely rare," Dr White said.

Filing in the gaps

Researchers used the fossilised tarsometatarsus, a fused foot bone found in birds, and tibiotarsus, the longest leg bone, to formally describe a new bird species, Tenuicruris piscanexum, which experts believe lived during the Cretaceous period about 100 million years ago.

Dr White said the bird likely had teeth and was roughly the size of a scrub turkey, with completed fossils found in China and Germany from the same period used to fill critical gaps in the animal's appearance.

"[There's] a little bit of artistic licence," he said.

"But we have had a lot of birds where we have more complete skeletons and we can do reverse dissection and go, right, these are roughly what the legs look like."

Matt White says the discovery of bird bones is "extremely rare". (Supplied: University of New England)

University of New South Wales Professor Mike Archer, who was not involved in the research, said primitive birds that lived during the Cretaceous period, such as Tenuicruris piscanexum, shared many features synonymous with their reptilian ancestors.

"Birds are dinosaurs," he said.

"Some of the birds have become so dinosaurian-like, like our cassowary, that you have to worry more about that than you would have had to worry about a velociraptor."

Against the odds

Despite the diversity of birds living in the country today, Dr White said Australia's Cretaceous bird record remains remarkably sparse.

Before the Richmond discovery, only a handful of bird bones from the period had been found in Australia, with just one other primitive species described in 1986.

Mike Archer says the fragile nature of bird bones means very few survive the fossilisation process. (Supplied)

Professor Archer said the same traits that allowed birds to fly made them less likely to survive fossilisation.

"The problem with bird fossils is that they're incredibly fragile," he said.

"Their bones are paper thin, and it's much harder and much less likely to have them survive the processes of fossilisation."

"Every time a fossil of one of these kinds these flying animals turns up, we all have to cheer because they're very rare."

Professor Archer said the location of the discovery also supported theories that some primitive birds in the group fed on fish and travelled across large stretches of water.

"It's quite likely that the part of the [inland sea] where it came from was not near the land," he said.

"It might well have been fairly far out to sea … reinforcing the idea that some of these birds could have been foraging for fish."

World.title: Mid-air stabbing, cockpit scrum and 'miracle' landing: Inside the flydubai flight
World.content:
A plummet in the air, a scrum in the cockpit, and a miraculous landing is how eyewitnesses describe the flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, now labelled by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz as "a jihadist terror attempt".

Warning: This article contains graphic images.

On Wednesday, local time, a commercial flight with 174 people aboard had to divert to Saudi Arabia after one pilot stabbed the other and "apparently tried to crash the plane".

The Boeing 737, operated by a sister airline of Emirates, took off from Dubai International Airport but mid-flight plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.

Customers and crew who then entered the cockpit foiled a co-pilot's attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, with a second pair of off-duty flydubai pilots landing the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Israel to 'ramp up' security after pilot attack A commercial flight carrying 174 people to Tel Aviv is forced to divert to Saudi Arabia after one pilot stabs the other and tries to crash the plane.

Passenger uses TV knowledge to steer plane

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun was among the first to step into action.

Mr Hayoun said he and others pushed their way into the cockpit where he saw the unharmed pilot apparently trying to destroy the controls, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported.

"The door apparently wasn't locked and we managed to open it somehow," Mr Hayoun told journalists.

"What made it difficult for us was the [other] pilot himself. He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door."

Israeli officials later identified the injured pilot as Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, who managed to click the release to open the cockpit, letting the passengers in.

As people wrestled with the attacker, Mr Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television.

Then other crew members took over.

Flydubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew "who diverted and landed the aircraft safely".

Hero passenger Yaniv Hayoun later met with Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu. (AP: Tomer Appelbaum)

Later, in a video released by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, the Israeli leader was shown at Ben Gurion Airport hugging Mr Hayoun.

"I see you and I see a lion — a big hero," Mr Netanyahu told Mr Hayoun, who was still wearing the blood-stained shirt he had on during the flight.

When asked by Mr Netanyahu whether he knew what he was doing, he answered: "I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister."

Loading...

Dentist, dad and sky marshals among flight's heroes

Another passenger in the scrum, Tzvika Manes, told Channel 12 it took many minutes to subdue the attacking pilot.

A third responder, dentist Shota Musayev, told journalists the passengers realised they had just seconds to take control of the plane before a "critical event".

He said they feared another attacker might be on the plane so "spread a few more people inside the plane so that if something happened we would be able to simply take control".

Mr Musayev also attended to the injured pilot who was "praying the whole time … and I was afraid we would really lose him".

Passengers gather around an injured man on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. (Reuters/Social media)

Among the passengers who intervened were members of Israeli security forces and sky marshals, according to a person familiar with a probe by Saudi Arabia and regional partners.

"This is something you do without thinking, just running to save your daughter's life, your family's life," said Asaf Rajuan, another passenger who helped restrain the attacker.

He spoke with a forehead still bloodied from the struggle and later told The New York Times there was a fear about where they would land.

"There was only desert below us," he added.

Israeli passenger Asaf Rajuan said he acted to save his family. (AP: Ariel Schalit)

Plummet felt like 'massive turbulence'

Describing the flight's sudden plunge, Almog Italie said it felt like the plane was passing through "massive turbulence" before he realised the life-or-death struggle unfolding in the cockpit.

"It was dropping like for 20, 30 seconds, and then balanced, and then started dropping again, and balanced again, and then we saw that [there were] people in the front, directly [in front of] the cockpit," he said.

Mr Italie said the reserve crew soon "took over the airplane and balanced it".

"It was quite scary, but not for long," he said.

"Most of the passengers kept calm and were very supportive to each other.

"We landed in Saudi Arabia, which we got a very very warm welcome with a lot of medical staff and food and anything we needed, and we're waiting for the flight back to Tel Aviv."

Hours after landing in Tel Aviv, Mr Italie said: "It has been a long day. Luckily for us it's ended."

Loading...

Terrified passenger felt 'not among the living'

Other passengers recounted their absolute fear as the incident took place.

Chaim Nazarovitz said the ordeal had been "very terrifying", adding for a moment he felt like he was "not among the living".

Loading...

"We're going to die," passenger Naama Bershadski recalled thinking as she closed her eyes and prayed.

Miryam Shira Ohayon described the plane as "pretty much out of control" while the incident unfolded.

"It was really on the way to crashing and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting in Tel Aviv.

Passengers rejoice after landing back in Tel Aviv. (AP: Ariel Schalit)

As they landed back in Israel, Lital Shachaf thanked God she was home.

"I just can say that it was a miracle," she said.

" It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it. We didn't think we will make it but thank God we are in Israel. "

ABC/Reuters/AFP/AP

World.title: Nation's love affair with coffee on shaky ground as cost of living bites
World.content:
At a Queensland coffee-processing factory, 10 people are employed to ensure every batch tastes exactly as it should.

Each day they gather in groups of three or four around a rotating table, which has a few sinks on the side so they can spit out the samples as they go.

"We do sample up to 100 cups per day, so you don't want to be drinking that much coffee on a standard day," quality assurance manager or "chief taste-tester" for Nestlé Glenn Jones said.

Nestlé Australia's Gympie factory employs 10 tasters who sample the coffee every day. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

The factory in Gympie, about two hours' drive north of Brisbane, has been producing instant coffee since 1997.

Mr Jones said even though drinking the beverage was part of his job description, he also enjoyed it when he was off duty.

"I need coffee before I come to work in the morning, then I taste it all day, and I'll have coffee on the weekends — I love coffee," he said.

Glenn Jones still drinks coffee outside of work hours. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

A national obsession

Mr Jones is not alone in his obsession, with an estimated three-quarters of Australians consuming coffee regularly.

Data shows more than 5 million Australians visit a cafe daily for their caffeine hit.

Martin Brown says cappuccino sachets have been the "fastest-growing part of the market" in the past five years. (Supplied.)

But Martin Brown, general manager of Nestlé's coffee and dairy business, said the company's sales figures showed a shift back to home consumption.

"[Australia has] one of the most sophisticated coffee cultures in the world, but we also have a cost-of-living challenge at the moment," Mr Brown said.

"A lot of households are having to make choices and find smarter ways to buy things."

He said cappuccino sachets had been the "fastest-growing part of the market" in the past five years, but there was also a shift back to more "traditional" soluble instant coffee.

"A cup of Blend 43 will cost you 12 to 15 cents a cup … it's super convenient and it's value for money and none of that goes out of fashion," he said.

Nestlé Australia's Gympie processing plant produces about 20 million cups of coffee each day. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Coffee price pinch

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 3 per cent in the 12 months leading up to August this year, with meals out and takeaway prices up 4.5 per cent.

The average price of a cafe-bought flat white in Australia is now about $6 a cup, despite warnings it could soar to double digits this year.

University students (from left) Elora Hemmer, Charlotte Cairns and Holly Durbidge have cut back on buying coffee out. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

On Queensland's Sunshine Coast, university student Charlotte Cairns said it was even more expensive to buy a cold coffee.

"I feel like when a coffee is $5 it's like, 'Oh that's alright'," Ms Cairns said.

" Whereas when it's like $9 dollars just for an iced latte it's like, 'OK, this is strictly a treat, I can't be doing this tomorrow as well'. "

Deann Mayfield said she and her partner had started to limit the amount of coffee they bought out.

"It's very expensive. We have one special coffee a day, so we try not to double up," Ms Mayfield said.

Deann Mayfield says she feels for cafe owners, who were also dealing with rising costs. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

A challenging environment

Coffee bean prices reached record highs last year, forcing importers and roasters to raise their prices, which was ultimately passed on to customers.

While green bean prices have dropped in 2026, they remain three times higher than in 2021.

More than five million Australians visit a cafe or coffee shop every day. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Australian Specialty Coffee Association president Bruno Maiolo said the drop had not offset the increase in "all of the other costs", including rent, electricity, milk and wages.

"We have a one-in-two failure rate [for coffee businesses]," Mr Maiolo said.

"People are going broke, not because they're necessarily bad operators; it's because they cannot keep the margins that are required to stay in business.

" They're running on a shoestring. "

Bruno Maiolo says it is a challenging time to be in the cafe business. (Supplied)

He said consumers in Australia had much cheaper coffee than in European countries, despite the fact that it was more expensive to make here.

"We have a phobia of putting the price up because we're all scared that everyone will stop drinking coffee and they'll go somewhere else," he said.

" No-one can absorb price increases forever. "

Simon O'Brien has made a conscious decision to offer $5 coffees to keep costs down for customers. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Simon O'Brien runs a coffee shop by the beach at Alexandra Headland and said he was able to still charge $5 for a cup due to the regular foot traffic.

"We've got coffee that people keep coming back for, and it's not so much about making a massive profit on each cup," Mr O'Brien said.

"It's the throughput over time and keeping that customer for as long as we can."

World.title: Jason Donovan is about to wrestle ‘a monster’. He just wishes his dad was here to see it
World.content:
The actor’s homecoming for One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest looks very different following the death of his father, Terence.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jason Donovan says “a lot of roads” have led him to Randle McMurphy, the charming, unruly psychiatric patient he will play in an upcoming stage production of One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “I’ve never worked so hard on a script in my entire life,” he says, speaking from Manchester, in the midst of his run as Coach Bolton in the stage production of High School Musical. McMurphy is a departure from the parts Donovan is best known for and he swings between excitement and apprehension. He is deliberately steering clear of studying Jack Nicholson’s Oscar-winning take on the character in the 1975 film, but he’s delved deeply into Ken Kesey’s novel. His review of the book, like most of his conversation, is candid, blunt and ends with a laugh. “I’ve read it. Not great on a first read. I reread it. Still f---ing … quite difficult to get your head around. [But] I sort of just threw caution to the wind. The biggest fear is fear itself. So I went, well, let’s go. You know, no risk, no magic. I think it’s the fear of the amount of work in it, the amount of dialogue. It’s a monster.” The script now resonates more on a personal level following the death of his beloved father Terence, also an actor, in July, at the age of 90. “There’s parts of my dad in this character … the craziness of this guy. I sort of channel a little bit of my father in that role. So there’s a lot of roads that lead to this moment for me.” Though he has lived in the UK now for longer than he ever lived in Australia, Donovan’s accent hasn’t changed. He speaks with a mixture of deep thought, candour, poetic turns of phrase and enthusiastic swearing. His conversation is liberally sprinkled with “you know?” and “do you know what I mean?” and when a reflection catches him off guard he happily punctuates with “f---!” On the atmosphere of Australia compared to his adopted home, he says: “Everything [in Australia] is in focus. It’s in focus. Here, it’s like a Turner painting. Then: “QF1 – you know I’ve been on that f---ing plane back and forth more than probably most people.” Later, he finishes off his carefully considered dissection of the themes of One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest – conformity and rebellion, the danger of institutions, freedom and redefining sanity, and the impact of the story being set against the backdrop of the Vietnam War – with a self-deprecating “blahdy blah”.



He first heard whispers that this show would happen the last time he performed in Melbourne – in 2023, when he was playing Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show. This time, stepping onto the Athenaeum stage will have a different resonance, with his father having also performed at the theatre – for Breaker Morant in 1978 and Certified Male as part of the Melbourne Festival in 1999. “The whole thing has, not weight, but it’s a wonderful bookend, really.” Boer War veteran Captain Hugh Woolf and Terence Donovan at the Athenaeum during the season of Breaker Morant in 1978. Age Archives Set in a psychiatric institution in the early 1960s, the story follows McMurphy as he challenges authority figures holding up a broken system. “McMurphy is a trailblazer for all his flaws,” says Donovan. Elements of Terence Donovan will make it into his performance in November. “I was very excited for my dad to see it,” he says. “You know with Dad you never quite knew somewhat what version you were going to get sometimes … he was feisty, strong, [and] had a sort of controlled madness about him. He embraced life – he went for it.” Donovan knew that his father would be remembered for his acting. But in a career that started in 1960, his work spilled not just across the stage and screen, but into what lay underneath it all. Gerard Kennedy and Terence Donovan (front) and other cast members of Homicide and Division 4 march through the centre of Melbourne in 1970 to demand local content quotas. “There’s a great picture of my dad holding a coffin,” he says. The photograph is black and white, and in it Terence Donovan is standing next to fellow actor Gerard Kennedy, the two of them leading a procession of pallbearers through the streets of Melbourne.



Taken in April 1975, this isn’t an image of a funeral; it’s a protest. Inside the coffin were rolls of film, spilling out from under the lid. The procession was made up of some of the biggest names in entertainment of the time, who had all come together to fight for mandated local content quotas to protect Australian jobs on the small screen. “I was pretty keen when Dad passed to make sure that he wasn’t just known as the guy who did Cop Shop and Home and Away and Neighbours,” says Donovan. He draws a line from the activism done in the ’60s and ’70s “lobbying successive governments to try and make sure that Australia told its own stories” to the industry we have today – one that helped pave the way for his own career. Though he is almost constantly working, the image we most often see of Donovan is from the late ’80s, in stills or videos from what is still one of the most iconic moments in Australian television. In 1987, Neighbours aired an episode in which Donovan’s character, Scott, married his on-screen love interest Charlene, played by Kylie Minogue. Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan as Charlene and Scott in Neighbours. Recently he’s been seeing a lot of posts on Instagram where “you can put in a picture of yourself and it pumps out you in 1988 with your mullet… I just put in me in 1988. I don’t need to AI it.” By now he’s used to occupying the strange space of being a figure in pop-culture history; it’s a normal part of his story that there is a band called Scott and Charlene’s Wedding. “I have heard about that,” he says, and adds that British electronic band KLF had a single called Kylie Said to Jason. Interest in his off-screen relationship with Minogue flared up again earlier this year when he took part in her Netflix documentary. Asked if it was a difficult choice to participate, Donovan doesn’t hesitate. “No,” he says. “I’ll tell you why it wasn’t difficult – because it was her documentary … there was no third party involved.” He clarifies: “I wasn’t telling her story for someone that might be able to misinterpret it … so I wasn’t fearful of it being manipulated or misconstrued.”



He was, however, surprised by how prominent he was in it. “I was a big part of episode one. That’s not a negative thing. That was a positive thing,” he says. “But I didn’t anticipate being probably such a big part.” Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan at the launch of her Netflix documentary series in London. John Phillips/Getty Images for Netflix The documentary covers the pair’s years on Neighbours, and the breakdown of their relationship. In it, Donovan is very open about his feelings at the time. “Love hurts, mate,” he says bluntly near the close of the first episode. “Maybe there’s an element of trust with her and I, which is a good thing. I think she trusts me to be honest and, you know, I trust her,” he reflects. “That’s a unique bond. That’s a good partnership … that even though there’s many years between us since those moments, there is still a trust and a respect; a mutual respect.” Today, he is just as open about the grief of losing his father. “It’s no surprise that I’ve had a bumpy few months,” he says. The pair were very close, walking back and forth in each other’s footsteps in careers that separated and intersected across the years. “I was brought up by my dad,” he says. “That’s quite unique, particularly in the ’70s in Australia.”



It meant that his childhood was spent in the company of creative people. “It was a nightmare!” he says with a laugh. “There were wonderful highs and sort of wonderful lows. I was surrounded by actors growing up, most of them pretty negative about the work and the life, but always passionate.” He pauses. “That’s something that I really latched onto. That passion. I watched my dad. I went to set. I went to plays. I watched him work, probably because I didn’t really have a mother figure around. So it was just him and I.” Jason and Terence Donovan. Jason Donovan Donovan started acting as a child, but it was when he was cast as Scott Robinson in Neighbours that fame quickly found him and he continued on to a career that has spanned stage, screen and music, including playing Joseph in Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat in London. But it isn’t what he imagined for himself. His sliding doors moment was enrolling at RMIT to study graphic design. “I never thought I was going to become an actor because every f---ing actor around me was out of work and depressed,” he says with a small smile. “All my dad’s mates were like, ‘Oh, it’s a terrible business’.” Donovan is more circumspect. “I’d love to have done a great film. Unfortunately, I made some pretty shit choices early on, and I turned down some jobs that might have gone in the direction to have had a career in film,” he says. “We all want to be sometimes something we’re not. I’d love to have done more film work. I’ve always harboured the idea of writing a great song, and I certainly tried in both those areas. And who’s to say in the future that can’t happen?” he reflects. “My dad always talked about versatility as a performer, and that’s something that I’ve really taken on board in my life … it’s a wonderful, full life when you get to make a living out of it.” In 1984, while he was still in school, he auditioned for Neighbours and was offered the part of Danny Ramsay. His teachers encouraged him to drop out and take the role. “I asked Dad, and Dad said, ‘You’re crazy. Finish school’.” So he turned it down. “It killed me!” he exclaims.

World.title: An Australian army veteran and an Afghan refugee met for coffee. What happened next changed both their lives
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend An Australian army veteran and an Afghan refugee met for coffee. What happened next changed both their lives Dani Valent October 1, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kat Rae, 45, served in Afghanistan, as did her husband, who died by suicide in 2017. Mursal Azizi, 33, came to Australia as an Afghan refugee. The pair, both artists, have found a deep comfort in their friendship.

Kat: In February, 2025, a friend introduced me to Mursal. We met at a cafe in North Fitzroy and connected straight away – as artists and as people with a connection to her homeland. She’d fled Kabul after the Taliban came to power in 2021. I was in the Australian Army for 20 years and had done two tours there. I wondered if Afghans would be mad at me, feel that we’d let them down, but Mursal was just grateful. The Afghans I’ve met understand loss and know we feel it, too. Mursal told me she felt lonely. It was painful for me to hear that. As a widow, I knew that feeling. She wanted to find a way to help the women over there. I love people with a mission and art that makes a statement, and hate the collateral damage of war, so we started working together. Sparks in the Dark [showing now at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance] features 260 handkerchiefs embroidered by women living in Afghanistan, one for each week since the Taliban took Kabul.



At its opening, I recited the words, “They shall not grow old as we that are left grow old” [from For The Fallen, by Laurence Binyon], which we’ve been reading every Anzac Day for generations but, this time, the people weren’t silent: Afghans were crying, their grief raw. Mursal gave me a hug and asked where I’d found those words; she said they were perfect. There’s an Afghan word, hamdard, which means shared grief, a shoulder-to-shoulder connectedness. Australians aren’t very good at expressing grief. They’re more like, “How can we get you back on your feet?” But there’s something beautiful about expressing grief together and trying to do some good with it. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Take it all the way’: the moment of supreme sibling sportsmanship that made Australia proud Seeing how the war affected my husband, losing him, cracking open with grief … you can’t help but be empathetic to people going through something, too. As a sole parent in Melbourne, I find I connect more with offbeat families – migrant families, widowed families or those impacted by domestic violence. And I always connected with the depth and warmth of the Afghan people. I missed their openness when I came back to Australia. Mursal is kind and generous. She invited me round for lunch one day and it was a huge banquet; she’d been slaving away in her little kitchen – I should have blocked out the whole afternoon. There’s this spiced milk pudding called firni that I first tried in Kabul. She knew I loved it and surprised me by cooking it for me. I cried: I was moved that she’d made it for the first time. There’s vulnerability there, no one guiding her by saying, “Oh, next time, do it like this and, by the way, our family always adds a bit of salt.” Making it for me is part of her fight to hang on to something that should be her birthright.



I’m glad and proud I can be one of Mursal’s first Melbourne friends. I love seeing her flourish as an artist and a mother. I’m also grateful that my daughter and partner get to know her and her family. I can say to them, “How cool are these people? How amazing is their food? How important are their art and their stories?” Mursal: I was lonely when I was introduced to Kat. She had been twice in Afghanistan and is an artist, too, which made it comfortable for me to talk to her. As a newcomer to Australia, I feel the differences between myself and people here. They savour and enjoy life, think about entertainment; we think about survival, our challenges, how we can mitigate risks. Mursal Azizi and Kat Rae at their exhibition, Sparks in the Dark. Courtesy of Kat Rae and Mursal Azizi With Kat, I felt understood: I knew she would understand what I say and who I am. She told me her husband had been in Afghanistan, too, and that he suicided on August 16 [nine years ago]. Kabul fell on August 15, four years later. The closeness of the dates was overwhelming for her. She created art about it. I understood that feeling as an artist – the need to get a message out, to get feelings out. I was working with female embroiderers in Afghanistan and had some samples of their work. I wanted to exhibit them in Australia. I showed Kat, I told her I wanted to do something to help them and she said, “I can help you, if you want. We can do this project together.” I agreed. The next day, she called me and we went to meet her mentor, talk about our project, apply for grants. If I’d been doing it by myself, maybe it would have happened, but it became very real, very quickly with Kat.



The kind of deep friendship we have, people usually develop over years. But it happened fast, with an intense and big connection as we worked on the exhibition. I’m a person of ideas: Kat made it real. The Australian system is new to me; she understands how to take it forward. She even invited the Governor-General to the opening. We complete each other, in a way. Related Article Opinion

Afghanistan ‘Gender apartheid’: Why we can’t forget the women of Afghanistan Liz Gooch Journalist I was pregnant with my first child, my daughter, Sarah, as we worked on the exhibition. Kat drove me places, found me a midwife to talk to, made me fresh food – broccoli with cheese, which was something new for me. One day, she was driving me home and I told her I was afraid about my baby coming, that I would be a full-time mum and wouldn’t be able to do my art. Kat told me she thinks her daughter, Imogen, is proud that she became an artist rather than losing herself in motherhood. That is always in my ears and on my mind. Sarah is nine months old now; I feel she needs a mother who follows her dreams. One day, when I was pregnant, we went to an Afghan restaurant in Lygon Street. Five of us: my husband, Asad, Kat’s partner, Mark, and Imogen. Being together as families, I felt closer to Kat; it was real. Kat likes the kebabs we do, with the meat and the fat together on a skewer. It was one of her favourite foods in Afghanistan and she tried the same thing here. It made me happy. When your food is appreciated, it feels like your country is appreciated, too. More than the food, what mattered was that we were there as families. We talked about Afghanistan, the situation of the women and how they live. The country has a rich culture. It’s historical, with so much beauty that people don’t hear about because of the politics and the war. Kat knows the beauty of Afghanistan, too, and that means she can know me.

World.title: ASX falls across the board as Wall Street slumps late
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX falls across the board as Wall Street slumps late Staff writers Updated October 1, 2026 — 10:47am ,first published October 1, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has fallen sharply at the open after Wall Street fell as it contended with the downside of a US economy that keeps powering through its many challenges. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 82.1 points or 0.9 per cent at the open, with industry sectors in negative territory. The ASX added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US69.58¢. Wall Street slid lower to wrap up a losing September. AP Overnight, the S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent to close its third losing month in the last four. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 443 points, or 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.2 per cent. US stocks turned lower after data reports suggested the US economy was even stronger during the spring than earlier thought. That helped yields remain high in the bond market, which in turn kept up the pressure weighing on stocks and all financial markets.



The financial sector was the heaviest weight on the ASX in early trade as the big four banks all fell sharply, with Commonwealth Bank and Westpac down 1.2 per cent while National Australia Bank and ANZ Bank shed 1.4 per cent. Mining stocks were mixed with BHP up 0.9 per cent while Fortescue fell 0.4 per cent and Rio Tinto lost 1.2 per cent. Gold miners fell with Northern Star down 1.5 per cent and Evolution Mining falling 1.4 per cent as the precious metal swung with softer inflation data tempering bets on further Federal Reserve tightening, while elevated bond yields kept it vulnerable to renewed selling. Bullion fluctuated between a gain of 0.9 per cent and a loss of 0.7 per cent. Traders now price in a roughly 40 per cent chance of a rate increase at the US central bank’s meeting next month. Energy stocks lost ground after oil prices steadied after gaining in the previous session amid uncertainty over whether a recovery in Middle East flows can be sustained. West Texas Intermediate traded near $US90 ($129) a barrel after rising 1.2 per cent, while the most-active Brent contract settled at about $US98. Woodside Energy dipped 0.6 per cent and Santos lost 0.2 per cent. Ampol fell 1.2 per cent as it announced it had reached a $225 million deal to acquire electric vehicle charging company Evie Networks. Technology stocks were mixed with WiseTech slipping 0.9 per cent while Codan lost 1.4 per cent, TechnologyOne dipped 0.1 per cent and NEXTDC shed 0.7 per cent. Life360 jumped 3 per cent while Xero added 0.2 per cent. Overnight, Wall Street’s day began with gains for stocks following an encouraging report that said inflation wasn’t as bad across the US last month as economists expected. It said the cost of living for US consumers was 3.4 per cent higher overall in August than a year earlier. That was not as high as the 3.7 per cent inflation rate that economists expected, even if it remained worse than the Fed’s 2 per cent target.



Related Article Mergers & acquisitions Giant gold miner eager to keep $38b Australian mega-deal alive The report followed others from earlier in the month about inflation during August, but it’s the one that the Federal Reserve prefers to use. Shorter-term Treasury yields fell as traders pared bets that the Fed will raise its main interest rate next month to get inflation further under control. That helped the yield on the two-year Treasury briefly fall towards 4.83 per cent before it pulled back to 4.89 per cent, where it was late on Tuesday. But longer-term yields rose in the bond market. That’s in part because worries about high inflation are just one of the reasons longer-term yields have jumped in the US and around the world.



The seemingly solid US economy is another. Besides Wednesday’s better-than-expected report, another update said growth in business activity in the Midwest was also stronger than economists expected. Much of the strength in the US economy is due to consumers, who are increasing their spending by more than their incomes are rising. “The consumer remains resilient, in a much better position than previously thought,” according to Gary Schlossberg, global strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Other factors sending Treasury yields higher continue to churn, including worries about the big debt loads that Washington and other governments worldwide are supporting. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the bond market, dropped as low as 5.20 per cent in the morning before rising to 5.29 per cent. That’s up from 5.26 per cent, and it’s back to where it was more than two decades ago in 2002.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which takes into account expectations for inflation and economic growth many years down the line, climbed to 5.64 per cent from 5.59 per cent late on Tuesday. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Higher yields slow the overall economy by making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while undercutting prices for all kinds of investments. On Wall Street, Cal-Maine Foods dropped 0.7 per cent after the country’s largest egg company reported a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected. With plenty of eggs available in the market, Cal-Maine Foods saw a sharp drop in prices it could charge, compared to a year earlier. Helping to limit the market’s losses was Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which rose 3.9 per cent. It increased its forecast for revenue from its networking business, which is benefiting from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology.



MongoDB climbed 3.4 per cent after the database company’s board boosted its program to send cash to shareholders by $US1 billion through buybacks of its own stock. That helped MongoDB recover some of its sharp loss from earlier in the week, after it said Chirantan “CJ” Desai was stepping down as chief executive for a senior role at Meta Platforms. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Silly season is here: Your club-by-club guide to AFL free agency
World.content:
SportAFLTrading and drafting Silly season is here: Your club-by-club guide to AFL free agency Jon Pierik October 1, 2026 — 10:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL’s silly season is upon us, and it officially kicks off on Friday when free agency opens. Heavyweight deals involving restricted free agents Zak Butters and Ben King have been a key point of discussion, while several stars, including dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene, are unrestricted free agents, meaning they have an easier path to a new home. Let’s look at where things sit at your club. On the move: Port Adelaide star Zak Butters is hoping to confirm a shift to the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos via Getty Images Restricted free agents



GOLD COAST

Ben King: The gun full-forward has told the Suns he is leaving and intends to join Hawthorn on a mammoth deal, which industry insiders say could stretch over seven years and be worth more than $9 million. Just how this deal is reached, in terms of whether the Suns opt to match the Hawks’ offer and force a trade, remains one of the more fascinating aspects of the trade period, particularly as it could impact the draft selections the Hawks will need to secure Essendon’s Zach Merrett. The AFL is keeping a close eye on this deal. Ben King is a free agent and wants to play for Hawthorn next season. AFL Photos PORT ADELAIDE

Zak Butters: Told the Power he would leave and later nominated the Western Bulldogs as his club of choice on what industry insiders say is a monster nine-year deal worth $18 million. “Zak Butters has informed the Western Bulldogs of his desire to join the club,” the Bulldogs said in a statement in September. “The club will work with Port Adelaide to facilitate a suitable outcome during the upcoming player movement period.” Just how this deal is structured also remains a point of debate, for if the Power let Butters walk, they would only receive pick five as an AFL free agency compensation pick, which they consider insufficient. Therefore, a trade could be their best option, potentially seeking up to three first-round selections. The AFL is in lock-step with both clubs. Unrestricted free agents ADELAIDE

Jordon Butts: Butts is headed to the Western Bulldogs on what insiders say will be a five-year contract after 94 games with the Crows. It could hasten Rory Lobb’s departure from the Whitten Oval, potentially to St Kilda, despite Lobb having a year remaining on his contract.

Mitch Hinge: Expected to remain.

Chayce Jones: Not offered a new contract.

Lachie Sholl: Delisted after not being offered a new contract.

Tyler Welsh: Not offered a new contract.



BRISBANE LIONS

Darragh Joyce: Faces an uncertain future.

Lincoln McCarthy: Weighing up retirement.

Lachie Neale: Confirmed in the minutes after Saturday’s third-straight Lions premiership that he was leaving the club and then on Wednesday that he would join Collingwood. Is expected to sign a three-year, $3 million contract with the Magpies. Lions’ great Lachie Neale was swamped by his teammates after they defeated Fremantle in a stunning grand final. AFL Photos CARLTON

Elijah Hollands: Officially delisted, and has stepped away from the game.

Zac Williams: Has been cut by the Blues and is open to a new club. COLLINGWOOD

Bobby Hill: Delisted free agent. ESSENDON

Jade Gresham: Delisted.

Matt Guelfi: Delisted.

Liam McMahon: Not offered a new contract.





HAWTHORN

None Melbourne

None NORTH MELBOURNE

Toby Pink: Out of contract.

Bailey Scott: Delisted free agent. PORT ADELAIDE

None



RICHMOND

Nathan Broad: Has technically retired, but now says he is keen to play on elsewhere, particularly in his home state of Western Australia.

Dion Prestia: While the Tigers said the midfielder retired, the triple-premiership star has left the door open to playing elsewhere next season. ST KILDA

Ryan Byrnes: Yet to be offered a new contract.

Jack Carroll: Yet to be offered a new contract.

Patrick Said: An active delisted free agent seeking a lifeline. Related Article AFL 2026 Giants put a price on Whitfield’s head as Blues, Demons circle star half-back SYDNEY

Joel Amartey: Will join Carlton on a five-year contract industry insiders say is worth up to $750,000 a season. The Blues hope he can be an ideal replacement for Charlie Curnow, the three-time Coleman medallist who has just finished his first year with the Swans.

Harry Cunningham: Off contract.

Joel Hamling: Off contract.

Dane Rampe: Off contract. WEST COAST

Matthew Flynn: Off contract.

Harry Schoenberg: Off contract.



WESTERN BULLDOGS

Oskar Baker: Not offered a new contract.

Ryan Gardner: Off contract.

Lachie McNeil: Off contract and exploring his options. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save flight FZ1073
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastAviation ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save flight FZ1073 David Crowe Updated October 1, 2026 — 10:47am ,first published October 1, 2026 — 7:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A gruesome brawl was under way at the front of Flight FZ1073 when one passenger chose to force his way into the cockpit to prevent a disaster. That passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, is now recognised as a hero who stopped one of the pilots from sending the flydubai Boeing 737 MAX crashing to the ground. Loading He did not act alone: several others joined him in a fight that lasted at least 20 minutes to defeat the co-pilot, who is now under arrest over a suspected act of terrorism. But Hayoun’s account reveals how close things came to a catastrophic mass murder of 174 passengers and crew, almost all of them Jewish.



“When I went in, I saw the terrorist on the controls, between the two seats. There were no pilots in the seats,” Hayoun said. “I grabbed the terrorist, put him in a hold, and first of all pulled him outside.” Yaniv Hayoun says he learned how to pull the plane out of a nosedive by watching a Canadian documentary series. AP Photo/Tomer Appelbaum The aircraft cabin was a scene of chaos at this time. The flight had left Dubai about two hours earlier and was above Saudi Arabia on its way to Tel Aviv. Israeli authorities say the key suspect, an Omani man working as the co-pilot, had turned on the lead pilot with a knife and begun stabbing him.



Witnesses said the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of the wounds took effect. Hayoun described what happened in several accounts including a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when the passengers and crew finally made it to Tel Aviv on a second flight. The plane’s captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, made a crucial decision that saved the flight. He unlocked the cockpit door before the worst of his wounds took effect. He saw what the pilot with the knife was attempting to do: “He was trying to destroy the controls in order to disable the plane.” The aircraft was racing toward the ground at this point. Flight tracking sites, including Flightradar24, show that the plane dropped 14,000 feet (4300 metres) in less than 30 seconds.



“I jumped back in there, grabbed the controls, started pulling the controls,” Hayoun said in his meeting with Netanyahu. He mimed his action with the controls as he gave his account. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayoun. AFP How did he know what to do? “I watch Mayday,” he said. This is a Canadian television documentary series that examines air crashes, hijackings and bombings. Another passenger, Assaf Rajwan, joined Hayoun in confronting the co-pilot. In an interview with Israeli news outlet Channel 12, he said he heard shouting from the cockpit when the plane was in its dive. “We kept the terrorist neutralised for 55 minutes,” Rajwan said, in an account reported by The Times of Israel.



“I can’t believe I was in Thailand a few hours ago on a family vacation. “Life is stronger than everything, and we decided to fight for it.” Passengers who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, during a flight on flydubai plane, arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit Assaf Regavim, one of the passengers who helped to overpower the co-pilot. Getty Images A third passenger, Tzvika Manes, said his wife and young daughter were in the bathroom when the struggle began in the cockpit.



Manes said the captain fell out into the cabin as the co-pilot was stabbing him, while the aircraft was falling rapidly and passengers were thrown about in the turmoil. Manes described his daughter screaming: “We don’t want to die.” He moved out of his seat to get to the cockpit. He said it took about 20 to 25 minutes for the three men to subdue the co-pilot. They used headphone cords to tie him up. In a video shared by one person on the flight, the captain is covered in blood as some passengers support him and praise him for saving the aircraft from disaster. The co-pilot is seen tied up nearby and apparently unconscious. The wall of the cabin is splashed in blood.



The flight tracking sites show it took another 90 minutes for the aircraft to land at Tabuk Airport in the far west of Saudi Arabia. Related Article Updated

Aviation Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster Another stroke of luck saved the passengers and crew. On board were two pilots. They joined the passengers at the front of the aircraft and took control. While these two pilots have not been named, some reports have described them as a South African and a New Zealander. One passenger, Daniel, told Channel 12 that he thought the aircraft would be destroyed in a repeat of the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington DC in 2001.



When the off-duty pilots took over, Daniel said, they kept to the cockpit and focused on securing the aircraft. Israeli passenger Haim Lazarovich celebrates a safe return home. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit People celebrate the arrival of the replacement aircraft in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit “The pilots locked themselves in the cockpit, and we had no contact with the pilots,” he said. He added that two of the flight attendants were of no help. “All kinds of thoughts were running through our heads, but [then] we heard the pilot start speaking to the passengers and telling them that they were going to land.” At that point, he said, things calmed down.



Once on the ground, the passengers and crew were helped by Saudi healthcare workers. “We immediately felt safe because they were really amazing and generous. So many soldiers and nurses and doctors,” said Lital Shahar, a passenger travelling with her four daughters. A plane carrying passengers from an earlier flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport. Getty Images Passengers embark on a flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit Shahar told The Times of Israel the passengers and crew survived due to two miracles.



“I felt sick. There are no words to describe what we experienced,” she said. “There were two miracles – that Israelis were on the plane who heroically went into the cockpit. And that there were off-duty pilots onboard who could land the plane in Saudi Arabia.” The captain of the flight is being hailed as a hero for resisting the co-pilot and opening the cockpit door. A photo showing Yaniv Hayoun on flydubai FZ1073 with blood on his shirt. Amichai Stein/Twitter Captain Machchhar was helped by an Israeli dentist, Doctor Shota Musayev, who went to the cockpit.



“When I heard screaming, after 10 seconds I ran – I didn’t wait,” Musayev told The Times of Israel. “When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape, with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head. “I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure.” Netanyahu praised Captain Machchhar for his bravery. The flight making its safe landing back in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” the Israeli prime minister said. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals. I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery. He is a true hero.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Ampol buys huge Australian EV charging network in $225m deal
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesEnergy Ampol buys huge Australian EV charging network in $225m deal Nick Toscano October 1, 2026 — 10:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fuel giant Ampol has struck a deal to acquire one of Australia’s most extensive electric-vehicle charging networks, a move that will more than triple the number of charging bays it owns just as local sales of battery-powered cars surge to record highs. Ampol, which runs hundreds of petrol stations across the nation and the Lytton oil refinery in Brisbane, on Thursday said it had agreed to acquire 100 per cent of Evie Networks for $225 million. The acquisition will add more than 1000 charging bays to Ampol’s existing AmpCharge network, creating a combined national platform of 1425 charging bays spread across more than 400 sites. Wolter Peeters The acquisition will add more than 1000 charging bays to Ampol’s existing AmpCharge network, creating a combined national platform of 1425 charging bays spread across more than 400 sites. The deal comes as Australians switch from petrol-powered to electric vehicles at an unprecedented rate, spurred by an influx of more-affordable EV models and sharp spikes in fuel prices caused by the war in the Middle East. EVs, which accounted for less than 10 per cent of Australia’s new car market just 12 months ago, now represent more than 25 per cent of new sales – or one in four – nationwide.



The rapid transition is putting pressure on retail fuel companies to rapidly scale up their public fast-charging infrastructure to keep up with booming demand. Ampol managing director Matt Halliday said the deal positioned the company to “capture growth” as the uptake of EVs and charging demand increased. Related Article Electric vehicles Electric cars are taking off in Australia. Charging stations are the next challenge “Our job is to be there for customers with what they need, when they need it, as they choose vehicle technology that suits their needs,” he said. There are more than 1300 public charging sites operational across Australia, housing more than 4000 individual charging ports. More than half are DC fast chargers rated above 50 kilowatts. Many of them are run by commercial operators including Evie Networks, EVX, Chargefox and Tesla. Others are owned by service station chains such as Ampol and BP, or motoring clubs like the NRMA and RACV.



However, with drivers making the switch to EVs “faster than ever, public fast-charging infrastructure is failing to keep up”, said Riz Akhtar, founder of EV data analytics firm Carloop. “That’s going to be the biggest challenge,” he says. Evie Networks’ current principal shareholder is Trevor St Baker, a long-time investor in Australia’s energy industry, with interests spanning coal-fired power stations and electric vehicle infrastructure. The rapid transition is putting pressure on retail fuel companies to rapidly scale up their public fast-charging infrastructure to keep up with booming demand. Ampol’s acquisition follows surging utilisation rates across its current AmpCharge network this year, in line with a doubling of the sales of EV and plug-in hybrids across the country. The number of charging sessions at Ampol sites, and the volume of energy supplied, had more than doubled in the first half of 2026, Halliday said. “This gives us confidence in the strength of the business case that complements our traditional fuels business,” he said.
