World.title: Cashmere Club holds onto liquor licence after man's fatal fall while heavy drinking
World.content:
A Christchurch bar has held onto its liquor licence following the death of a popular club member after a heavy drinking session but it will only be able to serve alcohol to diners for three months.

Longstanding club member Colin Hunt, known as Charlie, fell and hit his head after celebrating his 70th birthday at the Cashmere Club in September last year, dying in hospital a day later.

Last month, the Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority heard an application by police to strip or suspend liquor licences held by the Cashmere Club and the manager at the time, Rebecca Hine.

In reserved decision released on Thursday, the authority said the three month suspension from 1 February 2027 was a "sufficient, proportionate and reasonable response to the quite appalling and unlawful way in which the Club operated that night".

Hine's manager certificate was cancelled.

It stopped short of cancelling the club's licence as it was satisfied the circumstances around Hunt's death were a one-off, the authority said.

"It is a community hub and its response to the unlawful events of that night has just been sufficient to satisfy us that it is unlikely that there will be a repeat of this excessive and after hours drinking."

Records show the party ran up a bar tab of $2315.98 - Hunt had put down a bar credit of $3000 - with only three platters of food delivered to the pool room shortly after 10pm "presumably to Mr Hunt's group", the authority said.

"It is the tragic circumstances of this case that the death of Mr Hunt needlessly arose directly by the sale and supply of alcohol that was both unsafe and unreasonable."

The authority said a certificated manager must be on duty at all times when alcohol is sold and the club must extend its CCTV coverage to include the pool room and restaurant by the end of the year.

World.title: Opportunity party leader Qiulae Wong on recognising the good and the bad of AI
World.content:
Audio player for " Qiulae Wong’s vision for AI in New Zealand " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1670830%2Fopportunity-party-leader-qiulae-wong-on-recognising-the-good-and-the-bad-of-ai

Qiulae Wong’s vision for AI in New Zealand Midday Report Download MP3 19m

In the lead-up to November's election, Midday Report is speaking with the technology spokesperson for a range of parties about their biggest hopes and fears with artificial intelligence (AI) and the role of the Government in regulating the technology. On Thursday, Guyon Epsiner sat down with Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong.

Quilae Wong can see both sides of the AI debate - while she says it can be damaging, it can be used for a lot of good that could benefit Aotearoa and drive productivity.

In an interview with Midday Report, Wong said we had learnt through history that technology could be used for good or bad.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405782726112

She believed if the regulatory framework was right, AI could benefit New Zealanders while making sure the environment was protected along the way.

"But we have to be intentional about it," Wong said.

Referencing the recent hacking of medical records in Australia, Wong said there was a cause for concern and a need to take a "risk-based mindset" to the use of AI.

"We need to up cybersecurity in New Zealand... and make sure all our agencies are equipped.

"We take it incredibly seriously but we don't need to feel helpess about it all or hopeless."

She said a clear framework was needed on what was an acceptable standard for AI.

"We can't sit back and pretend we don't have agency in this we do, even as a small country.

"We need to regulate and there are clear international standards and we should implement those here. The Government needs to take a leadership role on what does good use of AI look like."

AI needed to be looked at by the Government as a tool for innovation and productivity, Wong said, not just a way to cut costs.

She said the main things her party was looking at were how to support AI to be used well, how to use it for good and how to capture as much of the value as possible for New Zealand.

There was a role for the Law Commission too, Wong said, to look at human rights in relation to AI and copyright and the human right to review work.

"It's moving so fast and I think a sit back and watch approach is just not appropriate anymore.

"We need to be active participants in this, and not sit on the sidelines."

Wong said the party also wanted to support businesses to roll it out by proposing a new tax credit for the adoption of technology like AI. The party had allocated $600m in its breakthrough policy for it, she said.

She also wanted there to be some rules around Government procurement of the technology to favour New Zealand suppliers.

In her day-to-day life Wong said she used AI for research and to draft things, but always reviewed it after.

World.title: Government reverses 'lethal' electrical rule change after inspectors' warnings
World.content:
The government has reversed a rule change following warnings from electrical inspectors that homes and businesses would be exposed to a new lethal risk.

As part of changes to electricity rules, regulators late last year lifted a ban on putting a switch or fuse into mains power earthing systems.

RNZ revealed at the time that inspectors in multiple meetings and letters had pleaded unsuccessfully with officials to do a U-turn.

The Electrical Inspectors Association said the removal of the Protective Earth Neutral (PEN) protections could render entire systems "lethal, possibly with multiple injuries or fatalities" even when they were operating normally.

Energy Minister Simon Watts said he was taking the feedback seriously.

WorkSafe commissioned an independent review by an international expert to provide assurance on its advice to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, which instituted the rule change.

On Thursday the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment said while WorkSafe has provided advice on how the risks associated with PEN switching could be managed, there remained significant concern within the sector about whether it can be used safely.

World.title: New Zealanders want to retain access to cash
World.content:
Audio player for " Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/personal-finance/1669001%2Fnew-zealanders-want-to-retain-access-to-cash

Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

New Zealanders want access to cash - and some want even stricter standards for its provision than the Reserve Bank had proposed.

The Reserve Bank has been consulting on its proposals for minimum standards for cash services in New Zealand.

It released a summary of submissions on Thursday.

Its proposal was to put a floor under the number and location of places where bank customers could withdraw, deposit or swap cash. It wanted 95 percent of people living in urban areas to have walking-distance access to a free cash point.

It identified a number of places that needed cash services including smaller settlements such as Ngakawau, Ongaonga, Omakau, Owaka, Whangaroa, Taipa, Te Araroa, Cheviot, Rotherham, Waikari, Kimbolton, Kawhia, Balfour, Ohai, Woodslands, St Andrews, Glenavy, Nuhaka, Tuai, Hampton, Kurow, Taharoa, Harihari, Fox Glacier and Ross.

It said meeting the standard would cost banks about $100 million a year but that was only 1 percent of their combined annual profit.

The Reserve Bank said 6106 submissions were received.

About half of the respondents were dissatisfied with the current cash services in their district and across New Zealand. Ninety percent agreed New Zealand needed a standard for cash access. About half said the Reserve Bank's proposed standard was about right but 28 percent said it was not enough.

The Reserve Bank said some banks supported the public having continued access to cash, with a voluntary approach from the industry to achieve that, but did not support the detailed Reserve Bank proposal.

Some respondents had concerns about the Reserve Bank proposal's estimated benefits and costs, and favoured digital payments services over cash services.

Karen Silk, assistant governor money, welcomed and thanked people for their views.

"New Zealanders use and value cash alongside digital ways to pay," she said.

"More than 6000 people completed our questionnaire and about 4000 wrote to us or gave extra information and we appreciate all contributions.

"Small business owners and market stallholders told us that cash was a secure, reliable way to get paid but that depositing cash, getting coins, and accessing bank services was becoming harder and more costly."

She said the submissions showed it was only a minority of people who never used cash, and some had started to hoard it in case of emergencies.

She said the Reserve Bank's preference was that banks voluntarily address the concerns that had been raised, rather than the Reserve Bank dictating what they must do.

"This is the way we said it could be dealt with, if you think about doing this in an efficient way this is an illustrative model of what that could look like. The way banks do that is up to them," she said.

"We're asking them to take that information... We're engaging with a working group of senior bank representatives on the topic."

She said there was a case for banks bearing a reasonable cost of providing cash services, and banks benefited from customers placing their money with them.

She said the Reserve Bank was now engaging with a Bank Working Group to improve cash services across New Zealand.

The Reserve Bank earlier said the number of bank branches around the country was down by 40 percent and the number of bank-owned ATMs had dropped 32 percent over the past decade. Between 2012 and 2017, total ATM numbers fell by 14.7 percent per million people.

RNZ research identified a number of dead zones where there were no cash points nearby for people to withdraw money.

World.title: 'I trusted him wholeheartedly': Remembering the life and times of Phil Gifford
World.content:
Two things should probably be made clear at the start of a reflection on the life and times of Phil Gifford - the broadcaster, sports journalist, raconteur and family man.

One is that virtually everyone who knew him has a story about him, and the second is that if he told you a story - and it could have been about rugby (his greatest sporting passion), but really it could have been about anything among his wide range of interests, including music - then it was best to prepare for the long version because he didn't have any other.

Gifford, who died in Auckland on Tuesday at the age of 79, was a journalist for more than 50 years and his recall for facts, figures and anecdotes was as remarkable as his personality was large.

He has also been remembered as an empathetic and kind-hearted man who had a hugely successful radio career, wrote many newspaper columns (including until very recently), plus no fewer than 26 books, including best-selling biographies on Alex 'Grizz' Wyllie, Dame Valerie Adams, Sir Wayne Smith and Sir Peter Leitch.

The relationships with whom he dealt throughout his long and industrious career were deep and long-lasting and few were more significant than his and wife Jan's with Dame Valerie, the two-time Olympic and three-time Commonwealth Games shot put champion during and after the book-writing process.

"Having to share your story can be quite tough but I trusted him wholeheartedly... he was the perfect person for it," Dame Valerie told RNZ on Thursday.

"I knew Phil before then - he had interviewed me in the past so he wasn't a stranger but equally I found so much comfort in telling him my story and then bonded with him and his wife Jan quite strongly after that.

"They came to Switzerland to see me when I was living over there training for the Games. They came to the Commonwealth Games to watch me, and I became pretty much part of the furniture and part of their family.

"They were my family. This is hitting home pretty hard. I lost a great man last year in [long-time coach] Jean-Pierre [Egger] and another one this year. He was a father figure to me. I used to call Phil and Jan my 'Palagi parents'. This one hurts."

When it was suggested to Dame Valerie that Gifford was a big personality and legendary storyteller while at the same time appearing inherently trustworthy, she replied: "Absolutely."

Dame Valerie competes at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics. John Cowpland / www.photosport.nz

She added: "Obviously, he had the gift of the gab - that's what he was paid to do. He was giving me rugby stats I didn't know I needed... but one thing you could guarantee is that it would be a pretty good story.

"His memory was phenomenal.

"I saw him last week and we had some good chats and banter. He was a massive personality but was a very empathetic and kind-hearted man at the same time. He was always very generous towards me and especially my children."

Originally from Waihi, where he got into journalism via his father, Ray, the editor of the Waihi Gazette, Gifford earned a cadetship at the New Zealand Herald in Auckland in 1965.

His fame was kick-started by his Loosehead Len character - a satirical rugby figure he created in 1973 and which featured alongside the equally notorious "Susan from Herne Bay" - and Gifford covered the great Auckland rugby sides of the 1980s and 90s.

But he then discovered a close and lasting affinity with the Crusaders rugby franchise during his time in Christchurch working alongside radio host Simon Barnett at 91ZM and More FM in the 90s, and he became a firm fan of coach Robbie Deans, among others, including Todd Blackadder - another book subject.

Phil Gifford and Sir Graham Henry, pictured in an event at Eden Park in 2012. Andrew Cornaga / Photosport.co.nz

Gifford's personality was such that despite his very public backing of Deans for the All Blacks head coach role over Sir Graham Henry after the 2007 Rugby World Cup, Henry, who got the job and subsequently led New Zealand to success in 2011, never held it against him (although he never let him forget it).

Tony Johnson, a fellow broadcaster and sports writer, told Morning Report: "He had guys like Grizz Wyllie and Sir Wayne Smith entrusting him with their biographies - that's how highly regarded he was as a writer but also as a rugby person.

"He was a great raconteur… and extremely popular wherever he worked."

This was confirmed by Rikki Swannell, who worked with Gifford at Radio Sport in Auckland in the mid-2000s, and who told RNZ: "Being one of the very few women in this industry for many years, and certainly one of the only women at Radio Sport and Newstalk ZB through all that time, people often want to hear the horror stories of how I may have been treated by men in the industry.

"But what I always had was someone like Phil who was absolutely my biggest champion and cheerleader.

"He texted me during the recent Commonwealth Games and after Northland won the Ranfurly Shield recently - I called that game for Sky. He said 'what a great job, the magic of the Shield…' He would always be in touch and was always happy to have a yarn for sure.

"He was a journo's journo - he always wanted the stories and the gossip."

All Blacks Will Jordan, left, and Ruben Love, compete with Cheslin Kolbe for a high ball during their team's win over the Springboks at Ellis Park last month. Catherine Kotze/BackpagePix

In the 2024 New Year Honours, Gifford was appointed an Officer of the New Zealand Order of Merit for services to broadcasting and sports journalism.

Gifford's dedication to the job was such that those working at Radio Sport at the time still recount when, after he fell ill during an All Blacks media session in Auckland immediately before the 2007 Rugby World Cup, an ambulance delivered the audio gathered from his interviews to the office reception.

He took pride in covering the first nine Rugby World Cups - from 1987 until 2019 - in person and was regarded as an astute observer of the game.

Herald deputy head of sport Cameron McMillan noted that Gifford was "as much a personality as he was a journalist" and that helped him gather stories and gain respect - not least that of Sir Graham Henry.

Gifford's final column for the Herald was published last month and covered New Zealand's test win over South Africa at Ellis Park which he described as "one of the great All Blacks victories".

Many will regard it as a fitting way for a remarkable career to finish.

World.title: 'Queens feeling confident': Cook Islands women dance their way to health
World.content:
Cook Islands women are dancing their way into healthier, happier lives through traditional dance.

CC Tamure Fitness was founded in 2019 by champion dancer Moana Taio, who found herself feeling disconnected as Cook Islands borders closed during the covid pandemic.

She launched free fitness classes through Facebook Live, combining tamure - traditional dance - with high cardio exercise.

Her first session attracted more than 400 participants worldwide. When restrictions eased, the classes moved into the real world, where there are now three classes a week, and virtual programmes offered online.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405787198112

The music is pumping, hips are swaying and the room is full of women working up a sweat. It is exercise, but with a distinct Cook Islands flavour.

For one CC Tamure Fitness instructor, Maria Ngatikao, the classes have become a place where women can come together and encourage each other to stay active while connecting with their culture.

"It's definitely a safe space for us as women. We can leave behind all our daily, everyday activities, worries, our children, our husbands, and come to a place where we can embrace our culture through fitness. And, you know, the benefits of it is we are healthier, we live a healthier lifestyle, we choose to live a healthier lifestyle, and by doing so, we are happier women."

The cultural connection can also make exercise feel less intimidating, according to fellow instructor Paige Taio.

Rather than walking into an unfamiliar gym environment, women are moving to music in ways that are already familiar.

"Our Cook Islands culture is part of who we are, and it's our traditions and our heritage. So embracing it by coming to this fitness class is definitely easier because this is who we are, and we're incorporating these things, these aspects, so we can have this fitness class."

Cook Islands women are dancing their way into healthier, happier lives through traditional dance. RNZ Pacific / Tiana Haxton

Zoe Hoff, a national dance champion and Miss International Cook Islands, said the programme offers a way to embrace Indigenous identities while improving physical fitness.

She said a big part of CC Tamure Fitness is creating a supportive community where people can work towards their health goals while celebrating culture and having fun.

"I do see CC Tamure as a way to embrace who we are, our cultural identity, and as well as improve our fitness levels. But I also see CC Tamure as our safe place where we are all able to empower each other and encourage each other and uplift one another."

For the three instructors, they hope the women that attend their classes leave feeling empowered, healthier and happier.

"I would love for them to take back like the light, the smiles, the encouragement that we share, who we are as Cook Islanders as well. It's just so full of life and giving," Hoff said.

Taio added: "Our queens leave feeling confident."

"I feel like that's so important to us, because we're just a small group and they come here from all their worries and stress and as soon as they leave, they have smiles on their faces, they're happier, they're going back home to their families and taking that same sort of energy back home."

Ngatikao agreed.

"Empowerment and uplifting each other. I mean that's one of the main purposes we come here is that it's just a place where we can come and be ourselves."

As the women leave CC Tamure classes, they are breathless and sweaty from an intense cardio workout, but confidence radiates through their smiles as they dance their way out the door.

World.title: Cities sinking due to too much groundwater extraction may eventually lift again - study
World.content:
Cities that are sinking because too much groundwater is being extracted may eventually lift again if the water is allowed to replenish, new research shows.

The study found the Japanese city of Osaka is rising again after decades of strict groundwater regulations, introduced after over-extraction caused some areas to sink by nearly three metres.

New Zealand earth scientist and co-author Jesse Kearse said the research had important implications for coastal cities in particular, because of accelerating sea-level rise and coastal flooding.

That included New Zealand, where nearly 80 percent of the coastline was already sinking, and pressure on freshwater - which was currently abundant - would grow as the climate warmed.

"We're not quite at that same stage as other countries around the world - I can't really point to a particular city in New Zealand and say, this city's sinking because we're using way too much groundwater," Kearse said.

"But the key message is, as we move into a world where we're getting more and more reliance on groundwater resources, we just need to be aware that that's one of the implications."

The link between over-extraction and land subsidence had long been known, but researchers had not been sure if allowing groundwater to replenish would reverse the subsidence over time.

The study used Osaka as a natural laboratory, because of its long history with groundwater and vertical land motion, Kearse said.

"The city realised in the early part of the 20th century that they were taking far too much water from underneath the ground, running out of water, and the city dropped by close to three metres in some places - which is really extreme subsidence - as a response to groundwater extraction."

Osaka put strict regulations in place in the 1960s and groundwater had gradually replenished over the last 50 or 60 years, he said.

The researchers combined long-term groundwater monitoring data from wells as deep as 500m with repeated satellite observations to measure the effect on land movement.

"The city has bounced back up again... Osaka is actually rising."

Kearse described the effect as "a gigantic water balloon" beneath the city.

"When we take up water from underneath the ground, that balloon deflates and the city sinks. But as the groundwater is replenished, that balloon reinflates and the city pops back up again - so it works in both directions," he said.

The patchiness of the subsidence meant it could cause great damage, Kearse said.

"If you've got pipes under the ground and some bits are moving differently to others, that can cause stress on the infrastructure. Roads are cracking, building are tilting, it's not a good thing."

The research showed it was possible to predict "quite precisely" where the damage would occur.

"The sharp barrier between uplift and subsidence tends to occur along the known mapped faultlines - they are acting as underground dams," he said.

That created corridors of damage - "not because of earthquakes, but because of how they're disrupting the groundwater flow."

The same subsidence could occur with any sub-surface fluid, such as oil and gas extraction, he said.

"It's essentially the same geomechanical process... The physical relationship there is really well-understood."

New Zealand's coastal subsidence had been mapped in detail as part of the NZ SeaRise project, which projected sea-level rise out to 2300.

World.title: Is it safe to charge your phone overnight?
World.content: It’s bedtime. You set your alarm, notice your phone is down to 23 percent battery, plug it in beside the bed and go to sleep. By the morning, it’s been connected to the charger for some seven to eight hours – much longer than it needed to reach 100 percent, especially if it’s on a fast charger.

World.title: Wallaby who overcame cystic fibrosis to play rugby diagnosed with MND
World.content:
Former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who defied cystic fibrosis to play international rugby, has been diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).

The 37-year-old, who played four Test matches for Australia in 2014, publicly announced his diagnosis during an interview with Stan Sport.

During the interview, Charles, who retired from professional rugby in 2018, said he had been experiencing challenges for eight months.

"For a long period there I just didn't know what it was," Charles told interviewer and former Wallaby Justin Harrison.

"I've had that many tests, seen that many doctors and it just wasn't getting any outcome. But my health just kept declining.

"And then recently, in the last few weeks, I was actually diagnosed with motor neurone disease, which has been extremely challenging and overwhelming. And, yeah, just at times quite cruel."

Nathan Charles speaking on Stan Sport about his MND diagnosis. (Stan Sport)

In the interview with Stan Sport, Charles said his first thoughts after being told the MND diagnosis were of his family.

"I felt as though this would impact them greater than it would me. So, yeah, that was my first thought," he said.

"I had a bad feeling going into that appointment and my fears were realised. It was the people around me that I felt worse for."

MND has dominated sporting headlines in 2026, with the death of 2025 Australian of the Year Neale Daniher, and the diagnosis for Queensland State of Origin representative Jai Arrow.

Loading...

"My first question was, 'How long have I got?' Charles said.

"I know that every person with MND has a different journey, a different path and it affects everyone differently.

"I know there's no cure and … your physicality, your body deteriorates and, yeah, your life cuts short."

Charles was a hooker who played Super Rugby for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels, and also had short stints in England and France.

His career in contact sport was remarkable considering Charles had been diagnosed with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder which impairs the lungs and can also affect the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine.

Prior to his first Test match in 2014, then Wallabies coach Ewen McKenzie described Charles as someone who had "defied science".

"If you look at the symptoms and classic outcomes of cystic fibrosis, it's not a great scenario from a sporting point of view, but he seems to have defied science and defied logic," McKenzie said at the time, as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald.

Speaking to Stan Sport, Charles said MND was affecting him.

"I'm already greatly impacted by it," he said.

"I'm getting around with mobility aids. I struggle to do a lot of daily tasks, and putting on shoes and socks and stuff like that is a bit of a challenge.

"So it's already impacted me, and I'm going to have my ups and downs."

World.title: Indian smashes fastest-ever ODI double century in huge run chase
World.content:
Shubman Gill has struck the fastest double century in one-day international history as India completed the second-highest successful chase in a ODI.

Wednesday's eight-wicket victory over West Indies was a run-filled second match of the three-game series in Guwahati.

Gill, the world's top-ranked ODI batter, remained unbeaten on 223 off 133 deliveries and brought up the quickest ODI century of his career (62 balls) before converting it into the fastest ODI double hundred (117 balls).

The 27-year-old scored his first ODI double century against New Zealand in Hyderabad in 2023.

"When it was 13 overs it felt like we had fielded for 25 overs, the way they were batting. Great game," Gill told reporters.

"At the half-time, 400 on the board, there was a bit of pressure. No matter the pitch or ground, chasing 400 is not easy.

"[I'm] very proud of that performance and happy to stay unbeaten till the end."

Rohit Sharma set the tone with a 72-ball century, passing 12,000 ODI runs during a blistering 255-run opening stand with Gill, before Jayden Seales ended his innings on 101 shortly after he brought up his 35th ODI hundred.

Virat Kohli made 29 off 19 deliveries before Shamar Joseph dismissed him with India well placed at 2-320.

Ruturaj Gaikwad chipped in with 31 off 37 balls, and with the Guwahati surface offering little assistance to the bowlers Gill guided India to their target with 39 balls to spare.

West Indies had looked in complete control after posting their first 400-plus ODI total with John Campbell, Shai Hope and Amir Jangoo scoring centuries.

Three batters making hundreds in the same ODI innings, only the sixth time this has happened, helped the touring side amass 7-405.

After Keacy Carty's early dismissal, Campbell blasted a 65-ball century, the fifth-fastest by a West Indian batter, racing to 101 with nine fours and five sixes before falling to Gurnoor Brar.

Captain Hope brought up his 20th ODI century and Jangoo hammered 114 off 77 balls.

Roston Chase maintained the momentum with a late cameo as the visitors plundered 76 runs from the final 10 overs.

Reuters

World.title: For love, not money — Tasmania's elite eight ready to represent the map
World.content:
He's the 202-centimetre, 17-year-old West Australian who was the raging favourite to be taken at pick number one in next year's AFL draft.

His name is Axel Walsh, and if Tasmanians are unfamiliar with the baby-faced beanpole, they won't be for much longer.

Axel Walsh says he's excited about playing with the Devils. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Rise of Tasmanian Devils, JackJumpers leads to sports academy Tasmania's sports sector is creating jobs at a scale not previously seen, galvanising academic pathways for those seeking careers in sports management.

Walsh is one of eight elite 17-year-old footballers who have been pre-listed by the Tasmania Devils, a year ahead of when they were due to be drafted, as part of the club's bespoke list concessions.

And if he turns out to be half as good as his football heroes, the Devils have a superstar on their hands.

"I think a lot of people would go Luke Jackson," he said, when asked what his closest AFL player comparison would be.

"I have a lot of respect for his game.

"But someone I've always looked up to is Max Gawn. You see the success he's had, and I've looked up to him as a leader off the field as well."

Axel Walsh has family connections in Tasmania, which he says made it an easy choice to accept the Devils' offer. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

It was an easy decision for Walsh to accept the Devils' invitation to join the team, a year ahead of his official draft year.

Family ties encourage decision

With an aunty, uncle and three cousins residing in the Hobart suburb of Glenorchy, Walsh already considered himself "somewhat Tasmanian" before signing on.

"I knew if the opportunity presented itself, it was going to be an easy option to say yes," he said.

Walsh said he got "goosebumps" at Tuesday night's draft-style event in Hobart, where he and seven other young guns were unveiled as the Devils' first-ever AFL-listed players.

He said he was struck by a club-produced hype video that chronicled Tasmania's football history, previous failed bids for an AFL team, and the importance of the state's famous "map" insignia.

"It's very important. The people of the island have wanted that for a long time so to have the opportunity to wear that on the jumper, it's very special and something I'm looking forward to," he said.

" It was a bit of goosebumps watching it; 1866 was where it all started, here we are in 2026, so it's feeling real now with the first eight being signed. "

Walsh was the first player unveiled at Tuesday night's event in Hobart. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Walsh was the first player unveiled on Tuesday, and is the highest profile player of the initial crop.

But he's not feeling the pressure to perform early.

"I'm really competitive. I want to win, and I hate losing," he said.

"I feel like pressure is a privilege, and we have that pressure because of the opportunity we've been given.

"I don't think there's pressure, just excitement."

It's a mindset reinforced by Devils' list boss, Todd Patterson.

Todd Patterson says each player's experience within the team will be customised to them. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

"We need to understand that each of them is on a different journey," Patterson said.

"Some of them might only have one kick in the VFL. That's OK. We just need to be patient with their development timelines.

"For some of them, it'll be really customised."

Walsh and his seven new teammates will split their time between the Devils' VFL, the Tasmanian under 18s, the gym, studying and visiting their home states next year.

Sales pitch began this year

Patterson was part of the team that lured the club's first players south — a process that started earlier this year with the delivery of "letters of interest" to about two dozen of the country's best under 18 players.

Part of the sales pitch was financial.

Each player will make about $150,000 next year, having penned four-year contracts with the club.

Hugh McCallum is the only Tasmanian from the pool of eight selected for the Devils. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

But Patterson insists the intentions of each of the players is pure.

"What they earn, what they'll end up earning and all that stuff, we are thinking about that and the strategy — but I think we could have offered them one dollar, and they would have been here," he said.

" They're just excited about the opportunity to leave a legacy. "

Each player signed has unique on- and off-field attributes.

Victorian Jake Miller is already a quasi-Tasmanian, boasting an impressive golf swing and having a mother who works for Cadbury.

Fellow Victorian midfielder Griffin Barker's highlight reel showcases a player who has perfected the "don't argue" — his favourite players are Harley Reid and Dustin Martin.

While on-baller Baxter Sruk accepted his Devils guernsey as AC/DC's Thunderstruck blasted throughout the venue.

Angus Brown at the Tasmanian Devils' team announcement. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

For another Victorian — gun small forward Angus Brown — moving to Tasmania was never a given.

"I wasn't in the initial interest letter back in the start of the year, I had to work my way up and find a patch of form," he said.

"I found out in May there was a letter of interest and then I pursued an interview with [recruiter] Derek Hine."

Even then, there was an element of trepidation for the Victorian who has placed an emphasis on finishing year 12, and pursuing higher education in tandem with a flourishing career in the AFL.

Tasmania Devils daring to dream The Devils weren't supposed to make the VFL finals. They were barely even supposed to be in the league.

"I'm someone whose pretty studious and I want to finish my studies," he said.

"The club has been open and flexible about my studying and pursuits academically, so that's probably my biggest thing.

"But when I got here and was able to experience the amounts of development, it was an easy sell."

It was the signing of Ken Hinkley as senior coach, and then the appointment of development guru Nigel Lappin that sealed the deal.

Momentum for the Devils is growing, boosted by their VFL and VFLW debuts this year. (Tasmania Football Club)

"The development opportunity here is something you're not going to get at any other club.

"I think the calibre of coaches and staff we've got is immense," he said.

"The sell is the experience, the dedication to the program and development was the biggest thing."

As for his on-field prospects, the 174-centimetre pocket rocket has this message for Devils fans:

"Something I pride myself on, is that while I'm not the biggest on the field, I think I have the biggest heart when I'm out there playing," he said.

"It'll be a dream come true," he says, of making his AFL debut.

World.title: Australia strikes back to avoid ODI whitewash ahead of Test series
World.content:
Australia avoided a whitewash in their ODI series in South Africa, with Pat Cummins's encouraging comeback and the return to form of Adam Zampa and Alex Carey inspiring them to a rain-interrupted win in Potchefstroom.

The final day-nighter was eventually called off under the lights on Wednesday as rain ruined the finale, but Australia could still celebrate a satisfying 45-run (DLS method) victory on a day when they were vastly improved after their capitulation in chases in the first two matches.

Half-centuries from the rejuvenated Carey (74 off 88 balls) and captain Mitch Marsh (56 off 42 balls), plus 48 from Ollie Peake, helped propel Australia to 9-322 after they had been put in, with South Africa at no point then threatening to pull off the highest successful ODI chase ever at the ground.

By the time the rain, which had also delayed the start by half an hour, returned to quite spoil the fun, Australia were already in full control.

Zampa (2-34 off six overs) rediscovered his best after recent struggles and Xavier Bartlett earned a couple of key early wickets (2-25 off five) as only Ryan Rickelton (71no off 81 balls) looked likely to trouble the visitors with South Africa limping to 4-145 off 28 overs.

Cummins may have returned as bowler only, not as the captain, with Marsh keeping the job for the third and final match, but his return seemed to enthuse everyone, with his 0-17 off five probing overs suggesting he'll be in fine shape to lead his troops in the first Test in Durban on October 9.

Stand-in Marsh again did his bit, leading from the front, as he powered to his third half-century of the series following his 60 and 84 in Durban and Johannesburg.

He and Travis Head (24 off 20) again provided an electric start with a 78 stand at nine runs an over, and this time the middle-order built much more assiduously against a Proteas side who weren't helped by resting key spinner, player-of-the-series Keshav Maharaj, and captain Temba Bavuma among four changes.

Cameron Green had an eventful time, taking a fearful beamer from Bosch straight into his box, but recovering to hit the next delivery, also a fast full-toss, courageously for six, only to then be bumped out next ball by a short one, seemingly suffering a muscle injury in the process.

Zampa was back to his squeezing, probing best, luring the dangerous first-match centurion Matthew Breetzke to be stumped on 25 and trapping Tristan Stubbs lbw for 14.

AAP

World.title: The AFLW is speeding up and these numbers prove it
World.content:
Ask a regular punter down the street what they think of AFLW and there's a good chance you'll get some version of "it's improving every year".

While this is not intended to be dismissive of those pioneers who helped lay the groundwork for the league a decade later, there is clear evidence that games are faster, more competitive, and more entertaining than ever.

And yes, there are teams still dwelling down the bottom, struggling to grow alongside the rest of the competition, but there is increasing pressure on those clubs to make adjustments in order to catch up.

The numbers are stark. Average scores are the highest they've ever been as metrics across the competition indicate increasing strategic control, and a growing desire to move the ball to attack, rather than focus wholly on defending the opposition.

Over the opening seven rounds of the 2026 season, teams are kicking an average of 45.6 points per game. This is an increase of 4.6 points compared to the previous all-time high of 41.1 points struck last year.

Of the 18 clubs, only four have failed to average a higher score in 2026 compared to 2025: Brisbane (-9.8 points per game), North Melbourne (-5.2), Port Adelaide (-18.5), and St Kilda (-7.2).

In line with this, inside 50s (avg. 35.1) and shots on goal (avg. 15.4) are at an all-time high, as are goal assists (avg. 4.2), all suggesting greater nuance in the attacking style employed by clubs.

Scoring is ultimately the end product of the way sides are moving the ball down the ground. Early days of AFLW were stoppage and tackle-heavy, keeping things caught in a rolling maul for extended periods of time.

But as we've seen fitness, skill, and strategy develop, the capacity to move the ball on the outside has become a weapon for a host of sides.

Rule changes last year — specifically, the adjudication of holding the ball — forced stoppages down from an average of 67 per game in 2024, to 44 in 2025.

That number has dropped again by 2.9 per game, which is another indicator of that desire to spread away from contest and use the ball in a more productive way.

Fewer sides are relying on resetting the ground via a stoppage in order to regain control.

Fremantle has been the clearest proponent of this shift. In 2025 it was caught out, relying heavily on a contested possession game, the late news that the holding the ball interpretation had been changed throwing the club out of sorts. No longer could heavy contest be the solution, and adjusting on the run was tough work.

This year, the Dockers have moved away from that contested game, averaging a positive uncontested possession differential for the first time in their 11-season history, and are reaping the benefits of the shift.

Slick ball movement by hand is now a strength for many AFLW teams. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

It is just one example of increased reliance on outside ball, with uncontested possession at an all-time high of 142.4 per game, up 10.2 on last year's record, while contested possession has marginally dropped. Disposal efficiency has also shot up to a record 63.6 per cent.

Teams are establishing far more control in game with ball in hand and enjoying a greater connection between lines.

Transition the key for improving sides

Clubs have opted to go one of two ways with their ball movement this year. The likes of Richmond, Hawthorn, and Adelaide have leaned into kick-mark football, choosing to control play with systematic build up. Whereas teams like Geelong, Gold Coast, and Carlton have taken the AFLW by storm with aggressive run and carry, moving the ball by hand and at speed.

Both methods have been beneficial in the increase in end-to-end transition throughout the season, with defensive half to inside 50 movement up to 20.6 per cent from 18.6 per cent last year, and defensive 50 to inside 50 movement also up by two per cent. This is combined with effective metres gained rising by 120 per game as well.

There has been AFLW-wide growth in handball metres gained with the average going from 160.7 last year to 224.5 this year, led by the Suns (+197) and Geelong (+130). A shift in Collingwood's game style has also seen it grow in this area (+119) and Carlton (+90) has doubled down on this after making its big move in this area last year.

The rolling mauls that characterised the early years of AFLW are decreasing. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Morgan Hancock)

It's hard to quantify the increased trust teams have in their system and willingness to attack, rather than simply rely on defence. With long kicks down the line marginally down — an indicator of the preference to build the ball up rather than opt for a bail out kick — and the aforementioned uncontested possession and stoppage metrics, there has been a clear move toward system, structure, and attack.

It requires teams to go into matches with faith that their system will do the job, rather than simply planning for how to stymie the opposition's style of play.

So, when that punter says that the AFLW is improving every year, they are correct, but this year more than ever. And the numbers back it up.

World.title: Nathan Cleary has no worlds left to conquer after Dally M win
World.content:
As Nathan Cleary sat on his couch, in between surgeries with his first Dally M medal around his neck on Wednesday night, the secret of his victory was that he didn't need it to prove his greatness.

That has been beyond dispute for some time now. It's very hard to argue otherwise against Cleary's four-straight premierships, five grand final appearances and two Clive Churchill Medals.

He and Cooper Cronk are the only halfbacks this century to win four titles, and he's the only halfback in history, and one of just three players, to win multiple man of the match awards in grand finals.

Nathan Cleary accepts maiden Dally M Medal from his dad's couch Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has claimed his maiden Dally M Medal, with Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton taking the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.

It's the same in rep football. His record for Australia is perfect, literally — the Kangaroos have won all eight games Cleary's played for them.

Cleary's time with New South Wales hasn't always been as smooth, and before this season it was the last thing his critics could point to because it was the only frontier left he had not totally dominated.

But if those same critics are still holding on, they're the rugby league version of the Japanese soldiers who hid out in the jungle for decades after World War II, refusing to admit the war was lost.

After his play in this year's series, where he became the third player ever — after Cameron Smith and Wally Lewis — to win two man of the match awards in one series en route to masterminding the Blues win in the Lang Park decider and claim his first player of the series award, his play for the Blues is now also beyond rebuke.

If all that wasn't enough, a Dally M wasn't going to make a difference either, even if it is richly deserved and now gives Cleary a complete set of all the major individual awards the NRL has to offer; at 28, he has no worlds left to conquer.

Cleary's record of success is astounding. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Cleary's 29 try assists this season marked a new career high as were his 14 line breaks, way up from his prior best of nine.

His 62 tackle busts were also his best-ever mark, and he led the league in goal-kicking percentage among full-time kickers while all the other heralds of his game — the boot that alternates between booming and clever, the roughneck physicality and on-field generalship — were constantly at the fore as Penrith stormed to the minor premiership.

When a player has been as good at club level for as long as Cleary has, it can be hard for individual seasons to stand out, but there's a reason nobody dared predict that anyone but him would take the medal home on Wednesday night.

Cleary was the runaway favourite to win the Dally M medal almost all season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Simply put, it's been the best year of his NRL career, and given he's been counted as one of the best players in the league for more than half a decade now, that's really saying something.

That first year he proved himself worthy of such a title also marked the closest he'd come to the Dally M before.

Back in 2020, when he and Penrith were first ascending via a regular season of 19 wins and one loss, Cleary was the hot favourite to win the medal but finished third behind Clint Gutherson and winner Jack Wighton.

Wighton won the award with Canberra's penultimate game of the season, where he earned three votes in a 26-14 win over the Warriors.

Blues write a new fate in blood Against all odds and with most of their state doubting them, Laurie Daley's New South Wales side has pulled off one of the greatest wins in Blues history.

Wighton set up a try but did little else of note besides being sin-binned. Elliott Whitehead, who was forced to play in the halves when Canberra halfback George Williams was sidelined due to an HIA and Wighton was in the bin, was the clear choice for best on ground but only received two votes.

Likewise, Gutherson was awarded two points in Parramatta's Round 1 over Canterbury, an 8-2 struggle where he did not score a try, set one up or make a line break.

He worked hard, running for over 200 metres, but in a game of such fine margins it would have been easy for the vote to go another way.

The details of forgotten Raiders and Eels wins from years past — the Parramatta match was so long ago it still had two referees and predates the set restart rule — seemingly have little to do with Nathan Cleary's story, but this is how the Dally M's work.

The six types of Dally M winners This week is the final round for NRL players to accumulate Dally M votes. Here are the six types of stars who can win the award.

The 3-2-1 voting system invites inconsistency, especially since an extra judge was appointed for each game and, given that said judges are anonymous, accountability is impossible.

One bad decision from one voter, just once, can decide the award and dictate how we talk about a player's legacy and place in history.

The flip side is a player doesn't need a Dally M to be considered an all-time great. Darren Lockyer, Brad Fittler, Allan Langer and Benji Marshall all never won one and because it's only been the official player of the year award since 1998, Andrew Johns is the only Immortal who's ever won it.

Even before Wednesday night, Cleary could exist in that mighty company and not feel ashamed.

He has achieved as much as any of them and more than some, and can match accolades with any player of modern times, including Johnathan Thurston (who won four Dally M's) and Johns himself (who won three).

This medal is not a validation or culmination. It is an affirmation, a glittering reminder of a truth we all knew already.

There's a reason Cleary's fitness dominated the talk leading into the preliminary final against Newcastle. There's a reason his every move on the bench was dissected like it was the Zapruder film.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

There's a reason the world seemed to stop when he suffered a compound fracture to his ankle following Phoenix Crossland's hip drop tackle and there's a reason his absence was felt so keenly, first through the final 45 minutes of Penrith's upset loss and right to the Dally M ceremony on Wednesday night.

He has the rugby league world in his hands, and he has for many years now. This era belongs to him more than it does to anybody else.

That was true before he was a Dally M winner and will remain true wherever his career goes next as he returns from his shocking ankle injury.

Where that is and what he does when he gets there remains to be seen.

All that's certain is that now he's ticked this final box: whatever spoils of war come his way are repeats.

There's long been nothing left to prove; now there's nothing new left to win.

The Dally M is one more thing on the pile of gold, a pile so large the medal could be lost amongst the glittering.

World.title: Jai Arrow told 'nothing' about pre-grand final tribute
World.content:
Jai Arrow says he has been told "nothing" about a tribute awaiting him ahead of Sunday's NRL grand final.

It was widely reported today that Arrow would do a lap of Stadium Australia while a selection of Australian musicians perform Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Earlier this year, Arrow retired from the NRL after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).

Speaking to the ABC at this evening's Dally M Awards in Sydney, Arrow said he was unsure of the details of the ceremony.

"[I know] nothing yet, apparently I'm going around … but I don't know anything," Arrow said.

"So it'll be interesting. It won't just be for me, it'll be for everyone fighting MND."

Loading...

Arrow was honoured with the Provan-Summons Medal at the awards night for embodying the spirit of the game, which is measured against the values of respect, honesty, bravery and sportsmanship.

He said the proposed pre-game tribute on Sunday would be an opportunity to continue raising awareness of MND.

"I can use my platform to spread awareness," he said.

Meanwhile, NRL executive chairman Peter V'landys was tight-lipped about the tribute but promised fans they would be "happy and impressed" with the performers selected.

"You'll see, there'll be superstar Australian performers, that's all that we'll say, and everyone will be very happy and impressed with what we've got," he said.

"But it's not about them; it's about Jai, it's about what Jai does; he inspires people.

"We've received a lot of correspondence at the NRL about how his inspiration has made them see their illnesses through."

V'landys also said the league will be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, as well as $1 million to a "fund for underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league".

"If we can lift a lot of other people with Jai's courage and leadership, that's what we're going to do on Sunday night," V'landys said.

The NRL was left without pre-match entertainment for the grand final after talks with Australian artist Tones and I broke down earlier this month.

World.title: Stawell Gift winner suspended for 12 months after positive drug test
World.content:
This year's Stawell Gift men's winner, Olufemi "Femi" Komolafe, has been suspended for 12 months after testing positive for ADHD medication.

The 21-year-old set a new personal best to claim his first major title in April this year, and also claimed the $40,000 prize for placing first in the annual 120-metre handicapped sprint.

Komolafe was given a 5-metre handicap in this year's race, starting behind all but one of his opponents in the final.

But Sports Integrity Australia has handed down a 12-month ban, confirming Komolafe had tested positive for the banned medication.

ADHD medications are banned in sport for their potential performance-enhancing effects, with athletes only able to use them if they have a medical diagnosis and it is part of treatment.

Stawell Gift organisers have not confirmed whether Komolafe will be asked to return his winnings or whether he will be stripped of his title.

The ban comes as Sports Integrity Australia expresses concerns over the prevalence of athletes using ADHD medications without a formal diagnosis.

In July, its chief executive, Sarah Benson, said she was seeing a "significant number" of inadvertent doping violations from high-level Australian athletes using ADHD medication.

Dr Benson said the consequences are severe for athletes found breaching the rules.

"Since these medications could be abused by athletes for performance improvement reasons, the tough reality is that they are banned under the World Anti-Doping Code if the athlete does not have a formal diagnosis," Dr Benson said.

"Under the Code, this is true even if they establish their diagnosis after the positive test, and they face a ban of one to four years."

Tech.title: The new and huger Paramount has a new co-CEO
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Paramount is appointing a new co-CEO ahead of the close of its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Ynon Kreiz, previously Mattel’s chairman and CEO, will be joining Paramount to lead alongside chairman and CEO David Ellison.

According to Paramount, “Ellison will focus on the company’s long-term strategy, creative vision and direction, including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. Kreiz will focus on the company’s day-to-day management and integration of the combined businesses.” The combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will “report jointly” to Ellison and Kreiz.

Kreiz joined Mattel in 2018. While he was leading the company, it launched the hit Barbie film in partnership with Warner Bros. Pictures. His first day at Paramount is October 5th.

Today, a judge also approved Paramount’s recently-announced settlement in a lawsuit with several states that had been blocking the Warner Bros. Discovery merger, according to Reuters.

On Tuesday, Paramount’s streaming chief, Cindy Holland, announced that she would be stepping down, and Variety reports that HBO boss Casey Bloys is “poised” to take over both Paramount Plus and HBO.

Tech.title: Neon sticks it to A24 by announcing a Creative Commons SCP Foundation movie
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A24 pissed off one of the internet’s largest horror communities when it announced it was working on an SCP Foundation film, but apparently hadn’t bothered to contact the SCP Wiki team, nor did it commit to releasing it under a Creative Commons license as required. Seeing an easy PR win, Neon is cashing in by announcing it’s making its own SCP movie. But unlike A24, it proactively reached out to the SCP Foundation Wiki team and has pledged to release it under the Creative Commons ShareAlike (CC BY-SA) license.

This is not an “official” SCP film. None of the wiki’s staff is involved in the writing or production, it is not receiving compensation, and the team’s official position is not to endorse such projects.

Other than the licensing details, there is almost no information about the upcoming film. Neon says it will be released theatrically in 2027, suggesting that this will be a quick turnaround, potentially low-budget affair. That’s not shocking considering the challenges of making a profit on a film made under a ShareAlike license.

In a statement, the SCP Foundation Wiki admin team said that, “The staff of the SCP Foundation Wiki and our community appreciate NEON’s excellent communication and commitment to following the requirements of our license as well as the spirit of collaboration at the core of the SCP Foundation project.“

Tech.title: Google announces Gemini 4 and says it’s so capable that only ‘trusted cyber defenders’ can have it right now
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google today revealed its next AI frontier model, which it’s calling Gemini 4 Argon. The new model delivers “frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense,” according to chief AI architect and Google DeepMind SVP Koray Kavukcuoglu. But the company is limiting access at first to a “set of trusted cyber defenders,” and Kavukcuoglu says that Google is “actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access while we gradually expand access.”

Kavukcuoglu says Gemini 4 Argon is already powering Google’s “internal workflows,” highlighting how the model has helped with tasks like large-scale codebase migrations. Google also shared a big chart showing many benchmarks where Gemini 4 fares better than competing models from OpenAI and Anthropic. (The AI community was buzzing earlier this week on X over what appeared to be leaked benchmarks for the new model.) Google will be strengthening “critical frontier safeguards” before a broader rollout, including defending against misuse and prompt injection attacks and monitoring for misalignment.

The launch of Gemini 4 Argon comes just a day after OpenAI’s splashy DevDay conference, where OpenAI launched its Dots AI agent and GPT-6.1 Sol AI model. (OpenAI also said this week that it wouldn’t be releasing a planned GPT-6.1 Astra model due to worries about safety.) It’s also arriving soon after Kavukcuoglu’s appointment as the new boss of DeepMind in August.

Tech.title: The AI Tamagotchis are coming
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

While AI has made plenty of inroads on people’s phones and computers, it’s largely failed in dedicated devices. But over the next year, two major AI companies, Meta and OpenAI, will attempt to change that. And they’re apparently betting on a similar path: testing appetites for physical hardware with their cutesy software agents.

“Hardware is hard” is a tech industry mantra. Dedicated AI devices like the Friend and Humane AI Pin have inspired mainly frustration and backlash, which may only worsen as public anger toward AI grows. Meta and OpenAI, however, are both pushing ahead. OpenAI is working with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive and plans to ship no earlier than February 2027, per a public filing. Meta aims to launch a pendant-like device sooner, before this year’s holiday shopping season.

While OpenAI’s hardware didn’t make an appearance at this year’s DevDay, the company debuted a major new AI agent platform called Dots, complete with personalizable colored blobs with eyes. During a Q&A with reporters after the keynote, when asked whether Dots would make their way into a future physical hardware device, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman replied that that “seems like a very reasonable thing to assume we may do someday,” declining to offer further details.

Meta, meanwhile, is more directly tying its hardware to the recently released Muse agent. Compared by CEO Mark Zuckerberg to a keychain, the device is called the Muse Charm, and it bears a screen featuring its cuddly-looking Muse AI agent, giving it the air of a Tamagotchi. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” Zuckerberg said onstage. “So, if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.”

Both OpenAI and Meta have likely learned from other companies’ failed hardware rollouts, and their resulting strategy seems to be soft-launching AI agents before hard-launching the hardware. Their solution for hacking the hardware problem is to prime the market by getting people used to AI agents, hoping people will spread the word that “yes, they really work now.” Once people find value in — and even get attached to — the cutesy agents, they might want them in a more physical form. Other companies, like Friend, have taken similar software-first strategies, but Friend was positioned mainly as a companion chatbot, not a productivity tool.

When asked during the DevDay press Q&A whether Dots will likely become the primary interface for interacting with ChatGPT, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said the company would be “evolving ChatGPT in place to be this incredible personal assistant very soon” and that he believes that as people are able to reach their AI agents via email, text, or phone call, the point of interaction is “all going to blur at some point.” It’ll be a “natural part of your life,” Sottiaux said.

Altman is banking on the fact that Dots will be more useful for long-term tasks than previous iterations of agents on the market have been. “This feels like an always-on helper, collaborator … that you can give very large pieces of work to and it gets to know you and helps proactively over time,” he said during the Tuesday press Q&A.

Both companies’ main bet is that, after years of less-than-impressive AI agents, they can finally deliver a useful everyday tool that will break through to a broader public market. But after Muse’s concerning exploits in Facebook Marketplace, and a Dots voice demo that went awry at DevDay, there’s apparently still some work to do.

Tech.title: Reddit says it has to cut back access to ‘Old Reddit’ because of AI bots
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Reddit is further limiting who can use the “Old Reddit” experience as part of its efforts to combat scraping and automated traffic. Reddit recently started forcing users to log in to be able to use Old Reddit, but in the “next few months,” the company says that you’ll have to be logged in and have used Old Reddit within the last six months from when the change rolls out to be able to continue browsing the platform with the classic experience.

Reddit says the six-month window covers “the vast majority of all Old Reddit users.” The announcement didn’t go into detail, but it’s clearly aimed at blocking not just new account creation for bots, but also any bots that might access unused or abandoned accounts. As part of the changes, Reddit will stop supporting RSS feeds on November 13th because RSS is “now a common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse,” and suggested replacements like Discord Relay for moderation help.

Reddit:

If you use RSS for feeds outside of a community you moderate, there is no replacement. We know RSS has been a beloved part of the open web for a long time, and we’re grateful to everyone who used it to stay connected to Reddit.

The company has been waging war against unsanctioned access to its data for some time, including blocking the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine to prevent AI scraping, suing Anthropic over alleged unauthorized bot access, and striking deals with Google and OpenAI to use Reddit data for training. Reddit knows that Old Reddit is beloved by many users, and in May 2025, CEO Steve Huffman said the company would “keep it online as long as people are using it.” But this past August, Huffman said that Reddit had gotten to a point where “we need to make some changes” because the experience was being used by “everyone who spams, scrapes, or does anything bad on Reddit.”

In its announcement today, Reddit said that the recent login requirement for Old Reddit “helped reduce scraping and automated abuse” but “still allowed any logged-in account to access Old Reddit, including accounts with no prior Old Reddit use.” Logged-in moderators, however, will still be able to use Old Reddit without a recent usage requirement.

Reddit also shared updates for the previously announced transition moving apps and bots that use Reddit’s public data API to the company’s developer platform. Reddit will begin removing API access for users that haven’t registered their apps by January 12th, 2027, and all remaining public API access “will end in March 2027.”

Tech.title: Amazon’s delivery driver smart glasses will reportedly take photos ‘almost constantly’
Tech.content:
Amazon deliveries could soon come with a new catch: the delivery driver’s smart glasses will be snapping photos of anything they see while they’re in use, including people and private property. Bloomberg reports that the glasses could take “several thousand captures in a single driver’s typical shift,” which Amazon plans to upload to its AI Wellspring platform. When asked if customers will be able to opt-out of this, Amazon’s Viraj Chatterjee told Bloomberg, “We haven’t thought about that.”

Chatterjee claimed Amazon’s only using the data from the glasses to “enhance the delivery process,” adding, “The intent has never been stuff like surveillance.” The impact of surveillance tech won’t be new to Amazon’s delivery drivers, who have had AI cameras watching in their vehicles and complained about it failing to register secured seat belts, or forcing them to pull over to take a sip of coffee, or having footage from the cameras leaked online.

Chatterjee also told Bloomberg that Amazon’s systems will blur any people and license plates in the images before they’re passed along for human review. Bloomberg says Amazon confirmed that “images from the smart glasses could be obtained with a warrant,” but wouldn’t specify how long it plans to store the images for. There reportedly won’t be a way for customers to see any images Amazon has of them or their property, or ask Amazon to delete those photos.

The photos from the glasses will reportedly be of a similar quality to the quick pictures delivery drivers snap when they drop off a package. Amazon says it’s planning to put 20,000 more pairs of the glasses in the field by the end of 2027, and drivers wearing them in a pilot program have already made over 275,000 deliveries.
